explanation: The sensitizer in rhus dermatitis is a pentadecacatechol found in the oleoresin of anacardaciae plants, including poison ivy/oak/sumac, mango rinds (but not pulp), cashew nutshells and oil, Indian marking nut oleoresin, gingko fruit pulp, and Japanese lacquer tree oleoresin.

question: Eccrine glands are found in all the following areas of the body except:
explanation: Eccrine glands are sweat glands innervated by cholinergic sympathetic nerves (i.e mediated by acetylcholine), thus they are functionally cholinergic but anatomically sympathetic. Eccrine glands are found everywhere on the body except: clitoris, glans penis, labia minora, external auditory canals, and the vermillion lips.

question: Elaboration of which of the following cytokines is characteristic of TH2 response?
explanation: Interleukin-4 (IL-4) is a cytokine involved in B-cell proliferation. Along with IL-5 and IL- 13, IL-4 is classified as a TH2 cytokine.

question: A patient presents with this skin eruption, started four days ago. It is extremely pruritic, but denies burning or skin pain. No associated facial swelling, shortness of breath or dermal/subcutaneous edema. The lesions appear to last for less than one day but recurs in other areas of the body. The patient reports no new medications, including NSAIDs and ACE-inhibitors. The eruption appeared spontaneously and no identifiable trigger could be identified based on the history. Dermographism was strongly positive. Based on the clinical images, history, and physical exam findings, which of the following mediators is responsible for this disease process?
explanation: The correct answer is histamine. This patient has urticaria based on the history and physical exam findings. Urticaria is classified based on duration: acute (<6 weeks) versus chronic (>6 weeks, 2+ attacks per week). Clinically, urticaria presents with evanescent pale to pink-red, edematous papules or plaques, often with central clearing and peripheral erythema. The lesions are extremely pruritic. When approaching urticaria cases, it is important to identify triggers, if any, which includes substances that trigger mast cell degranulation (aspirin, NSAIDs, codeine, morphine). Urticaria is mainly mediated by histamine release from mast cell degranulation. Urticarial vasculitis (UV) is differentiated from ordinary urticaria by lesion duration, with UV typically lasting >24 hours and other associated symptoms such as pain or burning, both are not typically seen in urticaria. Moreover, UV typically resolves with post-inflammatory pigmentary alterations due to the extravasated red blood cells from the vasculitis.

question: T-cell anergy occurs if:

choices.A: FasL is bound on the T-cell
choices.B: A HLA-DM facilitator is not involved with the binding
choices.C: MHC Class I or II is bound in the presence of IL-2
choices.D: MHC/TCR engagement occurs without costimulatory molecules
choices.E: Stimulation by a MHC Class III molecule is involved

correct_text: MHC/TCR engagement occurs without costimulatory molecules
explanation: MHC/TCR engagement occurs without costimulatory molecules. MHC Class III molecules are not involved in this process. The MHC III region encodes for soluble proteins of the complement cascade and the tumor necrosis family.

question: The first primordial hair follicles form on the eyebrows, upper lip and chin at which gestational age?
explanation: The first primordial hair follicles form at 9 weeks gestation on the eyebrows, upper lip and chin.

question: Which monoclonal gammopathy is most commonly associated with erythema elevatum diutinum?
explanation: A report of 13 patients indicated IgA is most commonly associated with EED.

question: Desmosine and isodesmosine are typical amino acids found in:
explanation: Desmosine and isodesmosine are typical amino acids found in elastic fibers. They crosslink fibrillin.

question: Rituximab works by targeting the CD20 antigen which is predominantly expressed on which of the following cells?
explanation: Rituximab targets the CD20 antigen which is predominantly expressed on mature B cells but not plasma cells, T cells, or dendritic cells. Therefore, even when used in antibody-mediated diseases (such as pemphigus vulgaris), the response to therapy requires a long duration of time as the drug targets B cells which must then differentiate into plasma cells that ultimately produce the pathogenic antibodies in their secreted form.

question: Which cytokine is chemotactic for neutrophils?
explanation: IL-8 is chemotactic for neutrophils.

question: This patient developed an acute vesicular rash after eating a mango. She has returned for a routine follow-up. She needs to be careful of exposure to:

choices.C: All of these answers are correct

explanation: Patients allergic to the peel of a mango can also be allergic to other plants/products of the Anacardiaceae family. Cross-reactions can occur with exposure to any plants of the genus Toxicodendron, to the oil from the cashew nut shell, to the Brazilian pepper tree, to lacquer from the Japanese lacquer tree, to ink from the Indian marking nut, and to the fruit pulp of the ginkgo tree, and others.

question: Embryologically, when do melanocytes begin to synthesize melanin?
explanation: Melanocytes begin to synthesize melanin in the 3rd month of gestation.

question: Melanocytes are derived from:
explanation: Melanocytes are derived from neural crest precursors and migrate to the epidermis, hair matrix, retinal pigment epithelium, ear (stria vascularis), leptomeninges, and mucous membranes. The other options listed are incorrect and are not involved with melanocytes.

question: Each of the following is true about melanosomes except:

choices.A: Are singly dispersed in the basal layer in lighter skin tones
choices.B: Most characteristic organelle of the melanocyte
choices.C: Are transferred to keratinocytes via phagocytosis
choices.D: Are larger in size in rich pigmented / darker skin tones compared to light skin tones
choices.E: Tyrosinase activity decreases as melanosomes mature

correct_text: Are singly dispersed in the basal layer in lighter skin tones
explanation: Several differences exist that may explain the heterogeneity of skin color. The number of melanocytes are the same; however, there are several differences in the melanosomes. Differences in skin color can be attributed to five factors. In heavily pigmented skin, (1) there is greater production of melanosomes in melanocytes, (2) individual melanosomes show a higher degree of melanization, (3) melanosomes are larger, (4) the melanosomes are dispersed to a greater degree in the keratinocytes, and (5) there is a slower rate of degradation.

question: Which mechanoreceptor found in hair bearing areas sense deep touch and vibration?
explanation: Vater-Pacini corpuscles sense deep touch and vibration.

question: The desmosomal connections of the epidermis are dependent on which of the following ions?
explanation: The desmosomal connections in the epidermis are calcium-dependent.

question: Keratinocytes express what class of major histocompatibility complex under normal conditions?
explanation: Keratinocytes express MHC Class I molecules and therefore can be attacked by CD8+ Tc cells, in particular after viral infection.

question: The human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is located on chromosome:
explanation: The MHC is highly polygenic and polymorphic, and this contributes to the ability of of the immune system to respond to a multitude of different and rapidly evolving pathogens. The MHC is located on chromosome 6 in humans.

question: Th2-related cytokines include:
explanation: Atopic dermatitis is considered a disease in which a Th2 pattern predominates, especially early on. Th2 cytokines are IL4, IL5, IL6, IL10, IL13.

question: Allergic contact dermatitis is caused by a T-cell response to topical exposure to compounds (haptens) that form complexes with host proteins. Which cell is responsible for initial sensitization of the T-cells?
explanation: The Langerhans cell phagocytizes the haptens in the epidermis or dermis, begins the process of maturation and migrates to the regional lymph node, where naïve T-cells are educated to expand to a clone of CLA positive memory T-cells. These cells then can expand and extravasate with subsequent exposure to the same allergen.

question: Which cytokine is responsible for fever in patients with sunburn?
explanation: IL-1 is a pyrogenic cytokine responsible for the fever in sunburn. It also is causes B cell maturation and proliferation and NK cell activation.

question: Which of the following cytokines is primarily involved in activating eosinophils?
explanation: Eosinophils provide many functions of the immune system, including protection against helminths. They are activated by IL-5.

question: Which of the following cytokines has been shown to be critical for epidermal acanthosis in psoriasis?
explanation: IL-22 has recently been shown to be critical in causing epidermal acanthosis. Interleukin (IL)-23, a cytokine involved in the development of IL-17-producing T helper cells (Th17 cells), was found to have a potential function in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. IL-22 is preferentially produced by Th17 cells and mediates the acanthosis induced by IL-23. IL-23 can directly induce the production of IL-22 in human naive T cells. Furthermore, IL-22 mediates IL-23-induced acanthosis and dermal inflammation through the activation of Stat3.

question: Which of the following is the best description of anagen effluvium?

choices.A: A scarring alopecia affecting only anagen stage follicles
choices.B: An abrupt transition of telogen to anagen in resting hair matrix cells
choices.C: An abrupt transition from anagen to catagen in rapidly dividing hair matrix cells
choices.D: A cessation of mitotic activity in resting hair matrix cells
choices.E: A cessation of mitotic activity in rapidly dividing hair matrix cells

correct_text: A cessation of mitotic activity in rapidly dividing hair matrix cells
explanation: Anagen effluvium is nonscarring alopecia, which results from an outside stimulus— most often an antimetabolite, chemotherapeutic drug—inducing an abrupt cessation of hair matrix cell mitotic activity. This process occurs within days to weeks of the stimulus and is reversible with cessation of the drug therapy.

question: What does a western blot identify?
explanation: A northern blot identifies RNA and a southern blot identifies DNA.

question: Occlusive moisturizers prevent evaporative water loss to the environment by placing an oily substance on the skin surface through which water cannot penetrate. This replenishes the stratum corneum by water movement from the viable epidermal and dermal layers. There are many different classes of chemicals that can function as occlusive moisturizers. What is the most effective occlusive moisturizer?
explanation: The most effective occlusive moisturizer is petrolatum, since it reduces transepidermal water loss by 99%. Petrolatum allows barrier repair while permeating throughout the interstices of the stratum corneum.

question: Which of the following immunoglobulins cannot activate the complement pathway?
explanation: Immunoglobulins (Ig) differ in their ability to activate complement. IgM is the largest Ig, is the major Ig in the primary immune response, and consists of a pentamer that activates the classic complement pathway. IgG is the most abundant Ig and the major Ig in the secondary immune response. Four subclasses of IgG exist based on the amino acid residue sequences of their constant region, IgG1 through IgG4. IgG1 and IgG3 are potent activators of the classic complement pathway, IgG2 is less effective and IgG4 is unable to do so.

question: The main collagen component of the basement membrane is:
explanation: Collagen IV is the main collagen component of basement membranes.

question: Krause end bulbs are:

choices.A: Located in the deep dermis and within the subcutis in weight-bearing sites of the body
choices.B: Adapting mechanoreceptors found on weight-bearing sites that respond to vibrational
choices.D: Located in the dermal papillae of digital skin
choices.E: Found on the vermillion border of the lips ? Found at the orifice of the hair follicle and particularly sensitive to cold

correct_text: Found on the vermillion border of the lips
explanation: Krause end bulbs are mucocutaneous receptors found on the glans penis, clitoris, labia minora, perianal area, and vermillion border of the lips. Papillary nerve endings are free nerve endings found at the orifice of the hair follicle and particularly sensitive to cold. Meissner's corpuscles are ovoid, elongated mechanoreceptors located in the dermal papillae of digital skin that detect touch and light pressure. Pacinian (Vater- Pacini) corpuscles exist in the deep dermis and within the subcutis in weight-bearing sites and function as adapting mechanoreceptors that respond to vibrational stimuli.

incorrect_rationales.D:
Located in the dermal papillae of digital skin

?. Found at the orifice of the hair follicle and particularly sensitive to cold

question: The function of glycosaminoglycans/proteoglycans in the dermis is:

choices.B: Facilitate COLVII binding to the anchoring plaques

explanation: The function of glycosaminoglycans/proteoglycans in the dermis is to regulate water-binding capacity. The other listed options are not functions of glycosaminoglycans / proteoglycans.

question: Which of the following is an apocrine gland?
explanation: Moll's gland is the term for apocrine glands located on the eyelids.

question: Psoriasis has been shown to be linked to:
explanation: Psoriasis is a T-cell-mediated immunological disease characterized by epidermal proliferation. The nature of the antigen(s) responsible for T-cell activation is still unknown. It has been suggested that the human papillomaviruses (HPVs) associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), including the oncogenic HPV5, may contribute to the pathogenesis of psoriasis. In one study, the early detection of several EV-HPV genotypes in children supports the link between psoriasis and EV-HPVs and suggests a putative role for these viruses in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

question: Hair grows at:
explanation: Hair grows at an average of 0.4 mm/day.

question: What is the most important cell for wound healing?
explanation: Macrophages are the most important cell for wound healing. They secrete TGFs, cytokines, IL-1, TNF, and PDGF. Neutropenic or lymphopenic patients do not have impaired wound healing, whereas macrophage-deficient (quantity or function) patients heal poorly.

question: Imiquimod has been used for many dermatologic conditions. It works by binding to toll-like receptor 7. What is the native ligand of TLR-7?
explanation: Toll-like receptors are pattern recognition receptors involved in innate immunity. They are most highly expressed on monocytes, dendritic cells, and B cells. Imiquimod works through binding to toll-like receptor 7. The native ligand for TLR7 is single-stranded RNA.

question: Which of the following cytokines shifts the immune response towards TH2?
explanation: IL-4 is the cytokine that polarizes the immune response towards Th2.

question: Which of the following is essential for the formation of granulation tissue?
explanation: Granulation tissue forms approximately four days after injury. It is composed of new capillaries, macrophages, fibroblasts, and blood vessels. The formation is dependent on the presence of fibronectin. There tends to be an ordered sequence of matrix deposition. Fibronectin is deposited first followed by collagen 3 and then collagen 1. Granulation tissue primarily contains type 3 collagen.

question: When does tissue contraction typically begin?

choices.A: After the 9th month of wound healing
choices.C: After the 3rd month of wound healing
choices.D: During the 2nd week of wound healing
choices.E: After the first month of wound healing

correct_text: During the 2nd week of wound healing
explanation: Wound contraction ensues during the second week of healing.

question: The pharmacologic activity of tacrolimus includes:

choices.A: Phosphorylation of NFAT (nuclear factor of transcription)
choices.B: Binding and inhibition of NF kappa B

explanation: Tacrolimus is similar to cyclosporine and pimecrolimus (Elidel). Calcineurin is a phosphatase that dephosphorylates the subunit on NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells). Dephosphorylated NFAT is active and causes the increase in IL-2. Tacrolimus binds macrophillin-1 which blocks calcineurin so NFAT is not dephosphorylated, meaning that it remains phosphorylated and is inactive therefore preventing transcription of IL-2.

question: Which of the following cells are associated with Sucquet-Hoyer canals?
explanation: Glomus cells are modified smooth muscle cells found in the dermis. They allow the shunting of blood from arterioles to venules directly, bypassing capillaries. A glomus body consists of an afferent arteriole, Sucquet-Hoyer canal, efferent arteriole, and nerve fibers.

question: The immunopathogenesis of inflammation in psoriasis is most likely to be associated with which of the following cytokines?
explanation: The response of psoriasis lesions to TNF-α inhibition underlies the role of this factor in the immunopathogenesis of psoriasis. TNF-α amplifies the cascade of inflammation from T-helper cells, ultimately leading to the production of multiple interleukins and other downstream targets of other therapies also implicated in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

question: Which of the following compounds is most likely to protect the skin from ultraviolet light in the 380-400 nm range?
explanation: Avobenzone is the only listed agent that can protect from ultraviolet light in the 380- 400 nm range.

question: Which of the following is an example of a delayed hypersensitivity reaction?
explanation: There are 4 types of Hypersensitivities: Type IV: Delayed (cell-mediated) type reaction: Examples -TB skin test, transplant rejection, allergic contact dermatitis, interactions and skin repsonsiveness to bacteria, fungi, viruses, and protozoa, photo-allergies, insect bites, etc.

question: In which of the following locations would you be least likely to identify melanocytes?
explanation: Melanocytes are found in the stria vascularis of the ear, iris, leptomeninges and retina.

question: The epidermis is comprised of what type of cells?

choices.A: Keratinocytes, Melanocytes, Merkel cells, Langerhan cells
choices.B: Keratinocytes, Endothelial cells, Merkel cells, Langerhan cells
choices.C: Keratinocytes, Melanocytes, Merkel cells, Goblet cells
choices.E: Keratinocytes, Endothelial cells, Merkel cells, Goblet cells

correct_text: Keratinocytes, Melanocytes, Merkel cells, Langerhan cells
explanation: The adult epidermis is composed of three basic cell types: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, and Langerhans cells. An additional cell, the Merkel cell, can be found in the basal layer of the palms and soles, the oral and genital mucosa, the nail bed, and the follicular infundibula.

question: A mother presents to your pediatric dermatology clinic for further evaluation of her daughter, who has red gums, episodic hair loss, and rough perifollicular papules on the arms and thighs. She reports a family history of similar findings. After a thorough assessment of this patient, you conclude the patient has:
explanation: Defects of the hair shaft include hereditary mucoepithelial dysplasia which is characterized by red gums, episodic hair loss, and keratosis pilaris.

question: Which type of collagen in mutated in osteogenesis imperfecta?
explanation: Collagen type I is mutated in osteogenesis imperfecta. The COL1A2 gene is located on 7q22 and the COL1A1 is on 17q22. The other listed collagens are not involved in osteogenesis imperfecta. Collagen II is in cartilage and vitreous, Collagen III is in fetal skin, blood vessels and intestines, Collagen IV is in basement membranes and Collagen VII in anchoring fibrils and amnion.

question: The T cell surface receptor CD2 binds to what partner on endothelial cells to assist with adhesion?
explanation: CD2 molecules are T cell surface receptors that bind to LFA-3 on endothelial cells and antigen presenting cells to participate in adhesion and activation.

question: The parents of an infant male patient bring him to the clinic for an itchy rash. It started shortly after birth with facial erythema and scale. He scratches his cheeks until they bleed, especially at bedtime. They are scheduled to see an allergist due to suspicion of food allergies. His 5-year-old sister has moderate flexural eczema and mild asthma. Which cytokine is correlated with the severity of the pruritus in this disease?
explanation: The case describes atopic dermatitis (AD) which can present with facial erythema, xerosis and pruritus. Topical corticosteroids and moisturizers are first line therapy. In AD, IL-31 is elevated and correlates with the severity of pruritus, but not the severity of AD itself. Nemolizumab is a monoclonal antibody directed against the IL-31 receptor.

question: All of the following statements regarding mast cells are true except:

choices.A: Mast cells reside near small blood vessels
choices.B: None of the above (all are true)
choices.C: Mast cells release substances that affect vascular permeability
choices.D: Mast cells have receptors for certain fragments of complement on their surface
choices.E: Mast cells protect mucosal surfaces against pathogens

correct_text: None of the above (all are true)
explanation: Mast cells are the central cell in immediate-type hypersensitivity, and are very important in cutaneous inflammation. They reside near small blood vessels, and when activated release substances that affect vascular permeability. They orchestrate allergic responses and protect mucosal surfaces against pathogens. They have receptors for IgE and certain fragments of complement on their cell surface.

question: Which of the following diseases does NOT respond with a Th1-type responses?
explanation: Lepromatous leprosy is Th2 biased. The remaining conditions are Th1 predominant responses. Leishmaniasis which show strong cell-mediated immunity to the parasite and with self-resolving lesions are Th1 responses. In indolent/progressive leishmaniasis, a Th2 pattern is predominant.

question: A 32 year-old woman presents with meningitis and palpable purpura. A diagnosis of meningococcemia is confirmed via culture of cerebrospinal fluid. Which complement component is most likely to be deficient in this patient?
explanation: Patients with deficiencies of late complement components (C5-9) are at increased risk of meningococcemia due to Neisseria.

question: Major histocompatibility complex class I molecules bind to:

choices.A: Peptides derived from proteins degraded in endocytic vesicles
choices.C: Peptides external to the cell membrane
choices.D: Peptides derived from proteins synthesized and degraded in the cytosol
choices.E: None of these answers are correct

correct_text: Peptides derived from proteins synthesized and degraded in the cytosol
explanation: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules bind to peptides derived from proteins synthesized and degraded in the cytosol. They present these processed peptides to CD8+ T-cells.

question: A patient with chronic atopic dermatitis is found to have elevated IgE levels. Which cytokine promotes isotype switching to IgE?
explanation: In a typical humoral response, isotype switching occurs subsequent to exposure to antigen. Switching is regulated by T cell derived cytokines. IgG is promoted by IL-4, IL- 6, IL-2 and IFN- gamma. IgA is promoted by IL-5 and TGF-beta. IgE is promoted by IL- 4.

question: Glomus cells are primarily found:
explanation: Glomus cells are derived from Susquet-Hoyer canals which function to shunt blood from the arterioles to venules and are primarily found on hands and feet. There are two types of glomus tumors, solitary and multiple. The solitary types tend to have paroxysmal pain which can be extreme. Multiple glomus tumors can be a autosomally dominant trait with incomplete penetrance and are less likely to be painful. Both have a predominance on the distal extremities, especially sub-ungual. Two tests are helpful in diagnosing glomus tumors: Hildreth sign - disappearance of pain following application of a tourniquet proximally. Love test - eliciting pain by applying pressure to a precise area with the tip of a pencil.

question: Which of the following cell types induce susceptibility to tumor growth?
explanation: The suppressor T-cells induce susceptibility to tumor. These cells appear to arise in UV-irradiated hosts prior to tumor developing, and play a role in carcinogenesis.

question: What is the significance of the critical line of Auber?

choices.A: It is the location of the insertion of the erector pili muscle
choices.B: The inner root sheath is formed above this line
choices.C: It is the widest diameter of the hair bulb
choices.D: The bulk of the mitotic activity in the hair occurs above this line
choices.E: It is where keratinization first occurs in the hair

correct_text: It is the widest diameter of the hair bulb
explanation: The critical line of Auber is at the widest diameter fo the hair bulb.

question: Which of the following TH2 cytokines is a B cell growth factor?
explanation: IL-4 is a B cell growth factor.

question: The greatest density of mast cells is found in the:
explanation: Mast cells are found in the greatest density in the papillary dermis, in sheaths of the appendages, and around blood vessels and nerves of the subpapillary plexus. These cells are derived from CD34+ stem cells residing in the bone marrow. They produce and store in secretory granules many inflammatory mediators such as histamine, heparin, tryptase, chymase, carboxypeptidase, neutrophil chemotactic factor and eosinophilic chemotactic factor of anaphylaxis. They also release, without storing, growth factors, cytokines and leukotrienes. Giemsa or Leder stains are used to identify mast cells in biopsy specimens. Giemsa stains mast cell granules purple. Leder stains granules red.

question: Which cytokine is most important in recruiting neutrophils?
explanation: Chemotaxis is the process of cells moving through a gradient of towards increasingly higher concentrations. IL-8 has activating and chemoattractant properties on neutrophils.

question: A medical student with a family history of psoriasis and severe plaque psoriasis would like to know if there are any hereditary disease associations with the major histocompatibility complex. You recall that psoriasis has the following associations with HLA types:
explanation: Psorsiasis is associated with a number of histcompatibility antigens. HLACw*0602– positive patients usually have a younger onset age, more severe psoriasis course, guttate or eruptive plaque psoriasis phenotypes, more frequent streptococcal throat carriage or infections, and streptococcal-associated psoriasis exacerbation. HLA-B27 is common in psoriatic arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and reactive arthritis. HLA-DQ2 is most frequently associated with dermatitis herpitformis. HLA-B51 most commonly with Behcet's. HLA-DR4 and HLA-DQ8 have been linked to chronic urticaria. Pemphigus gestationis has been assocated with HLA-DR3/DR4.

question: With which HLA type is psoriasis most definitively linked?
explanation: Psoriasis is most strongly linked with HLA-Cw6. Patients with this HLA type have a relative risk of developing psoriasis that is 9-15 times normal.

question: Cutaneous warts in renal transplant recipients show increased expression of which keratin?
explanation: Keratins are divided into acidic (type I) and basic (type II) subtypes. Keratin 13 is a type I keratin which is expressed suprabasally in adult epithelia and is associated with terminal differentiation. Renal transplant recipients have an increased risk of developing skin cancers and multiple warts. Factors contributing to this increased risk include human papillomavirus infection, immunosuppressive therapy, and exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Increased expression of K13 has been demonstrated in high-risk papillomas in this patient population.

question: The microflora of pilosebaceous unit consist of which of the following:
explanation: P. ovale is found within the acroinfundibulum, S. epidermidis is found within the midinfundibulum, and Propionibacterium spp. deep within the follicle.

question: Which one of the following is responsible for maintaining a barrier to water loss in the stratum corneum?
explanation: Odland bodies, also known as lamellar granules, keratinosomes, and membrane-coating granules, are small organelles that are discharged from granular cells into the intracellular space of the granular layer of the epidermis. These bodies have two known functions: they mediate stratum corneum cell cohesion and they form a barrier to water loss. Odland bodies are round to oval, measure approximately 300 to 500 nm in diameter, and possess a trilaminar membrane and a laminated interior. They contain neutral sugars linked to lipids and/or proteins, hydrolytic enzymes, and free sterols.

question: Which common contact allergen is detected via the dimethylglyoxime test?
explanation: Nickel is found in virtually all metals of common use. It is the most common sensitizer in women, and is detected by the dimethylglyoxime test.

question: What component is the major barrier in the stratum corneum?
explanation: The major component of lamellar granules of the keratinocytes is ceramide. These play a major role in the barrier function of the skin.

question: A 40-year-old male is started on voriconazole for fungal prophylaxis after receiving a stem cell transplant for non-Hodgkins lymphoma. Which of the following sunscreen ingredients will be most important to minimize the risk of immediate drug-induced phototoxic reactions?
explanation: Avobenzone is the only chemical blocker that absorbs the whole UVA spectrum from 310-400 nm. Avobenzone is typically degraded by UVA light, and thus is formulated with a photostabilizer. Because this is the chief spectrum responsible for phototoxic reactions, it is important for sunscreens to be broad-spectrum and include a UVA blocker. Physical sunscreen blocks such as zinc oxide or titanium dioxide are most preferred in this scenario but not included in the answer choices.

question: An 18 year old female presents to your office a day after returning from vacation in the Bahamas where she spent significant time laying in the sun. She presents with well demarcated erythematous patches in a photodistributed pattern sparing the areas covered by her bathing suit. Which of the following wavelength of light is primarily responsible for this patient’s subsequent sunburn?
explanation: This patient’s sunburn is primarily caused by UVB radiation. UVB wavelengths range from 290–320 nm (B) and are the main contributors to acute erythema and sunburn.

question: Which of the following absorbs ultraviolet radiation?
explanation: Urocanic acid is a chromophore that absorbs ultraviolet radiation (UVR) in the stratum corneum.

question: Meissner's corpuscles detect which of the following sensations?
explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are elongated mechanoreceptors located just below the dermo-epidermo junction in the dermal papillae. They detect light touch, and are highest in density in palmo-plantar skin.

question: Allergic contact dermatitis is a:
explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is an example of a Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction (delayed type hypersensitivity reaction). Type 4 reactions are mediated by T-cells. Other types of hypersensitivity reactions are described below.

question: All of the following are considered intermediate filaments except:
explanation: Intermediate filaments are composed of keratins, vimentin, desmin, peripherin, glial fibrillary acidic proteins, neurofilaments, nuclear laminins, and nestin. These are part of cytoskeletal elements.

question: A 5 year old patient is seen at a tertiary referral center for evaluation of a complex syndrome. Ultimately, he is diagnosed with IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked syndrome.) What gene is mutated in IPEX syndrome?
explanation: IPEX syndrome is a rare x-linked disorder. Mutation of FOXP3 results in absence of regulatory T cells and is the cause of this syndrome, which includes immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, and enteropathy.

question: This patient is not a candidate for systemic therapy and declines surgical treatment. Which of the following injectable agents is an oncolytic virus that is FDA approved for inoperable disease?
explanation: Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) is an oncolytic herpes virus bioengineered with GM-CSF to invade and destroy melanoma tumor cells. Although it is an FDA-approved injectable treatment for inoperable melanoma, it is only used for select patients with cutaneous, subcutaneous, or nodal metastases with limited visceral involvement.

question: When evaluating a foreign body, which substance would be PAS negative and have no birefringence on polarizing microscopy?
explanation: Starch, cactus spines, and wood splinters are PAS positive. Silica, talc, zinc, and wood splinters are positive for birefringence on microscopy.

question: A 24 year old female patient is referred for management of chronic idiopathic urticaria. Many cases of this disease are associated with autoantibodies against what?
explanation: Many cases of idiopathic urticaria have circulating autoantibodies directed against the chain of high affinity IgE receptor on the mast cell surface. By definition, chronic spontaneous urticaria has no known trigger. Causes include: Autoimmunity mediated by functional autoantibodies against the high-affinity immunoglobulin E (IgE) receptor IgE autoantibodies to autoantigens Non-allergic reactions to foods or drugs (pseudoallergy) Acute or chronic infections as a result of Helicobacter pylori, streptococci, staphylococci, Yersinia, Giardia lamblia, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, hepatitis viruses, norovirus, parvovirus B19, Anisakis simplex, Entamoeba spp. and Blastocystis spp. Chronic spontaneous urticaria may be due to a type I allergy in exceptionally rare cases.

question: Which of the following medications is not concentrated in the eccrine glands?
explanation: The above listed drugs, as well as beta-lactam antibiotics, antifungals such as ketoconazole and griseofulvin, are known to be secreted into eccrine sweat ducts. This feature may explain the development of neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis and eccrine squamous syringometaplasia in the context of chemotherapy.

question: A 23-year-old woman presents with the skin changes pictured. They have occurred on various parts of the body almost every day for the past 3 months. They are intensely pruritic. She has no known chronic medical conditions. Which antibody is most likely to play an important role in the development of this condition?
explanation: The patient has chronic idiopathic urticaria, which is defined as recurrent, spontaneous urticaria with or without angioedema for most days in a six-week period or longer. Urticaria, or hives, are pruritic, edematous wheals with surrounding erythema, which may present on any area of the body. Antibodies that release histamine are seen in 30-50% of patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria. The most common antibodies bind to the extracellular alpha domain of the FceRI on mast cells, cross-linking them and leading to degranulation. About 10% of patients have autoantibodies against the Fc portion of IgE itself.

question: Which of the following cytokines, together with IL-4, promotes isotype switching from IgM to IgE?
explanation: IL-13 (along with IL-4) promotes an isotype switch from IgM to IgE.

question: During embryogenesis, periderm cells of the fetus contain which of the following substances?
explanation: In week 7 of embryogenesis the surface ectoderm produces two layers. The external layer is the periderm which contains glycogen and gives rise to the stratum corneum by week 21. The other layer is the stratum germinativum.

question: The proteins that make up the cornified cell envelope are synthesized in the:
explanation: The proteins that make up the cornified cell envelope are synthesized in the spinous and granular cell layer. The stratum basale is not involved in production of these proteins and there is no protein synthesis in the stratum corneum. Melanocytes and Langerhans cells are components of the epidermis but are not involved in this process.

question: Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with Behcet’s disease?
explanation: HLA-B51 has been reported with increased relative risks in European, Asian and Middle Eastern populations.

question: All of the following locations have apocrine glands except:
explanation: Apocrine glands are found in the axillae, anogenital region, external ear canal, eyelids, breast, periumbilical region.

question: Which cytokine is the main macrophage-activating cytokine?
explanation: Interferon gamma is the main macrophage-activating cytokine, and is secreted by TH1 cells.

question: Embryologically, epidermal stratification begins at approximately what estimated gestational age?
explanation: Epidermal stratification begins at about 8 weeks estimated gestational age and is completed by the 2nd trimester. Epideral stratification occurs when an 'intermediate layer' develops between the epidermal basal cells and the overlying layer of periderm cells. The periderm is an embryonic structure that covers the primitive epidermis until keratinization begins, at which point the periderm sloughs off and contributes to the protective covering of the newborn, the vernix caseosa. This intermediate layer is highly proliferative, such that by 24-25 weeks estimated gestaional age, the epidermis consists of 4 or 5 layers, in addition to the degenerating periderm.

question: Gene rearrangement analysis is useful for determining:
explanation: Gene rearrangement studies are useful to detect clonality in antigen specific cell types (B cells, T cells).

question: Which signaling molecule mediates the transition of hair cycling from telogen to anagen phase?
explanation: Sonic hedgehog (Shh), a signaling molecule secreted by ectodermal cells of the developing hair follicle, appears to be critical in mediating the transition from telogen to anagen during postnatal hair cycling

question: People with darker skin show:

choices.A: A lessened production of melanosomes within melanocytes
choices.B: A higher degree of dispersion of melanosomes in keratinocytes
choices.C: A grouping of melanosomes with a low degree of melanization
choices.E: A more rapid degradation of melanosomes

correct_text: A higher degree of dispersion of melanosomes in keratinocytes
explanation: More darkly pigmented races show a greater production of melanosomes in the melanocyte, melanosomes with a higher degree of melanization, larger melanosomes, a higher degree of dispersion of melanosomes in the keratinocytes, and a slower rate of melanosome degradation.

question: Which cytokeratin would you expect to be preferentially expressed in the keratinocytes of a psoriatic plaque:
explanation: K16 and K6 act as markers for hyperproliferative keratinocytes. They are found in skin disease such as psoriasis, warts, actinic keratoses, and SCC's.

question: All of the following statements regarding neutrophils are true EXCEPT:

choices.A: Neutrophils are the most abundant leukocytes
choices.B: Neutrophils' major function is antigen presentation
choices.D: Neutrophils play an important role in wound healing
choices.E: Neutrophils have receptors for IgG and complement

correct_text: Neutrophils' major function is antigen presentation
explanation: Neutrophils' major function is phagocytosis.

question: Which of the following amino acids is most typically found in elastic fibers?
explanation: Desmosine and isodesmosine are the most typical amino acids found in elastic fibers.

question: Which T-cell subset is commonly found in Sezary syndrome?
explanation: Sezary syndrome is the leukemia phase of mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) and is usually a TH2-biased CD4+ leukemia with loss of CD7.

question: Which hair condition is associated with abnormal regulation of the peroxisome proliferator- activated receptors?
explanation: Lichen planopilaris is a chronic, scarring condition that results in permanent loss of hair and destruction of the hair follicles. Defect in lipid metabolism and peroxisome biogenesis may contribute to LPP pathogenesis. Medications that act as PPAR agonists, such as pioglitazone, may have a role in controlling the progression of this disease.

question: Which of the following is NOT a specialized type of sebaceous gland?
explanation: There are several types of specialized sebaceous glands that are not associated with a hair follicle. They include Montgomery's areolar tubercle, Fordyce spots of the lip, Glands of Zeis of the cutaneous eyelid, and Meibomian glands of the eyelid. Moll's gland of the eyelid are a modified apocrine gland.

question: Blocking which cytokine would be the most beneficial in this condition?
explanation: Nail psoriasis, characterized here by irregular nail pitting and distal onycholysis, responds to treatments against IL-17 including secukinumab, ixekizumab, and brodalumab.

question: Which cadherin is responsible for adhesion of Langerhan cells to the epidermis?
explanation: E-cadherin is responsible for the adhesion of Langerhan cells to the epidermis.

question: Apocrine glands:

choices.A: Are present everywhere on the skin except on the palms and soles
choices.C: The most abundant component of the secertion is proline.
choices.D: Have a two segment ducts that empties onto the skin

explanation: Apocrine glands are tubular glands that demonstrate decapitation secretion. The initial secretions are odorless with the odor being derived from C6-C11 acids. The most abundant being 3-methyl-2- hexenoic acid.

question: Which keratins are expressed in the stratum germinativum and are present but not made de novo in the stratum spinosum?
explanation: K5 and K14 are expressed in the stratum germinativum (basal layer) and are defective in epidermolysis bullosa simplex. They are still present in the stratum spinosum but are not made de novo in this layer. K4 and 13 are found in mucosal epithelium. K1 and 10 are expressed in suprabasal keratinocytes, K2e and 10 in the upper spinous and granular layers, and K3 and K12 in the cornea.

question: A feature of major histocompatibility complexes is best described by which of the following?

choices.A: The MHC region is located on chromosome 17 in humans
choices.B: Class I molecules are present on erythrocytes
choices.C: Class II molecules are present on all nucleated cells
choices.D: Class MHC I are not expressed on dendritic cells
choices.E: The level of Class I and II expression can be modulated by cytokines

correct_text: The level of Class I and II expression can be modulated by cytokines
explanation: Antigen presentation requires internalization of the pathogen, processing inside the cell, and display of a short peptide on the surface of the APC on a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule. There are two major types of MHC: MHC-I and MHC-II. MHC-I is found on all cells in the body and is used to display endogenous substances, such as viral or tumor proteins MHC-II is found on APCs (dendritic cells, monocytes/macrophages and B cells) and is used to display foreign non-self molecules The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) consists of a linked set of genes encoding for MHC Class I, Class II, Class III, and Class IB. The level of Class I and II expression can be modulated by cytokines.

question: Which of the following protein plays a major role in wound healing?
explanation: Fibronectin is a key player in wound healing, initially secreted by myofibroblasts. The bed/matrix of fibronectin provides an adherent base for migration into the wound, provides scaffolding for collagen fibrils and mediates wound contraction.

question: Which of the following is true regarding anagen effluvium?

choices.A: Patients being treated with nitrosurea agents are usually spared
choices.B: Occurs within 24 to 48 hours of exposure
choices.C: Stimulus induces the abrupt cessation of mitotic activity in the rapidly dividing
choices.E: Rarely seen following administration of cancer chemotherapeutic agents ? Entirely irreversible

correct_text:
Stimulus induces the abrupt cessation of mitotic activity in the rapidly
dividing
explanation: It is frequently seen following administration of cancer chemotherapeutic agents. Stimulus induces the abrupt cessation of mitotic activity in the rapidly dividing hair matrix cells.

question: Which eponym describes vestigial lines of pigmentary demarcation?
explanation: Futcher lines are vestigial lines in which the dorsal surface has more melanocytes than ventral surface.

question: An 80-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease develops a new pruritic eruption with these cutaneous findings. What is the antigenic target of the autoantibodies generated in this condition?
explanation: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common immunobullous disorder and presents with tense vesicles/ bullae and pruritus. There has been as association of neurologic disorders, such as Parkinson's disease and dementia, with bullous pemphigoid. Autoantibodies are most commonly directed against the NC16A domain of BPAg2, also known as BP180 or collagen XVII.

question: The immunoglobulin class most commonly found in mucous secretions is:
explanation: IgA is found in mucous membrane secretions and is able to agglutinate antigens and activate the alternate but not the classic complement pathway.

question: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) Class I molecules:

choices.A: Are present only on antigen-presenting cells
choices.B: Are recognized by receptors on CD4+ T cells
choices.C: Trigger cytotoxic T cells when complexed with antigen
choices.E: Bear peptides derived from pathogens taken up into vesicles

correct_text: Trigger cytotoxic T cells when complexed with antigen
explanation: MHC Class I molecules are present on all nucleated cells and, when complexed with antigen, trigger cytotoxic T cells (CD8+).

question: Psoriatic arthritis is most commonly associated with which HLA?
explanation: HLA-B27 is associated with psoriatic arthritis as well as pustular psoriasis and acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau.

question: The first cell type to migrate into a new wound in great numbers is the:
explanation: Neutrophils migrate with monocytes concurrently, but arrive first in great numbers because of their abundance in circulation. Chemoattractants for the neutrophils are fibrinogen, fibrin split products, C5a and leukotrienes. If wound contamination is controlled, neutrophil migration ceases within a few days and they become entrapped within the wound clot, undergo apoptosis or are phagocytosed by macrophages.

question: After an antigen penetrates into the skin, it may couple with host proteins to be able to act as a full antigen. This coupling is called a hapten. The first cell type to take up the hapten is a:
explanation: Most of the contact allergens are low-molecular weight chemicals, which after penetrating into the skin, have to couple with host proteins to be able to act as full antigens. These are called haptens. Upon epicutaneous application to a naive host, Langerhans cells take up the hapten, process it and migrate towards the regional lymph nodes, where the antigen is then presented to naive T cells.

question: Langerhans cell adhesion to keratinocytes is mediated by what adhesion molecule?
explanation: Langerhans cells are found in the epidermis and on mucosal surfaces. After antigen exposure and activation, they migrate to regional lymph nodes where they mature into antigen presenting cells. Adhesion to keratinocytes in the epidermis is mediated by e-cadherin.

question: Natural killer (NK) cells eliminate infected cells in all of the following ways EXCEPT:

choices.C: NK cells adhere to and kill target cells coated with IgG
choices.E: NK cells do not target cells expressing major histocompatibility (MHC) class I molecules

explanation: NK cells focus on the destruction of infected or malignant cells. They achieve this via recognition of IgG on target cells, the so-called 'antibody-dependent cellular toxicity.' NK cells also eliminate cells by secreting perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane, through which granzyme is injected. Granzyme induces apoptosis by activating the caspase cascade. In addition, NK cells do not target cells expressing MHC class I molecules on their surface; some virus downregulate MHC class I molecules to evade recognition by cytotoxic T cells, which may make them susceptible to NK cell attack.

question: Which cell type is most important for wound healing?
explanation: The macrophage is required for wound healing. Without macrophages, there is no healing. Macrophages debride tissue through phagocytosis and digestion of organisms, tissue debris and effete PMN's. They secrete collagenase and secrete growth factors that facilitate transition from inflammation to repair.

question: Which of the following keratins would most likely be expressed in the nail bed?
explanation: Keratins 6b and 17 are expressed in the nail bed. K6a/16 is expressed in the nail bed, outer root sheath, and in hyperproliferative keratinocytes. Keratins 6a and16 are mutated in pachyonychia congenita type-1.6b. Keratins 6b and 17 are mutated in pachyonychia congenita type-2. Both are characterized by nail thickening and palmoplantar keratoderma while type-1 also has benign leukoplakia and type-2 has steatocystomas.

question: The best screen for classical pathway complement deficiency or dysfunction is:
explanation: The appropriate screening test for a complement deficiency is the CH50. The CH50 will detect deficiencies in the classical pathway and membrane attack pathways.

question: Anti-Ro (SS-A) antibodies are most commonly found in:
explanation: Ro 60 kDa autoantigen is a major target for patients with SLE and Sjogren's syndrome. Neonatal lupus occurs in newborns of mothers with anti-Ro antibodies and leads to children with photosensitive skin lesions and a cardiac conduction defect, a third degree heart block.

question: Excessive sebum production is most likely to result from stimulation of receptors for which of these peptides?
explanation: Sebaceous glands are androgen-responsive and hormone-responsive holocrine glands that enlarge at puberty and produce sebum. Alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, in addition to adrenocorticotropic hormone and prolactin, is a neurohormone involved in the production of sebum.

question: The Epstein-Barr virus utilizes which cell surface receptor to gain access to cells?
explanation: EBV utilizes the CR2 receptor for cell entry and infection. the CR2 receptor (also known as CD21) presents antigen to B cells and is a co-receptor for B cell signalling.

question: This wound is in the first phase of healing. What is the best term to describe this initial phase?
explanation: Wound healing can be described with 3 phases: inflammatory, proliferative, and remodeling. The other options represent different phases or aspects that are critical to wound healing, but inflammation is the initial stage.

question: Eccrine glands are found on the:
explanation: Eccrine glands are present all over the body except on the vermilion of lips, glans, labia minora, nail beds, and inner prepuce.

question: This patient has metastatic colon cancer and biopsy was done to rule out cutaneous metastases. Pathology showed abundant granulation tissue. What is the best description of the cellular composition of this healing tissue?
explanation: Granulation tissue is composed most correctly of macrophages, fibroblasts, endothelial cells. Eosinophils, keratinocytes, and mast cells are less prominent in the makeup of granulation tissue.

question: Which part of the matrix gives rise to the dorsal nail plate?
explanation: The proximal matrix gives rise to the dorsal nail plate. The distal matrix gives rise to the ventral nail plate.

question: What is the major determinant of sodium chloride concentration of eccrine sweat that is secreted onto the surface of the skin?
explanation: The composition of human eccrine sweat includes inorganic ions (sodium chloride, bicarbonate, potassium), urea, lactate, ammonia, amino acids, proteases, and other proteins. The sweat rate is the major determinant of sodium chloride concentration of eccrine sweat that is secreted onto the surface of the skin. Eccrine sweat is secreted from eccrine glands via merocrine secretion. The substance secreted is initially isotonic but becomes hypotonic as NaCl reabsorption occurs in the eccrine duct. The sweat rate determines how much reabsorption occurs, and thus determines the final concentration of eccrine sweat that reaches the skin surface. Eccrine glands play an important role in the regulation of body temperature. They are distributed over the entire body skin, but are highest in density on the palms and soles. Eccrine glands secrete a salty solution, which reaches the skin pores via an eccrine duct. Eccrine sweat is a sterile electrolyte solution primarily containing sodium chloride, potassium and bicarbonate, with smaller quantities of various other components such as glucose and antimicrobial peptides. Sweat rate differs depending on site on the body, the degree of thermal or physical stress, and between individuals. Under maximal stimulation, the body can produce 3 liters of eccrine sweat per hour.

question: A mother presents to your pediatric dermatology clinic for further evaluation of her daughter, who has red gums, episodic hair loss, and rough perifollicular papules on the arms and thighs. She reports a family history of similar findings. After a thorough assessment of this patient, you conclude the patient has:
explanation: Defects of the hair shaft include hereditary mucoepithelial dysplasia which is characterized by red gums, episodic hair loss, and keratosis pilaris. Pili annulati is known as banded hair. Uncombable hair syndrome results in triangle-shaped hair. Naxos syndrome is characterized by wooly hair, hyperkeratosis of the palms & soles, and cardiac arrhythmias.

question: Occlusive moisturizers prevent evaporative water loss to the environment by placing an oily substance on the skin surface through which water cannot penetrate. This replenishes the stratum corneum by water movement from the viable epidermal and dermal layers. There are many different classes of chemicals that can function as occlusive moisturizers. What is the most effective occlusive moisturizer?
explanation: The most effective occlusive moisturizer is petrolatum, since it reduce transepidermal water loss by 99%. Petrolatum allows barrier repair while permeating throughout the interstices of the stratum corneum. a- Glycerin: Humectants are substances that attract moisture; they include: glycerin, honey, sodium lactate, urea, propylene glycol, sorbitol, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, and some vitamins and proteins. Some astringents designed for dry skin contain a humectant liquid moisturizer, such as propylene glycol or glycerin, and skin soothing agents, such as allantoin, guaiazulene or quaternium-19. Glycerin is not the most effective occlusive moisturizer. c- Vegetable oil: There are many different classes of chemicals that can function as occlusive moisturizers, such as vegetable oils (castor oil, corn oil, grape seed oil, soybean oil). Vegetable oil and wax is a moisturizer type that composes castor oil, corn oil, ozokerite, beeswax, paraffin and carnauba wax. There are many different classes of chemicals that can function as occlusive moisturizers such as vegetable oil. Vegetable oil is not the most effective occlusive moisturizer. d - Dimethicone: There are many different classes of chemicals that can function as occlusive moisturizers such as silicones (dimethicone, cyclomethicone). Dimethicone and ceramides are moisturizer types that compose water, petrolatum, dimethicone, and ceramics. Dimethicone is not the most effective occlusive moisturizer. e - Ceramide: There are many different classes of chemicals that can function as occlusive moisturizers such as sterols (cholesterol and ceramides). Dimethicone and ceramides are moisturizer types that compose water, petrolatum,dimethicone, and ceramics. Ceramides are not the most effective occlusive moisturizers.

question: What structure is indicated by the arrow in this Mohs frozen section?
explanation: A collection of elongated smooth muscle cells at a 45 degree angle in associated with a hair follicle is consistent erector pili muscle. Nerves are a bundle of spindled cells and are typically not seen in the upper dermis, and are not at a 45 degree angle, nor in connection with a hair follicle. Veins consistent of endothelial cells that would be lining a lumen; the lumen may appear collapsed. A hair shaft should be surrounded by various layers and sheaths, and is not made up of spindle cells. Sebaceous glands a a round collection of lobulated cells, not spindled cells, and are seen in association with a hair follicle.

question: The desmosomal connections of the epidermis are dependent on which of the following ions?
explanation: The desmosomal connections in the epidermis are calcium dependent. The other options are not required for these connections. Desmogleins and desmocollins are cadherins (calcium-dependent adherence molecules)

question: A patient presents with a chronic pruritic papular eruption in both axillae. You suspect she may have Fox-Fordyce disease, due to an occlusion of apocrine ducts. Which of the following is also true of apocrine glands?

choices.D: Denervation abolishes response to emotive stimuli
choices.E: Distributed over the entire cutaneous surface

explanation: Apocrine glands are innervated by sympathetic fibers. They are present at birth but do not enlarge until hormonal stimulation from puberty. Apocrine glands stain positive for S100, keratin, CEA, and lysozyme. Secretion is in response to emotive stimuli through action of epinephrine/ norepinephrine. Denervation does not abolish this response although apocrine sweating requires intact nerve supply. Apocrine sweat glands are confined to certain anatomic locations (axillae, anogenital region, periumbilical region, areolae, nipples, vermilion border of the lip).

question: As the shown wound heals and matures, which cell type is most important for wound contraction?
explanation: Myofibroblasts are modified fibroblast with smooth muscle like features. Myofibroblasts play the important role in the contraction of the wound that occurs during the proliferation phase. The contraction is considered one of the important events in wound healing because it results in the closure of the wound. The correct balance between too little contraction, which leads to non-healing wounds, and too much contraction, which leads to contractures, is important for optimal healing. The other cell types do not play a large role in wound contraction.

question: Which type of collagen is the first to be deposited in a healing wound?
explanation: During the proliferative phase of wound healing, granulation tissue is formed, which relies on presence of fibronectin. Fibronectin is then replaced by collagen type III, and ultimately by collagen type I. Wound contraction then ensues during the second week of wound healing, a process that is mediated by myofibroblasts. The remaining answer choices are incorrect.

question: Which of the options below, per high concentrations noted in recent studies, is the most important factor in the pathogenesis of SJS/TEN?
explanation: While the pathogenesis of SJS and TEN is not exactly understood, Granzyme B has been shown to be a key factor due to high concentrations present in affected skin. TNF-alpha, perforin and FasL have also been shown to be key to the development of the adverse drug dermatosis. The other cytokines listed are not as critical in the development of SJS/TEN.

question: This patient presents with chronic swelling of the lower extremities, and circumferential lesions on both lower legs as shown in this image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Elephantiasis nostras verrucosa is complication from chronic ymphedema. It commonly affects distal feet and lower extremities leading to verrucous changes with papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis. The other options would not lead to circumferential verrucous lesions on both lower extremities.

question: A child with a stahylococcal infection has an exfoliative dermatitis. The pathogenesis of this eruption is similar to what disease?
explanation: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is descibed, a staphylococcal infection that has exfoliative properties, and the pathogenesis involves serine proteases binding desmoglein 1. This explains the clinical similarities between pemphigus foliaceous and SSSS. The other answer choices are not similar in pathogenesis to that of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

question: Botulinum toxin acts by reducing the amount of acetylcholine release from nerve endings and can be targeted for use on sweat glands for hyperhidrosis. Which of the following sites has the greatest density of these sweat glands?
explanation: A is correct. The question refers to eccrine glands, which are innervated by postganglionic sympathetic fibers and use acetylcholine as their neurotransmitter. They are targeted by botulinum toxin for hyperhidrosis (in contrast to apocrine glands; innervation of these glands is less clear). All of the following sites except for the nipple (A) lack eccrine glands.

question: An 80-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease developed a new pruritic eruption with these cutaneous findings. What is the antigenic target of the autoantibodies generated in this condition?
explanation: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common immunobullous disorder and presents with tense vesicles and bullae and pruritus. There has been as association of neurologic disorders, such as Parkinson's disease and dementia, with bullous pemphigoid. Autoantibodies are most commonly directed against the NC16A domain of BPAg2, also known as BP180 or collagen XVII.

question: Which of the following absorbs ultraviolet radiation?
explanation: Urocanic acid is a chromophore that absorbs ultraviolet radiation (UVR) in the stratum corneum.This question assesses the examinee’s basic science knowledge of the function of skin proteins and their breakdown products. In the stratum corneum, urocanic acid (choice 4) functions as a chromophore that absorbs UVR and also mediates UV-induced immunosuppression. None of the remaining answer choices absorbs UVR. Urocanic acid is a degradation product of filaggrin (choice 1). Filaggrin cements the keratin filaments composing the stratum corneum; it is mutated in atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris. Loricrin (choice 2) is the most plentiful component of the cornified envelope. Involucrin (choice 3), another component of the cornified envelope, is crosslinked to loricrin by transglutaminase 1. Laminin 332 (choice 5), found within the lamina lucida and densa, connects anchoring filaments to collagen VII.

question: Which of the following is NOT a degranulating stimulus for the largest cells seen in the image?
explanation: The largest cells in the image are mast cells, which can be identified based on their size and presence of many intracellular granules. Captopril, and ACE-inhibitor, is not a degranulating stimulus for mast cells. The remaining answer choices are all mast cell degranulating stimuli, thus patients with mastocytosis should be counseled to avoid these medications if possible.

question: Which of the following medications is not concentrated in the eccrine glands?
explanation: The above listed drugs, as well as beta-lactam antibiotics, antifungals such as ketoconazole and griseofulvin, are known to be secreted into eccrine sweat ducts. This feature may explain the development of neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis and eccrine squamous syringometaplasia in the context of chemotherapy. Doxycycline does not accumulate in eccrine glands.

question: Which of the following is a conservative and effective treatment for chondrodermatitis nodularis helicis?

choices.D: Cushion pillow support on either side of the lesion to reduce focal pressure

correct_text: Cushion pillow support on either side of the lesion to reduce focal pressure
explanation: Chondrodermatitis nodularis helices presents as a tender nodule usually on the helix or antihelix of the ear. It is thought to be a result of pressure to the local, affected area. Multiple treatment modalities have been noted with conservative, effective treatment seen with cushion pillow application to reduce the focal pressure. The other options listed are either too invasive (Mohs, aggressive liquid nitrogen) or are less effective (TCA peels and cantharidin).

question: At any one time, the approximate proportion of hair follicles in anagen phase is:
explanation: Most (~90%) hair follicles are in anagen (growth) phase. The longer a hair follicle is in anagen phase, the longer the hair can grow. Hairs of the scalp grow approximately 0.4 mm per day, and thus the date of one's next hair cut can be accurately calculated. Approximately 1% of hairs are in catagen (transitional) phase, whereas ~9% of hairs are in telogen (resting) phase. The remaining answer choices (60% and 95%) are distractors.

question: All of the following are increased in psoriasis EXCEPT:
explanation: Loricrin is the major protein component of the cell envelope. It is decreased in psoriasis. The remaining answer choices are increased in psoriasis.

question: Detection of immunoglobulins, complement, or both at the basement membrane zone in lesional skin by direct immunofluorescence occurs in approximately half of cases of which dermatologic condition?
explanation: The key diagnostic sign of neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE) is the erythematous and annular clinical appearance of lesions. The histopathologic findings may be subtle in NLE compared with discoid or subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Direct immunofluorescence testing may be useful in supplementing the histopathologic evaluation. Detection of immunoglobulins, complement, or both at the basement membrane zone in lesional skin by immunofluorescence occurs in approximately half of cases; a negative study does not preclude the diagnosis of NLE syndrome. Clinical and serologic evaluation of both the infant and the mother are important in establishing a diagnosis of NLE syndrome, particularly when histopathologic findings are subtle. DIF (direct immunofluorescence) of lichen planus is positive in the vast majority, with granular DEJ (dermal-epidermal junction) deposition and IgM and fibrinogen staining within cytoid bodies in the superficial dermis. In MCTD DIF shows IgG deposits within epidermal cell nuclei, and rarely along the DEJ. In SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus), while serology is more reliable, DIF can show DEJ deposition in the lupus band test. DIF of erythema multiforme shows immunoglobulin within superficial vessel walls, DEJ, and cytoid bodies.

question: A 16-year-old female presents with severe scarring, cystic acne. Which of the following immunologic factors are involved in the pathogenesis of acne?
explanation: TLR-2 is a key aspect in the pathogenesis of acne. The other options listed are not key parts of the pathogenesis of acne, some are specifically involved in the pathogenesis of rosacea (KLK5, MMPs and TRPV channels).

question: All of the following locations have apocrine glands except:
explanation: Apocrine glands are found in the axillae, anogenital region, external ear canal, eyelids, breast, periumbilical region. Apocrine glands produce an oily fluid rich in triglycerides and fatty acids – subsequent colonization by anaerobic bacteria results in body odor. Apocrine sweat glands are androgen-dependent for their development and have an unclear function in humans; primary locations are the axillae, anogenital region, periumbilical region and nipples Apocrine glands, whose apical portion (acrosyringium) drains into terminal hair follicles, continuously secrete a sterile odorless viscous fluid that is rich in precursors of odoriferous substances.

question: Subcorneal pustular dermatosis type IgA pemphigus is caused by a defect in what antigen?
explanation: IgA pemphigus has two types subcorneal pustular dermatosis type which is due to ab to desmocollin 1 and intraepidermal n eutrophilic IgA dermatosis which is due to ab to desmoglein 3 and 1. Sneddon- Wilkinson disease, also known as sub-corneal pustular dermatosis has an unknown etiology. Desmoglein 1 defect is seen in pemphigus foliaceous and staph scalded skin syndrome. Desmoglein 3 defect is seen in pemphigus vulgaris and intraepidermal neutrophilic IgA dermatosis. BPAg1 is seen in paraneoplastic pemphigus and bullous pemphigoid. BPAg2 is seen in bullous pemphigoid, cicatricial mucous membrane pemphigoid and linear IgA disease. IgA pemphigus (or immunoglobulin A pemphigus) is an autoimmune blistering disorder. It is also called intercellular IgA dermatosis among other names. IgA pemphigus has two major subtypes:

question: What is the most abundant amino acid in collagen?
explanation: Collagen is composed of 3 chains of amino acids combined into a triple helix configuration. It contains Gly-x-y repeats (glycine is always the 3rd residue). Thus, glycine is the most abundant amino acid in collagen. The remaining answer choices are not the most abundant amino acids in collagen.

question: Which of the following medications is concentrated in the eccrine glands?

choices.E: All of the answers are correct

correct_text: All of the answers are correct
explanation: The above listed drugs, as well as beta-lactam antibiotics, antifungals such as ketoconazole and griseofulvin, are known to be secreted into eccrine sweat ducts. This feature may explain the development of neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis and eccrine squamous syringometaplasia in the context of chemotherapy.

question: Which element is necessary for function of matrix metalloproteinases?
explanation: Matrix metalloproteinases are required for normal tissue architecture and normal turnover of the extracellular matrix. All of them have zinc at the active site and require octahedral binding of calcium ions to maintain structural integrity.

question: What is the most important cell for wound healing?
explanation: Macrophages are the most important cell for wound healing. They secrete TGFs, cytokines, IL-1, TNF, and PDGF. Neutropenic or lymphopenic patients do not have impaired wound healing, whereas macrophage-deficient (quantity or function) patients heal poorly. Neutrophils however are the first cell type to flood the wound during phase I of inflammation (within first 6-8 hours); this movement is facilitated by TGF-beta. Fibroblasts migrate into the wound by stage II (granulation) where they produced glycosaminoglycans and fibronectin.

question: Which of the following is true in or associated with Apert Syndrome?

choices.A: Secondary to a mutation in FGFR3
choices.C: Acne localized to buttocks and thighs

explanation: Apert Syndrome is an AD syndrome secondary to a mutation in FGFR2. Also known as acrocephlosyndactyly, this condition includes synostoses of the hands, feet, back and skull as well as generalized acne. Mosaicism of this gene causes nevus comedonicus. There is associated cutaneous and ocular hypopigmentation.

question: What is the most abundant collagen found on fetal skin?
explanation: Type III collagen is found in the fetal skin. It is also present in the gastrointestinal tract, blood vessels, and the basement membrane. A defect in this collagen results in the Ehlers-Danlos, vascular type.

question: Which component of hair is positive for citrulline?
explanation: The inner root sheath stains red because it contains citrulline. The cortex and medulla along with the cuticle make up the hair shaft. The outer root sheath is the most peripheral cellular structure. The glassy vitreous layer is the basement zone equivalent of hair and is the outermost layer.

question: The major protein component of the cornified envelope is:
explanation: Loricrin is the major component of the cornified envelope (CE). The proteins of the CE are synthesized in the spinous and granular layers. The CE is primarily a protein/lipid polymer formed within the differentiating layer of keratinocytes. The CE eventually exists outside of the cornified cells after the granular cell undergoes a programmed destruction (apoptosis). Self-destructing granular cells are called transition cells.

question: The most common type of pityriasis rubra pilaris in childhood is type:
explanation: Type IV, or circumscribed juvenile, accounts for 25% of total PRP cases. The most common type is Type I, classical adult, which accounts for 55% of cases. Types II, III, and V account for less than 10% each.

question: Elastic fibers contain the specific amino acids:
explanation: Desmosine and isodesmosine are the typical amino acids of elastic fibers. Elastic fibers are comprised of elastin that is wrapped by fibrillin microfibrils. Elastic fibers form a complex meshwork extending from the lamina densa of the dermo-epidermo junction through the dermis. Elastic fibers return the skin to a normal shape after being stretched.

question: Anchoring fibrils are primarily composed of:
explanation: Anchoring fibrils are found in the sublamina densa and are made up of collagen type VII. This collagen type is mutated in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, and targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita and bullous lupus erythematosus.

question: A child presents with a 1 cm yellow-red nodule on the face. Pathology shows Touton giant cells. What is the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement in this disease?
explanation: The eye is the most frequent site of extracutaneous juvenile xamthogranuloma. The second most common site of extracutaneous disease is the lungs. Ocular involvement is typically unilateral.

question: Keratinocytes are derived from which of the following:
explanation: As implied by the root 'ecto', a prefix meaning "outer", the keratinocytes of the epidermis are derived from the ectoderm. The other layers do contribute cell populations that are present in the skin.

question: Which epidermal layer do pilar cysts generally not have a:
explanation: Pilar cysts do not have a granular layer, they do have all the other layers.

question: Fragmentation and/or loss of elastic fibers in not seen in:
explanation: Cutis laxa results from decreased desmosine and lysyl oxidase and demonstrates fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers. Marfan's sydnrome results from decreased fibrillin I and demonstrates fragmentation of elastic fibers. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum demonstrates increased glycosaminoglycans on elastic fibers and the accumulation of fragmented and calcified elastic fibers. Anetoderma has decreased desmosine and demonstrates loss and fragmentation of elastic fibers. Buschke- Ollendorf syndrome exhibits increased desmosine and an increased amount of thickened elastic fibers.

question: Which of the following protein plays a major role in wound healing?
explanation: Fibronectin is a key player in wound healing, initially secreted by myofibroblasts. The bed/matrix of fibronectin provides an adherent base for migration into the wound, provides scaffolding for collagen fibrils and mediates wound contraction. Band-6 protein is a constituent of the desmosomes intracellular plaque. Entactin and nidogen are synonyms and are found in the dermal-epidermal junction, binding to laminin 1s alpha chain. Uncein is associated with anchoring filaments.

question: Keratinocytes have been shown to secrete all of the following cytokines except:
explanation: Keratinocytes have been shown to secrete all of the above cytokines, except IL-2, IL- 4, and IFNgamma.

question: The microflora of pilosebaceous unit consist of which of the following:
explanation: All the above bacteria and fungi are found within sebaceous glands; the Malasssezia spp. and P. ovale are found within the acroinfundibulum, S. epidermidis is found within the midinfundibulum, and Propionibacterium spp. deep within the follicle.

question: Regarding dermal-epidermal junction, which of the following statements is true:

choices.A: There are no anchoring filaments in lamina lucida
choices.B: Lamina fibroreticularis lies above lamina densa
choices.C: Lamina fibroreticularis comprises of anchoring fibrils and the elastic microfibrils
choices.D: Blood vessels cross the dermal-epidermal junction to reach the epidermis
choices.E: Lamina lucida is an electron-dense layer

correct_text:
Lamina fibroreticularis comprises of anchoring fibrils and the elastic
microfibrils
explanation: Lamina fibroreticularis comprises of anchoring fibrils and the elastic microfibrils. Lamina fibroreticularis lies below lamina densa. Blood vessels don't cross the dermal-epidermal junction to reach the epidermis. Basement membrane contain both: 1)Lamina basale which include a.lamina lucida and b.lamina densa ( which contain collagene IV & other glycoproteins like laminins,fibronectin etc.) 2)Lamina fibroreticularis contain collagen type III and anchoring fibrils (collagen type VII).

question: Direct immunofluorescence staining of intercellular spaces and the basement membrane zone, in combination, is seen in:
explanation: Paraneoplastic pemphigus and drug-induced pemphigus demonstrate direct immunofluorescence staining of the intercellular space and the BMZ, in combination. Anti-epiligrin pemphigoid demonstrates BMZ staining (dermal staining on salt-split skin). Pemphigus vegetans, pemphigus foliaceous, and IgA pemphigus all show intercellular space deposition without staining of the BMZ.

question: Keratohyalin granules contain:
explanation: Keratohyalin granules are found in the stratum granulosum (the granular layer), and contain the proteins profilaggrin and loricrin. Profilaggrin is converted to filaggrin during the transformation of the granular layer to the cornified layer. This is a calcium-dependent process. Loricrin comprises 75% of the cornified envelopeï¿½s mass.

question: Which eponym describes vestigial lines of pigmentary demarcation?
explanation: Futcher lines are vestigial lines in which the dorsal surface has more melanocytes than ventral surface. Wallace's lines are the well-demarcated lines around the margin of the foot and hand.

question: Sebaceous glands are located in each of the following locations except:
explanation: Sebaceous glands secrete their contents in a holocrine fashion and are primarily under the influence of androgens. They secrete triglycerides, phospholipids, esterified cholesterol, waxes but not free cholesterol. They may be found in association with hair follicles or in some areas of modified skin such as the nipple/areola, labia minora, prepuce, vermilion border, and eyelids.

question: All of the following pertain to Odland bodies EXCEPT:

choices.B: Are found intracellularly in upper level keratinocytes
