choices.A: Serum protein electrophoresis should be performed
choices.B: The palms and soles are usually affected
choices.C: Dapsone will likely be an effective treatment
choices.D: The diagnostic histopathological findings include acanthosis and hyperkeratosis
choices.E: The face is usually is affected

correct_text: Serum protein electrophoresis should be performed
explanation: This patient likely has nephrogenic fibrosing dermopathy (NFD). NFD is an acquired, idiopathic disorder that occurs in renal disease patients. It resembles scleroderma or eosinophilic fasciitis clinically, and scleromyxedema histopathologically. Large areas of indurated skin with fibrotic nodules and plaques develop. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis results are negative unlike scleromyxedema, and thus may be helpful to distinguish the two diseases.

question: A 70-year-old farmer presents with cysts and comedone formation in sun-damaged skin, most prominent under and around the eyes and on the back of the neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The scenario describes Favre-Racouchot, also known as "nodular elastosis." It is characterized by cysts and comedone formation in sun-damaged skin, often prominent under and around the eyes or on the back of the neck.

question: A patient presents with recurrent genital and oral ulcerations and a diagnosis of posterior uveitis. What HLA type is associated with the diagnosis you suspect?
explanation: The patient has Behcet's disease. Behcet's disease is diagnosed based on recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 times in a 12 month period) plus 2 of the following: recurrent genital ulceration, posterior uveitis, skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustular lesions, or acneiform nodules), and a positive pathergy test. Behcet's disease is associated with HLA-B51.

question: Hydrogen peroxide is often chosen for treatment of which of the following?

choices.A: Post-operative follow-up of a full thickness skin graft with a bolster
choices.B: Cleaning a chronic wound on the lower extremity
choices.D: Treatment of a chronic venous ulcer

correct_text: Post-operative follow-up of a full thickness skin graft with a bolster
explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is used to remove crusts on healing wounds such as a bolster on a skin graft.

question: Which of the following molecules have been shown to play a role in the development of TEN/SJS severe drug reactions?
explanation: All of the molecules have been implicated in playing an important pathogenic role in development of SJS/TEN.

question: A patient with multiple lentigines and blue nevi may also have:
explanation: This patient may have a constellation of features associated with NAME syndrome, otherwise known as Carney complex or LAMB syndrome. This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and is due to a defect in the PRKAR1A gene. This condition is characterized by the following features: blue Nevi, Atrial myxomas, cutaneous Myxomas, and Ephelides. In addition, testicular tumors are seen as well as sexual precocity. Finally, patients may have endocrine abnormalities including pigmented nodular adrenocorticoal disease and Cushing syndrome as well as pituitary adenomas.

question: What condition is depicted in the image?
explanation: The image shows cutaneous larva migrans. The causative organism is larvae of hookworms from cats and dogs (Ancylostoma braziliense or Bunostomum phlebotomum). Physical examination shows pruritic, serpiginous tracks which move 2 mm-2 cm/day. This is much slower than larva currens which moves 5-10 cm/hour. Due to the lack of collagenase, the organisms are unable to penetrate past the basement membrane. Albendazole can be used to treat this condition.

question: Patients that experience hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita can be due to all of the following except:
explanation: Tetracyclines are not associated with hypertrichosis lanuginosa aquisita.

question: One might see all of the following laboratory and clinical abnormalities in cryoglobulinemia associated with hepatitis C virus infection EXCEPT:
explanation: Laboratory abnormalities of HCV include an elevation of liver enzymes, positive rheumatoid factor (70-90%), and DEPRESSED C3 levels. Classical clinical presentation includes palpable purpura, arthralgias, and glomerulonephritis. Livedo reticularis, hemorrhagic bullae, acrocyanosis, and urticarial plaques can also be found.

question: Which of the following may be an early cutaneous manifestation of Sipple syndrome (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A)?
explanation: Sipple syndrome (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of pheochromocytomas, medullary thyroid carcinomas, and hyperparathyroidism. The associated mutation is found in the RET proto-oncogene. An early cutaneous manifestation includes the development of lichen or macular amyloidosis (both keratin-derived cutaneous amyloidoses) often localized to interscapular patches, which may be pruritic (similar to notalgia paresthetica). The latter arises during teenage years and may be the earliest presenting sign of this disease.

question: Which of the following carcinomas has been most associated with erythema gyratum repens?
explanation: 80% of cases of erythema gyratum repens have been associated with underlying malignancy. Lung cancer is the most common neoplasm. The skin eruption preceedes the detection of malignancy by an average of 9 months

question: A 22 year old woman presents with a rash on her cheeks that encompasses her cheeks and nasal bridge. She has scattered telangiectasias and the rash worsens in the sun. There is no ulceration but she appears to have some atrophy in certain areas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The cutaneous manifestations of SLE typically present with a photosensitive malar rash in a butterfly distribution on the cheeks and nasal bridge that spares the nasolabial folds. Although rosacea can present with a similar type of rash, atrophy is not seen in rosacea but can be seen in chronic SLE lesions.

question: What is the most common internal cause of intractable pruritus?
explanation: Chronic renal failure is the most common internal systemic cause of pruritus. Up to 49% of patients with chronic renal failure have pruritus. Other systemic causes of pruritus include liver disease, hepatitis C, hypo and hyperthryoidism, iron deficiency anemia, polycyhtemia vera, Hodkin's lymphoma, leukemia, carcinoid, internal malignancy, AIDS, and internal parasites.

question: This caterpillar has spines, which can cause hemorrhagic papules in a grid like pattern:
explanation: Megalopye opercularis, also known as the puss caterpillar, has spines, which can cause hemorrhagic papules in a grip like pattern.

question: The substance that is responsible for the yellow tattoo color is:
explanation: Cadmium sulfide is responsible for the yellow color in tattoos.

question: In a patient suspected of having multiple endocrine neoplasia type IIb, which lab test would be appropriate?
explanation: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome type IIb, also called multiple mucosal neuroma syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition due to a defect in the RET protooncogene on chromosome 10q11.2. This rare condition is associated with mucosal neuromas on the tongue and lips, medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and gastrointestinal ganglioneuromatosis. In addition, patients can also present with a marfanoid habitus and facial dysmorphism. Mucosal neuromas can be a dermatologic clue to the underlying diagnosis as these lesions appear during early childhood and present as pink, pedunculated nodules. As the major cause of mortality in these patients is medullary thyroid cancer, which nearly all patients will have by early adulthood, aggressive screening, with serial calcitonin level, and prophylactic thyroidectomy are warranted.

question: A 34 year old woman complains of recurrent painful blisters on her lower lip. These occur 4 times per year, and are preceded by painful sensations for a day before the blisters appear. What is the most common trigger of recurrent orolabial herpes simplex virus infection?
explanation: Recurrent orolabial herpes simplex virus infection is a very common problem. In many cases, the cause of the recurrences is idiopathic. Identifiable triggers include light exposure and emotional stress, among others. UVB is the most commonly implicated factor.

question: A 6-year-old male has painful edema and erythema of his posterior forearms, dorsal hands, and face several hours following sun exposure. He says a tingling and intense, painful burning sensation precede the rash when it occurs, starting immediately after sun exposure. These episodes recover in a few days. Episodes appear seasonal, with increased symptoms in the spring and summer months. Blood levels of protoporphyrin IX and metal-free protoporphyrin elevated, but no porphyrins are detected in the urine. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this patient?
explanation: This pediatric patient has erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), characterized by the rapid onset pf painful burning followed by erythema and edema after sun exposure. Urinary porphyrins are not elevated in EPP patients unlike other porphyrias, such as hereditary porphyria and variegate porphyria. It is associated with jaundice and the development of pigment gallstones, a leading cause of gallstones in the pediatric population. It is caused by a genetic, either autosomal recessive or dominant, deficiency in the enzyme ferrochelatase. Ferrochelatase normally converts protoporphyrin into heme in the mitochondria of erythrocytes as part of the heme synthesis pathway.

question: A patient presents with hyperpigmentation on the leg. What is the most likely culprit?
explanation: This is an example of phytophotodermatitis. The linearity indicates an "outside job," and appears as though something dripped down this patient's leg. Given the morphology it is likely that this is a phytophotodermatitis. Lime (Rutaceae family) would be the most likely culprit of all of the options.

question: What is the appropriate and necessary medical management for a seborrheic keratosis diagnosed by biopsy?
explanation: Seborrheic keratoses are benign lesions that do not require additional treatment.

question: Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is most commonly associated with which of the following:
explanation: Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is associated with a monoclonal IgG kappa paraproteinemia in approximately 80% of cases. It is less commonly associated with an IgA gammopathy. Myeloma or myelodysplastic syndromes may resultantly occur. A hallmark feature of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is the associated paraproteinemia, an IgG monoclonal gammopathy, which is found in at least 70% of cases. The paraproteinemia can be detected by serum protein electrophoresis and/or the more sensitive immunofixation electrophoresis. Other common findings include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, an increased ESR/CRP, leukopenia, hypocomplementemia, and an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia (including multiple myeloma). Less commonly, cryoglobulinemia and/or an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder are observed.

question: A common cause of a medication induced photoallergy is:
explanation: All of the listed medications are causes of photosensitivity, but only piroxicam is a cause of photoallergy (can be both phototoxic and photoallergic).

question: Which of the following proteins is a 160kDa cadherin?
explanation: Desmogleins and desmocollins belong to the cadherin family of proteins, which are calcium-dependent adhesion molecules. Desmoglein I is a 160kDa cadherin, while Desmoglein 3 is a 130 kDa cadherin. Desmoplakin, envoplakin, and plectin belong to the plakin family of adhesion proteins.

question: Patients presenting with horizontal parallel ridges on the nail, often accompanied by an absent cuticle have:
explanation: Patients with horizontal parallel ridges, often accompanied by an absent cuticle, is called habit tic deformity. It is caused by trauma to the cuticle. Patients can have anxiety and obsessive compulsive disorder associated with this finding.

question: A 28-year-old man presents for evaluation of an 8-mm painless pink ulcerated plaque on his right forearm. He is a refugee from Mexico who recently arrived in the United States. There is no mucosal involvement or adenopathy on the exam. A punch biopsy of the ulceration is performed, and diagnostic amastigotes are observed in the stain. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: A patient from an endemic area with a painless pink ulcerated plaque on the forearm, along with histopathologic findings of amastigotes, should be most suspicious for cutaneous leishmaniasis. Given the patient’s country of origin, this is most likely to be a non-diffuse form of leishmaniasis; given the size of the lesion being less than 1 cm, local therapy with intralesional sodium stibogluconate is the most appropriate treatment.

question: This is the term that is used from tuberculosis of the skin and is spread by hematogenous, lymphatic, or contiguous spread. The clinical characteristic is brownish red plaque, apple jelly color on diascopy.
explanation: Lupus vulgaris spreads from hematogenous, lymphatic, or contiguous spread from distant site of tuberculous infection. It is sensitizes the host with moderate to high immunity. It is pauci-bacillarry. It also involved the head/neck in 90% of cases.

question: A patient has epidermal cysts, a desmoid tumor, fibromas, lipomas, and dental cysts. Which of the following malignancies is most likely in this patient?
explanation: This patient has Gardner syndrome with a mutation in the tumor suppressor APC gene. These patients develop adenomatous polyposis of the colon and rectum with 100% transformation to carcinoma by the age of 30. Gardner syndrome is an autosomal dominant syndrome with the characteristic eye finding of congenital hypertrophy of retinal epithelium (CHRPE).

question: A patient is diagnosed with Loiasis. This patient most likely has clinical features such as:

choices.A: Ocular involvement that leads to blindness
choices.C: Depigmented macules/patches also known as "leopard skin"
choices.D: Adult worm migrating across the conjunctivae
choices.E: Nodules over bony prominences on the extremities

correct_text: Adult worm migrating across the conjunctivae
explanation: Loiasis is caused by the organism Loa Loa. The vector is mango flies. The clinical characteristic is calabar swelling and adult worm migrating across conjunctivae or "eye worm". The treatment is DEC or diethylcarbamazine.

question: A 35 year-old woman who works in the animal product industry presents with a painless hemorrhagic bulla. A diagnosis of anthrax is suspected. Gram stain of the vesicle fluid should reveal which of the following?
explanation: Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, which is a gram-positive spore-forming rod.

question: What name is commonly used to describe this condition of nodular elastosis with cysts and comedones?
explanation: Favre-Racouchot syndrome is a condition that generally affects elderly white males with a history of chronic sun exposure and smoking. It is characterized by multiple open comedones on the temples and forehead with a background of actinically damaged skin.

question: A 42-year-old Caucasian female with no past medical history presents to the emergency department with diffuse, painful sloughing erosions and ulcers involving the mucosa, conjunctiva, and 15% of the body surface area. She admits to taking NSAIDs 3 weeks ago for a sprained ankle. She is admitted to the hospital and transferred to the burn unit. Her vitals, serum BUN, and serum glucose are within normal limits, but her serum bicarbonate is 13. What is her calculated mortality rate related to this condition?
explanation: The condition described in this vignette is Steven-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). SCORTEN scale can be used to predict the mortality rate in patients with this eruption (see table 2.3.12 in DIR). All the following are considered risk factors: age >40, associated malignancy, heart rate >120, serum BUN >28, detached body surface >10%, serum bicarbonate <20, and serum glucose >252. This patient has 3 risk factors: age >40, detached body surface >10%, and serum bicarbonate <20. The mortality rate on the SCORTEN scale for 3 risk factors is 35.3%.

question: Which of the following is correct about eosinophilic folliculitis?

choices.B: Associated with P. acnes infection of hair follicles

explanation: Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis is a non-infectious eosinophilic infiltrate of the hair follicle. It is characterized by intense pruritus. The 3 variants of eosinophilic folliculitis include classic eosinophilic pustular folliculitis, immunosuppression-associated (mostly HIV-related), and infancy-associated eosinophilic folliculitis. The classic type (Ofuji) is more common in Japanese men. The male-to-female ratio of eosinophilic folliculitis is 5:1. It is associated with immunosuppresion and has been classified as an AIDS defining illness. Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis should be viewed as a possible cutaneous sign of immunosuppression.

question: A 65 year-old woman is referred to your office for evaluation of a skin lesion that has been increasing in size over the past 5 years. You perform a skin biopsy that results as poorly- differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Risk factors for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) include all of the following EXCEPT:

choices.D: Fitzpatrick skin types I and II

explanation: Kidney disease in and of itself is not a risk factor for cSCC, however a patient who has had a kidney transplant is at higher risk for the development of cSCC, 65x increased risk over the general population due to the use of immunosuppressive agents to prevent organ rejection. Other risk factors for SCC include: chronic sun exposure, skin types I and II, chemical carcinogens (arsenic, tobacco, coal, tar), immunosuppression, chronic ulcers, burn scars, genetic syndrome (e.g. xeroderma pigmentosa), male gender, and older age.

question: A 45-year-old male presents with numerous yellow papules on his face, chest, and back. Biopsy reveals lobules of sebaceous glands within the dermis. He reports a strong family history of colon cancer. What is the function of the mutated genes in the associated condition?
explanation: The vignette describes a patient with multiple sebaceous neoplasms and a strong family history of colon cancer, suggesting the diagnosis of Muir-Torre syndrome (MTS). MTS is an autosomal dominant condition associated with colon, breast, head and neck, and GI tract adenocarcinomas. Cutaneous manifestations include sebaceous neoplasms and keratoacanthomas. MTS is caused by heterozygous mutation in DNA mismatch repair (MSH2, MLH1, MSH6).

question: A 12 year old boy has a pruritic bullous eruption on his feet. A KOH is positive and a fungal culture shows microconidia in grape-like clusters. The etiology is:
explanation: Trichophyton mentagrophytes is the dermatophyte primarily responsible for bullous tinea pedis. It typically has septate, spiral hypahe with cigar or grape like thin-walled microconidia.

question: A 27-year-old woman presents with a linear, verrucous plaque present since birth. The lesion is biopsied and shows hyperkeratosis, broad papillomatosis, and clumping of keratin filaments in the suprabasal cells. What is the next best step in management or counseling this patient?

choices.A: Counsel the patient that she will develop diffuse, chronic blistering condition of the skin
choices.B: No further treatment or counseling necessary
choices.D: Counsel the patient that the findings on pathology may indicate a risk of passing skin disorder to her children
choices.E: Counsel the patient that there is a small risk for developing a malignancy within the biopsied lesion in the future

correct_text:
Counsel the patient that the findings on pathology may indicate a risk of
passing skin disorder to her children
explanation: The vignette describes an epidermal nevus with epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (EHK) on pathology. EHK is due to a mutation in Keratin 1 and 10. If present within epidermal nevi, especially if extensive or on the abdomen, can involve germinative cells and this mutation can be transferred to offspring resulting in epidermolytic icthyosis. Therefore patients with these findings on pathology should be counseled regarding the risk of passing the gene mutations to their children.

question: Which of the following should NOT be included on the differential diagnosis of this patient?
explanation: Solar urticaria produces erythematous, edematous papules/plaques, not erythematous, eczematous patches/plaques, in sun exposed areas.

question: Which of the following statements about multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes is FALSE?

choices.A: MEN IIa is related to a defect in RET proto-oncogene
choices.B: MEN IIa is associated with multiple mucosal neuromas
choices.C: MEN I is associated with angiofibromas and collagenomas
choices.D: MEN I, IIa and IIb are all inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion
choices.E: MEN IIa and IIb are both associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma

correct_text: MEN IIa is associated with multiple mucosal neuromas
explanation: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are divided into types I, IIa and IIb. All are autosomal dominantly inherited. Type IIb displays multiple mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, Hirschsprung disease, medulloblastoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and ocular neuromas.

question: A 43-year-old woman presents to the dermatologist with an itchy erythematous rash in sun- exposed areas. The patient recently purchased a new sunscreen brand and has been using it over the last several weeks. Patch testing is performed and reveals the cause of the patient’s reaction. Which of the following is most responsible for the patient’s reaction?
explanation: Oxybenzone is the most common contact allergen among sunscreen.

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with tender nodules on her anterior shins. Biopsy reveals a septal panniculitis. She reports minimal relief with NSAIDs and would like a different option as the lesions are cosmetically bothersome. She has diet-controlled diabetes and normal renal function. In addition to screening for triggers, what is a reasonable second-line treatment option?
explanation: Potassium iodide is a reasonable addition to the treatment of erythema nodosum in appropriate patients. EN typically runs a self-resolving course but sometimes treatment is warranted. In this patient with mostly cosmetic concerns, super saturated potassium iodide is an option with a safe side-effect profile.

question: What is the likely etiology of the pictured lesion?
explanation: This is a SCC of the tongue. SCCs most commonly have mutations in p53.

question: A patient presents to clinic with a new onset of bullous lesions on his ankles. He notes immediately prior to the onset of these lesions, he was taking a walk through a local park. Which of the following is the most common association?
explanation: This question stem is describing a bullous arthropod reaction. This is typically seen in the setting of CLL.

question: Which of the following medications is a cause of hirsutism without virilization?
explanation: Phenytoin, diazoxide, cyclosporine and hexachlorobenzene all can cause increased hair growth in patients. In addition, oral (and topical) minoxidil can cause hirsutism.

question: Patients that have this form of acne, seen affecting young males, have suppurating nodules and plaques that ulcerate and form blackish eschar on the trunk. These patients can have leukocytosis, fever, arthralgia, and lytic changes in the bone most commonly affecting the:
explanation: Patients with acne fulminans can have severe acne with lytic lesions indicative of sterile osteomyelitis seen on x-ray and bone scans. The sternoclavicular joint and the chest wall are most frequently affected. Treatment includes oral prednisone, antibiotics, and isotretinoin.

question: A 58 year old female with lifelong Type 1 diabetes mellitus has end-stage renal failure. What is the most common cutaneous manifestation of end stage renal disease?
explanation: There are may cutaneous manifestations of end-stage renal disease. Chronic anemia can cause skin pallor. Deposition of carotenoids can give the skin a yellowish hue. Photo-distributed hyperpigmentation and ecchymoses are also commonly seen. The most common cutaneous manifestation, however, is pruritus. Other cutaneous findings include metastatic calcification, acquired perforating dermatosis, and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

question: A 63-year-old man presents with a hyperkeratotic, poorly-defined plaque on the abdomen. A biopsy of the lesion is performed, consistent with metastatic cancer, and staining reveals CK20 positivity and CK7 negativity. Which of the following is the most likely source of the patient’s malignancy?
explanation: Colon adenocarcinoma is associated with a CK20+, CK7- staining pattern on histopathology. Further evaluation should include age-appropriate evaluation, such as a colonoscopy.

question: Autoantibodies to ECM-1 may be associated with which of the following phenotypic alterations?

choices.A: Pruritic, atrophic scarring of the genitalia
choices.B: Tense blisters arising within urticarial plaques
choices.C: Hoarse cry at birth, with beaded papules at the eyelid margins noted later in life
choices.D: 1-3mm yellow papules and wrinkled skin of the lateral neck and flexures
choices.E: Thickened toenails with painful plantar keratoderma

correct_text: Pruritic, atrophic scarring of the genitalia
explanation: Antibodies to ECM-1 are associated with lichen sclerosus. Lichen sclerosus is characterized by pruritic, atrophic plaques of the vulva, though this condition can affect the male genitals or extragenital skin as well.

question: A patient with a CD4 count of 48 presents with several dozen umbilicated papulonodules and complains of fatigue and fever. Which of the following is the least likely underlying infectious process?
explanation: C is the correct answer. The remaining choices are in the differential diagnosis of molluscum-like lesions, especially in AIDS or immunocompromised patients.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common food or environmental allergen implicated in atopic dermatitis?
explanation: While most AD patients do not have food allergy, food allergens exacerbate AD in at least a subset of patients, particularly infants and young children. Eggs, milk, peanuts, soybeans, tree nuts, fish, and wheat are the most common food allergens implicated. Dust mites (Dermatophagoides pteronyssimus) are among the environmental allergens that may exacerbate AD. Corn is not a common allergen associated with atopic dermatitis.

question: What is the most likely ocular finding associated with this condition?

choices.D: Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium

explanation: This photo depicts the plucked-chicken skin appearance of Pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Histologically, it presents with fragmented distorted calcified elastic fibers within the deep dermis. Fibers stain with von Kossa. It occurs due to a ABCC6 gene defect. Angioid streaks or rupture of Bruch's membrane can occur with PXE.

question: A patient presents for treatment of a melanoma on the cheek with Breslow depth of 0.7 mm and ulceration on pathology. There is no evidence of nodal metastasis. Based on the 8th edition AJCC, what is the correct staging for this patient?
explanation: Tumors less than 0.8 mm WITH ulceration OR tumors 0.8 - 1mm (regardless of ulceration) are a T stage of T1b. If there is no nodal or distant metastasis then the patient is a cancer Stage IB. Patients with tumors 1.01 - 2mm without ulceration are T2a, and if there is no nodal metastasis they are also considered Stage IB.

question: A 23-year-old Peace Corp volunteer returns from Africa with an extensive undermined, non- healing ulceration on the right lower leg. Which of the following infections is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation: The most likely cause of a non-healing ulceration in someone who has been in a tropical location is M. ulcerans. M. marinum causes inflammatory nodules following injury in an aquatic environment. M. chelonei is a rapidly growing organism most commonly found in soil, water, dust and animals which presents as single/multiple erythematous SC nodules on an extremity or following a surgical procedure. M. kansasii rarely causes skin lesions. L. donovani is a causse of visceral leishmaniasis in India and Kenya (kala-azar).

question: A 64-year-old woman presents with lichenified keratotic plaques on the bilateral lower extremities. Biopsy reveals suppurative inflammation and collagen extending from the dermis through the epidermis. Which is the most likely associated systemic disease:
explanation: Chronic kidney disease is associated with perforating disorders. These disorder are characterized by pruritus and a biopsy revealing collagen and inflammatory cells broaching the epidermis. The other disorders are not closely associated with perforating diseases.

question: Patients with a type I reaction to latex may have cross-reactions with which of the following foods?
explanation: Latex allergy is a TH2 form of contact sensitivity that is IGE mediated. Using the old Gel and Coombs classification, it was classified as type I hypersensitivity. Foods that contain cross-reactive allergens to latex include, banana, kiwi, avocado, chestnut, papaya, white potato and tomato.

question: Apocrine hidrocystoma may be associated with which of the following syndromes?
explanation: Schopf-Schulz-Passarge is a syndrome of ectodermal dysplasia which presents with keratosis palmoplantaris with hypodontia, hypotrichosis, and cysts of the eyelids.

question: You are evaluating an 8-year-old female patient. On exam you note short stature, a narrow face with a bird-like nose, and photosensitivity that is followed by telangiectatic erythema in a malar distribution. You find that a RECQL3 was identified by a genetics consult. What monitoring is most important for this patient?
explanation: The clinical picture and RECQL3 mutation support a diagnosis of Bloom syndrome. Although many organ systems are affected, these patients have 150-300x increased risk of lymphoma/leukemia and are likely to pass away from malignancy.

question: Mutations in which of the following receptors are most likely to be associated with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis?
explanation: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis disease (CMCD) is characterized by recurrent or persistent infections of the skin, nails, and oral and genital mucosae caused by Candida albicans and, to a lesser extent, Staphylococcus aureus, in patients with no other infectious or autoimmune manifestations. Mutations in IL-17 receptor A (IL-17RA, autosomal recessive) and IL-17 receptor F (IL-17F, autosomal dominant) have been reported. IL-17RA deficiency is complete, abolishing cellular responses to IL-17A and IL-17F homodimers and heterodimers. By contrast, IL-17F deficiency is partial, with mutant IL-17F-containing homodimers and heterodimers displaying impaired, but not abolished, activity.

question: Patients with this HLA type, which has the most definitive association with psoriasis, have a relative risk of having psoriasis that is 9-15 times normal.
explanation: HLA-Cw6 is the HLA type most definitively associated with psoriasis. It carries a relative risk 9-15 times normal.

question: A middle-aged female presents with purplish pruritic plaques on her dorsal wrist and whitish plaques on her buccal mucosa. A diagnosis of lichen planus is made. Which type of lichen planus is most strongly associated with Hepatitis C virus infection?
explanation: Lichen planus presents a wide variety of cutaneous morphologies that share common histologic findings of a lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate, basal vacuolization, and dyskeratotic keratinocytes. The form of lichen planus most strongly associated with Hepatitis C virus infection is mucosal ulcerative lichen planus.

question: Median rhomboid glossitis is most likely associated with which of the following organisms?
explanation: Median rhomboid glossitis is most likely associated with Candida albicans. Candida can also cause angular cheilitis, chronic paronychia, erosio interdigitale blastomycetica, and vulvovaginitis.

question: Which of the following is most common location of an angioleiomyoma?
explanation: Angioleiomyomas are benign tumors that originate from smooth muscle in vascular structures and are difficult to definitively diagnose clinically. Although these lesions are rarely encountered in the foot, the lower extremity is the most common site of occurrence. An angioleiomyoma typically manifests as a small, painful, solitary, mobile lesion. Owing to the ambiguous nature of the clinical findings, angioleiomyoma should be included in the differential diagnosis of lower-extremity tumors.

question: Which of the following statements regarding candidal infection is FALSE?

choices.A: Candida albicans is the number one cause of mucocutaneous infections
choices.B: Candida species may be associated with granuloma gluteale infantum
choices.C: Candidal infections typically do not spare the scrotum
choices.D: Predisposing factors for candidal infection include diabetes mellitus, hyperhidrosis and broad spectrum antibiotics
choices.E: Candida species displays true hyphae on potassium hydroxide examination

correct_text: Candida species displays true hyphae on potassium hydroxide examination
explanation: Candida species are part of the resident flora but they are also the most common cause of opportunistic mycotic infection. Cutaneous clinical manifestations include thrush, perleche, paronychia, onychomycosis, intertrigo, and folliculitis. Candida albicans is the most common organism; however, C. dubliniensis is often implicated in mucosal disease in AIDS patients. C. parapsilosis causes chronic paronychia and C. glabrata is fluconazole resistant. Infection is most common in the extreme of age, and the mucosal disease is prevalent in HIV patients. Factors predisposing patients to infection include impaired mucocutaneous barrier function, immunodeficiencies, broad spectrum antibiotic use, malignancies, heat, humidity, friction, diabetes, and indwelling catheters. Groin infections often involve the scrotum unlike tinea cruris caused by dermatophytes. Predisposing factors for granuloma gluteale infantum include occlusion, topical corticosteroids, and possibly Candida diaper dermatitis.

question: Which medication is not associated with the condition depicted in the image?
explanation: The image shows Acanthosis nigricans. The following medications have been shown to be associated with this condition: testosterone, oral contraceptives, glucocorticoids, niacin, protease inhibitors, aripiprazole, and palifermin.

question: A 40-year-old patient presents with a rash on his hands, as shown. It has developed in the past 6 months and is gradually becoming more severe. He describes intense pruritus. The patient is a construction worker, working primarily with concrete. He was prescribed clobetasol ointment, which provides some relief but does not clear the rash. He notes that he recently took a week- long vacation at a resort in the Dominican Republic, and notes that his hands had improved at the end of the vacation, but flared again after he returned. Which of the following is most likely allergen to react on patch testing?
explanation: The questions describes a case of allergic contact dermatitis due to occupational exposure to potassium dichromate, also known as chromium, in wet cement. This allergen is present in wet cement as well as leather, such as leather gloves.

question: What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
explanation: The condition depicted is lichen sclerosus et atrophicus (LSetA) which most commonly affects the genital region. High potency topical steroids are the treatment of choice.

question: This 32-year-old man has two sisters each with melanoma, and his father died from metastatic pancreatic cancer. You suspect a germline mutation in which of the following genes?
explanation: Malignant melanoma is considered the most lethal skin cancer if it is not detected and treated during its early stages. About 10% of melanoma patients report a family history of melanoma; however, individuals with features of true hereditary melanoma (ie, unilateral lineage, multigenerational, multiple primary lesions, and early onset of disease) are in fact quite rare. Although many new loci have been implicated in hereditary melanoma, CDKN2A mutations remain the most common. Familial melanoma in the presence of multiple atypical nevi should raise suspicion for a germline CDKN2A mutation. These patients have a high risk of developing multiple primary melanomas and internal organ malignancies, especially pancreatic cancer; therefore, a multidisciplinary approach is necessary in many cases. The value of dermoscopic examination and total body photography performed at regular intervals has been suggested by a number of studies, and should therefore be considered for these patients and their first-degree relatives. In addition, genetic counseling with the possibility of testing can be a valuable adjunct for familial melanoma patients. This must be performed with care, however, and only by qualified individuals trained in cancer risk analysis.

incorrect_rationales.D:
PTCH

?. MITF

question: Frontal bossing, saddle nose, hypoplastic midface, peg shaped or conical teeth and hypopigmented short sparse scalp and body hair are prominent features of which of the following?
explanation: Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome also known as hypohidrotic ectodermal dysphasia or anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is an X-linked recessive disorder that presents in infancy to early childhood. Features include hypo-anhidrosis with increased body temperature, hypopigmented sparse scalp and body hair, frontal bossing, saddle nose, hypoplastic midface, abnormal ears, hypo-anodontia, and increased bronchopulmonary inections.

question: Which of the following is the most common treatment for sporotrichosis?
explanation: Sporotrichosis (also known as “rose gardener’s disease”) is an infection caused by the fungus Sporothrix schenckii. Cutaneous (skin) infection is the most common form of the infection. It occurs when the fungus enters the skin through a small cut or scrape, usually after someone touches contaminated plant matter. Skin on the hands or arms is most commonly affected. The first symptom of cutaneous sporotrichosis is usually a small, painless papule that can develop any time from 1 to 12 weeks after exposure to the fungus. The papule can be red, pink, or purple, and it usually appears on the finger, hand, or arm where the fungus has entered through a break in the skin. The papule will eventually grow larger and may look like an erosion or ulcer that is very slow to heal. Additional papules or ulcers may appear later near the original one. The most common treatment for this type of sporotrichosis is itraconazole, taken by mouth for 3 to 6 months.

question: Pseudo-pili annulati with light reflection off periodic flattening of the hair shaft is seen in:
explanation: Pseudo pili annulati is seen in blond hair, due to the light reflection off the periodic flattening of the hair shaft. Pili annulati is the alternating of light and dark bands, secondary to air spaces, seen in normal light as opposed to "tiger-tail" hair in trichothiodystrophy, seen only under polarized light.

question: What is the best treatment for this condition?
explanation: This is melasma and the best treatment option is aggressive photoprotection with hats and sunscreen. Hydroquinone may work if it is only epidermal melasma. Melasma is made worse by any irritation of the skin therefore aggressive procedures and treatments are typically not recommended.

question: Tinea imbricata is most frequently caused by:
explanation: Tinea imbricata or Tokelau, an unusual type of tinea corporis causing polycyclic scaly lesions, is endemic in the South Pacific Islands, Far East and C. & S. America. The etiology is usually infection caused by Trichophyton concentricum.

question: Keratins 1 and 10 are important intermediate filaments in suprabasal keratinocytes. Genetic mutation of these keratins can lead to which of the following disorders?
explanation: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (also known as bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma) is caused by a genetic mutation in keratins 1 and 10.

question: What is the treatment of choice for porphyria cutanea tarda?
explanation: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Phlebotomy is the treatment of choice and may improve enzymatic activity by removing iron, an inhibitor of the enzyme. Antimalarials and erythropoietin are alternative therapies. Oral iron supplementation may worsen PCT. Naproxen is a common cause of pseudoporphyria.

question: What range of ultraviolet radiation has been shown to be most efficient in inducing neoplasia in mice?
explanation: Midrange UVR 280-320nm (UVB range) has been shown to be most efficient in inducing neoplasia in mice. Long-wave UVA, when added to UVB may accelerate carcinogenesis.

question: The patient has the findings shown localized to the head and neck. What is his risk of developing systemic complications?
explanation: This patient has discoid lupus, which can present with atrophy, scarring, dyspigmentation, and telangiectasias. Localized variants of DLE typically occur on the head and neck & carry a 5% risk of systemic involvement.

question: The genetic predisposition for patients with pemphigus vulgaris is:
explanation: Patients with HLA-DRQ402, HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRw6 can be predisposed to the development of pemphigus vulgaris. Pemphigus vulgaris is a severe potentially fatal disease with blister formation on the skin and the mucosa

question: A 17 year old high school cheerleader returns to clinic for follow up of her acne and management of her isotretinoin. She denies depression or any GI complications. She is pleased with her progress but does mention painful red bumps on her lower legs for 1 week. She attributes these to her cheer practice. What is the most likely cause of her lower extremity lesions?
explanation: The patient is likely experiencing erythema nodosum (EN), a delayed hypersensitivity response to a wide variety of eliciting factors. They consist of an eruption of erythematous, tender nodules, typically over the anterior tibial areas. Common causes include oral contraceptives, which is a probable choice given that the patient is likely taking them as part of her isotretinoin treatment.

question: A 42-year-old female with keratosis follicularis has a severe disease flare after starting a new medication. She has a history of epilepsy, bipolar disorder and gout. What is the most likely new treatment that induced the flare?
explanation: Keratosis follicularis (or Dariers disease) is known to worsen with initiation of certain medications including lithium.

question: The portion of the electromagnetic spectrum that produces a particular biologic effect is known as the:
explanation: The action spectrum is the portion of the electromagnetic spectrum that products a particular biologic effect (e.g. erythema, delayed tanning).

question: Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: This is erythema infectiosum, shown with the characteristic "slapped cheek" appearance, caused by parvovirus B19.

question: A 42-year-old man presents with milky white macules and patches in his periorbital area surrounded by normal skin. The lesions have discrete margins and are irregular in shape. On Wood’s lamp examination, the contrast between the affected areas and the surrounding skin is striking. Which of the following statements is not true in this condition?

choices.A: The epidermal melanocyte density can be assessed via incubation of biopsy specimens with dihydroxyphenylalanine
choices.B: Segmental vitiligo is significantly increased in adults compared to children
choices.C: Vitiligo vulgaris is the most common clinical type of vitiligo observed in children
choices.D: In lesions of vitiligo, melanocytes are typically absent or present in small numbers
choices.E: The epidermal melanocyte density can be assessed with Melan-A, MITF, and HMB-45

correct_text: Segmental vitiligo is significantly increased in adults compared to children
explanation: Segmental vitiligo is significantly increased in children compared to adults. Although vitiligo vulgaris is the most common clinical type observed in children, the frequency of segmental vitiligo (~15–30%) is significantly increased compared to that in adults (<5–10%). The incidence of associated endocrinopathies is less than in the adult vitiligo population. A family history of vitiligo is associated with an earlier age of onset.

question: Which of the following ethnic groups are commonly diagnosed with dermatosis papulosa nigra?
explanation: Characterized by the presence of multiple, small, hyperpigmented, sessile SKs on the face, DPN is typically diagnosed on the African-American and Hispanic population.

question: A patient with a stage III melanoma is being treated with Vemurafenib monotherapy. The patient presents for a full body skin examination. A lesion suspicious for a squamous cell carcinoma is biopsed. Which of the following gene mutations is most common in this lesion?
explanation: In contrast to spontaneous SCCs (where RAS mutations are relatively uncommon), most BRAFi-associated SCCs have a RAS mutation (60%). Vemurafenib and Dabrafenib are BRAF inhibitors. Up to 30% of patients on BRAFi monotherapy develop SCCs and keratoacanthomas due to paradoxical activation of MAPK when keratinocytes are exposed to BRAF inhibitors. Adding a MEK inhibitor to the BRAF inhibitors decreases this risk.

question: A 21 year old college student returning back to school from a spring break trip presents with 12 days of headache, fever, and a skin lesion with annular erythema on her upper back measuring 15 cm in diameter. This multi-system disease is most likely caused by?
explanation: Lyme disease is a multisystem disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi that is transmitted to humans by ticks of the genus Ixodes. Patients present with variable constitutional symptoms including headache, fever, malaise, and arthralgias. 75% of patients develop erythema chronicum migrans that begins as an erythematous papule that can progress to an annular erythema reaching 20 cm or more in size.

question: A six year old girl presents after being sent home from school for "lice". On examination, there are structures on the hair which are freely slide along the hair shaft. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hair casts present most commonly in young girls between the age of 2 and 8 years old. These casts are freely sliding along the hair shaft and are not adherent.

question: Which of the following is a fluorescent ectothrix dermatophyte?
explanation: Fluorescent ectothrix dermatophytes include M. canis, M. audouinii, M. distortum, M. ferrugineum, and sometimes M. gypseum and T. schoenleinii (sometimes, T.Schoenleinii is endothrix and ectothrix) ("Cats And Dogs Fight and Growl Sometimes.")

question: Which of the following immunosuppressive agents has been most effective in cicatricial pemphigoid?
explanation: Cicatricial pemphigoid is a heterogeneous group of subepithelial blistering diseases involving the mucous membranes and skin. The treatment of cictracial pemphigoid is predicated upon the extent, severity, and location of disease. Most regimens used are empiric and are based on clinical experience. With severe ocular involvement, most experts recommend aggressive treatment with the combination of cyclophosphamide and steroids.

question: Which of the following features is not associated with Cornelia de Lange Syndrome?

choices.E: Characteristic facies with downturned mouth, hirsutism, synophrys, trichomegaly, anteverted nostrils, long philtrum and low set ears

explanation: Children with Cornelia de Lange are usually severley mentally retarded with an IQ <35.

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with the following findings on exam. After a thorough history, physical, and family history evaluation to confirm the syndrome, which of the following is the most appropriate screening exam to refer the patient to?

choices.D: No additional screening at this time

explanation: This photo depicts numerous neurofibromas, consistent with a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis. Many malignancies have now been associated with neurofibromatosis, but in a 35-year-old female, consideration must be given to breast cancer. Women with NF-1 <50 years of age have up to 5x increased risk of developing breast cancer compared with the general population. Due to this increased risk, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommends annual breast MRI from age 25 in patients with NF1.

question: Christ-Siemens-Touraine Syndrome is most commonly linked with defects in which of the following genes?
explanation: Ectodysplasin (EDA) on Xq12-q13 is transmitted in an X-linked recessive fashion and is the most common cause of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (aka Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome or anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia).

question: Which eye findings would be expected in an individual with this disorder associated with atherosclerosis?
explanation: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is an autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutation in ABCC6 (adenosine triphosphate-binding cassette subfamily C member 6). Associated findings include gastric artery hemorrhage, angioid streaks, retinal hemorrhage, atherosclerotic disease, and a possible increased risk of first-trimester miscarriage.

question: Which paraprotein is found most commonly in patients with pyoderma gangrenosum?
explanation: IgA paraproteinemia has been reported in over 10-18% of pyoderma gangrenosum.

question: Biopsy reveals absence of follicles, a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, and dermal fibrosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp (EPDS) is a rare, inflammatory, and chronic slow-onset disease that causes scarring alopecia and mainly affects the scalp of older men. Clinical diagnosis can be challenging since it mimics more common diseases and due to its nonspecific clinical features. Different histologic findings can be seen depending on the stage of disease, with EPDS potentially being characterized by an atrophic epidermis and chronic inflammation consisting of lymphocytes, neutrophils, and occasional foreign body giant cells. Dermoscopy (or trichoscopy) has been recently reported as a useful aid for the diagnosis, as it shows absent follicular ostia with marked skin atrophy, with consequent visualization of dermal vessels, although histology is mandatory for the final diagnosis.

question: Which of the following is not a formaldehyde-releasing preservative?
explanation: Methylchloroisothiazinolone, also known as Kathon CG, is the only non-formaldehyde releasing preservative. It is found in cosmetics, skin/hair products, "acid" permanent waves, soaps, latex emulsions, and biocides.

question: All of the following plants commonly cause a phytophotodermatitis except:
explanation: Ananas comosus (pineapple) commonly produces irritant contact dermatitis as it contains both bromelin and calcium oxalate. It is not known to cause phytophotodermatitis.

question: On cutaneous exam, angiokeratoma corporis diffusum is characteristic of which of the following conditions?

choices.A: None of these options are correct
choices.E: All of these options are correct

correct_text: All of these options are correct
explanation: Findings of angiokeratoma corporis diffusum are found in all three listed conditions. They cannot by distinguished by skin exam. Angiokeratomas are one of the earliest signs of Fabry disease, typically beginning to appear during childhood or adolescence. They develop in most male patients and ~30% of female heterozygotes. Angiokeratomas present as punctate, dark-red to blue–black macules or papules. The lesions do not blanch with pressure and may become slightly keratotic as they enlarge. The angiokeratomas of Fabry disease, referred to as angiokeratoma corporis diffusum, tend to be concentrated between the umbilicus and the knees but can develop at any cutaneous site; oral and conjunctival lesions are also seen. Less frequent vascular findings include linear telangiectasias favoring the face, lips, and oral mucosa; episodic acral vasospasm resembling Raynaud phenomenon, typically accompanied by pain and paresthesias; and peripheral edema and lymphedema. Hypohidrosis is an early and almost constant feature of Fabry disease that can result in heat intolerance. Decreased body hair has also been described.

question: Which of the following is the most useful morphologic feature in identifying the mycelial phase of Histoplasma capsulatum?

choices.B: Microconidia laterally along the hyphae strand
choices.D: Small oval conidia on long thin conidiophores

explanation: On artificial media the mold form of Histoplasmosis produces hyphae with tear drop microconidia and round thick wall tuberculate macroconidia.

question: A 70-year-old female develops green-black to green-blue discoloration of her great toenail. She works as a janitor at a seaquarium and thinks she may have developed the discoloration due to frequent and prolonged exposure to water. Which of the following is not a treatment option for green nail syndrome (chloronychia)?

choices.D: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID x 2 weeks

explanation: Avoidance of bleach is not recommended as a treatment option for green nail syndrome. In green nail syndrome (chloronychia), the nail develops green–black to green–blue discoloration due to pyocyanin, a blue–green pigment produced by P. aeruginosa. Predisposing factors include frequent or prolonged exposure to water, excessive use of detergents and soaps, nail trauma and other causes of onycholysis. The diagnosis of green nail syndrome is usually clinical; if necessary, it can be confirmed by Gram stain and culture of exudate and nail fragments. The differential diagnosis includes a subungual hematoma, melanocytic nevus, melanoma, and Aspergillus infection. Treatment involves avoidance of predisposing factors, clipping the nail, and topical application of 2% sodium hypochlorite (household bleach diluted 1:4), a quinolone, or aminoglycoside (e.g. tobramycin) solution for 1–4 months. In refractory cases, removal of the affected nail may be required. file:///tmp/Quiz_Questions_1778874819.html Page 492 of 1,559

question: An 11-year-old boy presents with numerous venous malformations, on the left side of his body, especially on his hands and feet. Radiographs reveal cystic structures in his bones that are consistent with enchondromas. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
explanation: This case scenario describes Maffucci syndrome, also known as enchondromas with multiple angiomas. Maffucci syndrome is a sporadic congenital disorder. Maffucci syndrome is characterized by venous malformations in early infancy, seen on hands and feet, and enchondromas due to dyschondroplasia, a developmental abnormality in cartilage formation. Somatic mosaic mutations of isocitrate dehydrogenase( IDH1 and IDH2 )have been associated with Maffucci syndrome. Maffucci syndrome results in bone fractures secondary to nonossification, and 50% of patients are at risk of chondrosarcoma (which occurs within enchondromas).

question: This is found in both desmosomes and adherens junctions:
explanation: Plakoglobin is a plaque protein of the armadillo family that is found in desmosomes; it can also substitute for beta-catenin in adherens junctions. Plakoglobin co-precipitates with desmogleins. It is 85 kDa.

question: A 34-year-old man with no past medical conditions presents with lesions as shown. Of the following, what is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: Ecthyma is a deep or ulcerative type of pyoderma commonly seen on the lower extremities and buttocks and is caused most often by group A beta-hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. Ecthyma can present as small punched-out ulcers or a deep-spreading ulcerative process. The disorder begins in the same manner as impetigo, often following infected insect bites or minor trauma, but penetrates through the epidermis to produce a shallow ulcer. The initial lesion is a vesiculopustule with an erythematous base and firmly adherent crust. Removal of the crust reveals a lesion deeper than that seen in impetigo, with an underlying saucer-shaped ulcer and raised margin. The lesions are painful and heal slowly over a few weeks, often with scar formation.

question: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis is caused by which human papilloma virus (HPV) types?
explanation: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis is caused by HPV types 5, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 17, 19-26.

question: Which disorder does the image indicate?
explanation: This photo depicts blue lunulae which is characteristic of Wilson's disease. This is an autosomal recessive condition due to a disorder in the ATP7B gene, which encodes an ATPase copper-transporting polypeptide. It leads to copper accumulation in the liver.

question: You are managing an 80-year-old man with mycosis fungoides. He has slowly advanced and after being lost to follow-up for almost a year, now has the disease over 80% of his body surface area and has a firm lymph node on his left axilla. He reports discomfort from his pruritis. What is the best next treatment?
explanation: This patient has Stage 3 MF, extracorporeal photopheresis is the recommended first-line for patients with this severity of disease.

question: An internal hordeolum can be painful and erythematous. It is an infection of the Meibomian glands and is most commonly caused by:
explanation: Internal hordeolum are a secondary infection of the Meibomian gland in the tarsal plate. The infectious agent is Staphylococcus aureus in 90- 95% of cases.

question: A 56-year-old male with HIV presents with multiple umbilicated brown papules on the face. Which of the following is the LEAST likely cause of his lesions?
explanation: This patient has molluscum-like lesions on the face in the setting of immunosuppression. The differential for such papules includes cryptococcus, histoplasmosis, coccidiomycosis, and penicilliosis. Blastomycosis can cause sporotrichoid lesions, warty vegetations, papillomatous proliferations, and osteomyelitis; it usually does not produce molluscum-type papules.

question: A 48-year-old man with hepatitis C infection developed the shown rash on his lower extremities, which progressed over the last 6 weeks across the entire lower extremity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in establishing the diagnosis?

choices.B: Potassium hydroxide preparation of skin scrapings

explanation: The image shown with a petechial rash on the lower extremities is most consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis. As such, the most appropriate next step is a skin biopsy.

question: Malignancies of which of the following organs is most associated with the presence of hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita?
explanation: Hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita is the abrupt onset of downy, soft, non-pigmented hair on the face, trunk, and extremities. It may have associated glossitis. It is most often associated with underlying lung carcinoma or colon adenocarcinoma. It may resolve with treatment of the underlying malignancy.

question: Herpangina is caused by which of the following?
explanation: Herpangina, typically presenting with high fever and oral vesicles, is usually caused by Group A coxsackievirus.

question: What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Granuloma annulare is a benign condition characterized by annular dermal plaques. They are often pink to skin-colored. High potency topical or intralesional steroids may be used, though often observation and reassurance is the treatment of choice.

question: Which of the following methods of direct microscopic examination is chitin specific?
explanation: Chlorazol black E is chitin specific.

question: The gene defect in LEOPARD syndrome is:
explanation: PTPN11 gene is mutated in LEOPARD syndrome. This syndrome consists of the complex of Lentigines, EKG abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormal genitalia, Retardation of growth and Deafness.

question: A skin biopsy of a rash in a patient with known HIV infection reveals a predominantly dermal eosinophilic infiltrate that is most prominent around hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Blood tests show a mild elevation in eosinophils and immunoglobulin-E with reduced IgG and IgA levels. What is the most effective treatment given this patient's diagnosis?
explanation: Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis is a recurrent skin disorder of unknown cause but has been associated with HIV. It is also known as eosinophilic folliculitis and Ofuji disease. Skin biopsies of this disorder demonstrate eosinophils around hair follicles. In patients with HIV, eosinophilic pustular folliculitis is likely to improve or resolve with HAART (Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Treatment), as CD4 cell counts rise above 250/mm3. Adjunctive treatments that may be effective include: Indomethacin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are reported effective in up to 70% of cases of eosinophilic folliculitis Dapsone Tetracycline antibiotics Other antimicrobials including metronidazole Phototherapy Topical steroids Calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus ointment Oral antihistamines such as ceterizine Colchicine Itraconazole Permethrin cream Nicotine patches Isotretinoin and acitretin

question: Which of the following is the vector of lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti?
explanation: Lymphatic filariasis is spread by mosquitoes belonging to genera Aedes, Anopheles, Culex, or Mansonia.

question: Bullous diabeticorum typically presents on the:
explanation: Bullous diabetocorum presents as tense blisters on the legs. They are typically non-inflammatory and appear suddenly.

question: Which of the following statements about the spectrums of UVR that cause of solar urticaria is MOST correct?

choices.A: Both UVA and UVB cause solar urticaria
choices.D: Patients can react to visible light, UVA and/or UVB

correct_text: Patients can react to visible light, UVA and/or UVB
explanation: Some patients react with wheals to either visible light or UVA or UVB. Others react to both UVA and visible radiation. Some react to both UVB and UVA, and some patients react to UVB, UVA and visible light.

question: Chloroma is a characteristic cutaneous manifestation of:
explanation: Chloromas, also termed granulocytic sarcomas, are a localized tumor composed of immature granulocytic cells. They frequently have a greenish coloration due to the presence of myeloperoxidase and most commonly affect the bone. The condition most often occurs in patients with acute leukemia of the myeloid type.

question: A patient recently had pharyngitis and now has an eruption of guttate psoriasis. Which of the following tests would be helpful in determining that this patient had a Streptococcal infection?
explanation: The DNAse B, hyaluronidase or streptolysin O (ASLO) antibodies in serum can be helpful for confirming streptococcal infection in situations where streptococci cannot be isolated.

question: A patient comes to the office for a rash on the face consisting of persistent centrofacial erythema and scattered papules and pustules. A biopsy of the rash is performed. Which of the following medications should be prescribed to specifically address the findings seen in the biopsy below?
explanation: Topical ivermectin. The organism is a Demodex mite. Demodex mites (folliculorum and brevis) are normally present on the face as commensal microbes, but in rosacea, greater numbers of these mites are detected by skin surface biopsy techniques. In routine histologic sections, the mites often appear prominently within pilosebaceous follicles and follicular infestation with multiple mites can be associated with an intense perifollicular infiltrate of predominantly CD4 helper T cells. Antigenic proteins from a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from Demodex mites can stimulate inflammation in patients with papulopustular rosacea. It has been suggested that Demodex mites and their associated bacteria upregulate local proteases, thereby potentiating dysregulation of the cutaneous innate immune response.

question: A pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with nonpruritic erythematous plaques and pustules in the intertriginous regions, the trunk, and the extremities as well as systemic symptoms of malaise and fever. Which complication is most associated with this condition?

choices.B: No risk to fetus or mother

explanation: This patient has pustular psoriasis of pregnancy which is also called "impetigo herpetiformis." It is characterized by red plaques with a peripheral ring of pustules that are distributed symmetrically in flexural areas and trunk and extremities. Patients can have elevated ESR and leukocytosis as well as hypocalcemia. There is a risk of fetal morbidity and mortality secondary to placental insufficiency and maternal mortality secondary to cardiac or renal failure. Premature labor may be associated with cholestasis or pregnancy. Patients with herpes gestationis may have a risk of premature labor and small for gestational age. Microcephaly may occur with isotretinoin taken during pregnancy.

question: The combination of painful palmoplantar keratoderma and pseudoherpetic keratitis is characteristic of which of the following syndromes?
explanation: Richner-Hanhart syndrome (hereditary tyrosenemia type II) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency in hepatic tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT gene), the first enzyme in the tyrosine degradation pathway. As a result, plasma tyrosine and its metabolites are elevated. This disease is characterized by painful PPK and pseudoherpetic keratitis or ulcers, which can result in blindness. Treatment is low-tyrosine/phenylalanine diet; this approach can result in resolution of the skin and eye lesions.

question: A 30-year-old male with a history of unprotected sex with multiple male partners presents to your clinic with a truncal erythematous eruption and malaise for 1 week. Human immunodeficiency virus antibody and viral load were negative. Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay was positive and rapid plasma reagin test was positive at 1:128 titer. Cranial nerve examination findings were unremarkable. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed uveitis. What is the next best step in management

choices.B: Start intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units weekly for 3 weeks
choices.C: Start intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units in a single dose
choices.D: Perform lumbar puncture and CSF examination
choices.E: Start prednisone 1 mg/kg daily for 2 weeks

correct_text: Perform lumbar puncture and CSF examination
explanation: Syphilitic uveitis or other ocular manifestations can be associated with neurosyphilis. Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid examination should be performed when ocular syphilis is suspected, even in the absence of clinical neurologic findings. The majority of cases of ocular syphilis have been among HIV-infected men who have sex with men; a few cases have occurred among HIV-uninfected persons including heterosexual men and women. Clinical recognition is important to avoid sequalae such as blindness. Treatment of ocular syphilis is similar to that of neurosyphilis and requires intravenous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days.

question: A 60-year-old patient develops a green-black to green-blue discoloration of one of her toenails. You suspect she may have green nail syndrome. Which of the following is not a predisposing factor to the development of green nail syndrome?

choices.B: frequent and prolonged exposure to water

explanation: In green nail syndrome (chloronychia), the nail develops green–black to green–blue discoloration due to pyocyanin, a blue–green pigment produced by P. aeruginosa. Predisposing factors include frequent or prolonged exposure to water, excessive use of detergents and soaps, nail trauma and other causes of onycholysis. The diagnosis of green nail syndrome is usually clinical; if necessary, it can be confirmed by Gram stain and culture of exudate and nail fragments. The differential diagnosis includes a subungual hematoma, melanocytic nevus, melanoma, and Aspergillus infection.

question: A 50 year-old female patient presents with a red-brown indurated plaque located on her right clavicular area (see image). The biopsy shows the presence of monomorphic spindle cells in a storiform pattern, and deep subcutaneous infiltration. According to the aforementioned information, the most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: DFSP intially arises as an asymptomatic, red-brown or skin colored indurated plaque, which may later enlarge, and become raised, firm and multinodular. DFSP is histologically characterized by the presence of monomorphic spindle cells arranged in a "storiform" or "cartwheel" pattern.

question: A patient develops herpes zoster in the V1 distribution. A few days after development of the classic vesicular rash, her family brings her to the emergency room because of new onset seizures. She had been complaining of confusion, headache, fatigue, and loss of appetite prior to the convulsions. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: The question stem describes signs and symptoms of hyponatremia. The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is a known, albeit rare, complication of varicella-zoster virus infection. The other four answer choices are also known complications of varicella-zoster virus infection, but do not cause the disease presentation as described.

question: Reactive arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease similar to psoriasis with arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. Which of the following is the most common cause of the urethral form of reactive arthritis?
explanation: Reactive arthritis classically presents with the triad of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis. It occurs most commonly in young men with the HLA-B27 genotype. Among the genitourinary infections associated with reactive arthritis, Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common. Ureaplasma urealyticum is also a possible cause, though it is less common than C. trachomatis. Enteric infections caused by Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter are also possible triggers.

question: Necrosis may be seen in which of the following:
explanation: Necrosis may be seen in severe acute irritant reactions such as chemical burns.

question: What is the risk of transmission of HSV from active cervical lesions when a C-section is performed?
explanation: When a C-section is performed in the setting of active cervical lesions of HSV, the risk of maternal-fetal transmission is decreased to 1%. If a child were delivered vaginally in such a setting, the risk of transmission is approximately 8%.

question: Which one of the following can develop into squamous cell skin cancer over time?
explanation: Actinic keratosis can develop into squamous cell skin cancer, thus it is a pre-cancerous lesion.

question: Which of the following dermatophytes causes endothrix tinea capitis?
explanation: T. tonsurans, T. violaceum, T. soudanense, T. gourvilli, T. yaoundei, and occasionally T. rubrum cause an endothrix pattern. T. schoenleinii causes favus in which hyphae and air spaces are seen in the hair shaft. A bluish-white fluorescence pattern is seen with Wood’s lamp. Clinically, patients have thick yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula); scarring and secondary infection may result. M. canis, M. audouinii, M. ferruginosum, M. distortium display a yellow fluorescence on Wood’s lamp examination.

question: This lesion is hypoesthetic and is associated with which of the following:
explanation: The lesion is high immune or tuberculoid leprosy, which is associated with Th1 cytokines including IFN-gamma, IL2, IL12, IL15, IL18 and IL23.

question: A patient is referred for these findings. Which study is the most appropriate in this setting?
explanation: This kodachrome is of blue lunulae, which can occur with zidovudine, silver, or Wilson’s disease. The test for Wilson’s disease would be decreased ceruloplasmin. It is caused by an autosomal recessive ATP7B gene defect (copper-transporting ATPase). It causes an accumulation of copper, resulting in blue lunulae, Kayser-Fleishcher rings, neurologic sequelae, and liver failure.

question: A 66-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for painful oral erosion and eroded plaques on the body. He has recently had unintentional weight loss of 10 pounds. Biopsy for routine histology reveals intraepidermal blister formation and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate in the superficial dermis. What is the pattern noted on direct immunofluorescence testing in this patient?

choices.A: Homogeneous staining of blood vessel walls and the dermal-epidermal junction with IgG
choices.B: Basement membrane zone staining with C3 and/or IgG
choices.D: Both intercellular and basement membrane staining with C3 and/or IgG
choices.E: Intercellular staining with C3 and/or IgG

correct_text: Both intercellular and basement membrane staining with C3 and/or IgG
explanation: This patient has paraneoplastic pemphigus, an autoimmune blistering disorder commonly linked to non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Oral blisters, erosions, and ulcerations may be painful and characteristically involve the vermillion lip. Skin lesions occur anywhere on the body and are highly variable in appearance. Histology of paraneoplastic pemphigus characteristically reveals a lichenoid tissue reaction combined with suprabasal acantholysis and clefting. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular and basement membrane staining with C3 and/or IgG.

question: Which of the following statements about blue-gray pigmentation of the lunulae is correct?

choices.A: Can be seen in patients on amiodarone
choices.B: Is a rare side effect of treatment with tricyclic antidepressants
choices.C: Occurs only after many years of treatment with chlorpromazine
choices.E: Can be seen in patients on doxycycline

explanation: Blue-gray pigmentation of the skin, sclera, lunulae, or mucous membranes, can be seen in argyria (prolonged contact with or ingestion of silver salts).

question: Which of the following is an innate antimicrobial peptide expressed by keratinocytes in response to injury or inflammation?
explanation: Human beta-defensin (HBD) and cathelicidins are innate antimicrobial peptides in human skin. HBD-1 is constitutively expressed. HBD-2 (and the cathelicidin LL 37) is expressed in response to skin injury and inflammation.

question: Regarding eruptive xanthomas, which of the following is true?

choices.A: They are most commonly found on the eyelids
choices.C: They occur in the setting of familial hyperlipidemia types I, IV, and V
choices.D: They occur in the setting of familial hyperlipidemia types II and III
choices.E: They are not related to alcohol consumption

correct_text: They occur in the setting of familial hyperlipidemia types I, IV, and V
explanation: Eruptive xanthomas generally occur in patients with triglyceride levels of 2000mg/dl or greater. Associations include poorly-controlled diabetes mellitus, retinoids, estrogens, excessive alcohol consumption (leading to pancreatitis) and familial hyperlipidemias types I, IV and V. Clinically, they appear as crops of firm, non-tender yellowish papules with an erythematous border. Most commonly, they occur on the extensor surfaces, but they can be diffuse. A reduction in triglycerides and/or tight glucose control usually results in a reduction in the number of lesions.

question: A 40-year-old male with HIV (CD4 <200) presents with asymptomatic, slowly enlarging yellow- pink papules and nodules localized to his perianal skin. A skin biopsy is performed, which reveals foamy dermal interstitial histiocytes with characteristic basophilic laminated inclusion bodies. The latter are noted to stain positively with von Kossa, Perls, and PAS stains. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Malakoplakia is a multi-organ inflammatory granulomatous disease that most frequently arises in the setting of immunosuppression. Common sites of involvement include the genitourinary, lung, lymph nodes and bone. Cutaneous involvement is rare, and typically presents as asymptomatic papules, nodules, or plaques. Lesions may have associated erosions or ulcerations, and sinus tracts may be seen. While skin lesions are non-specific, histopathology reveals foamy dermal histiocytes known as von Hansemann cells which contain basophilic granular inclusions. The latter are known as Michaelis-Gutmann bodies and are considered pathognomonic for malakoplakia. Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are comprised of calcium, iron, and phosphate salts, and hence stain positively with von Kossa, Perls, and PAS, respectively. The pathophysiology of malakoplakia is thought to arise from an acquired defect in macrophage activation in response to bacterial infection, most commonly E. coli. Treatment for cutaneous lesions is surgical excision, although recurrence is not uncommon.

question: Which of the following is NOT part of the Carney complex?
explanation: Peg/conical teeth are not part of the Carney complex. This is found in incontinentia pigmenti and anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia.

question: A child presents with macroglossia, exopthalmos and gigantism. He has a history of omphalocele repair and has circular depressions on the rim of the posterior helices. Although this syndrome is most often transmitted in a sporadic manner, 15% of cases have defects in which gene?
explanation: KIP2 can be mutated in 15% of cases of Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome. KIP2 is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor gene which acts as a negative regulator of cell proliferation. These children have an increase risk of Wilms' tumor and organomegaly. In addition to the circular ear depression, they can also have a linear earlobe crease.

question: A patient has cutaneous amyloidosis, parathyroid tumors, pheochromocytoma and medullary carcinoma. The patient also had notalgia paresthetica as a child. The child most likely has:
explanation: This patient has MEN type IIA also known as "Sipple's Syndrome". It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by the RET gene. Work up should include calcitonin, calcium, PTH and urine catecholamines.

question: A 48-year-old man is admitted for fever and malaise and is treated with antibiotics. Approximately 10 days after initiation of antibiotics, the patient’s skin, including the mucous membranes, blisters and desquamates, as shown. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely to prognosticate the patient’s mortality?
