The lesions tend to appear in infancy and childhood and stabilize during adolescence. Mutations in the double-stranded RNA-specific adenosine deaminase gene (ADAR1 or DSRAD) underlie DSH. The ADAR1 protein catalyzes the deamination of adenosine to inosine in double-stranded RNA which is important for alternative splicing or alternations of codons for protein translation. However, the precise mechanism by which these mutations lead to actual disease remain unknown. There are two diseases that are phenoptypically similar to DSH and previously thought to be related. The first is dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH) which is characterized by a mixture of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules that are widespread. DSH can be distinguished from DUH by its localization to the face and distal acral sites. The second disease is acropigmentatio retiticularis (AR, also known as acropigmentation of Kitamura). AR is also characterized by hyperpigmentated macules on the dorsal hands and feet as well as palmar pits. However, in contrast to DSH, it is notably devoid of hypopigmented macules. Suzuki et al. sequenced 20 cases of patients presenting with DSH, DUH, and AR. All patients with DSH demonstrated mutations in ADAR1, however, none of the patients with DUH or AR demonstrated mutations. Based on these studies, they proposed that these diseases are in fact distinct and separate from DSH. There are no effective therapies for DSH. However, it is important to distinguish DSH from other more serious disorders that can present with pigment alterations such as dyskeratosis congenita and xeroderma pigmentosum. Both of these conditions present with photosensitivity and squamous cell carcinomas which are not present in DSH.

question: Refsum syndrome is due to a deficiency in phytanyl coenzyme A hydroxylase. Treatment for this condition is:

choices.A: No treatment is available at this time
choices.C: Diet low in green vegetables, dairy and ruminant fats
choices.E: Diet high in green vegetables, dairy and ruminant fats

correct_text: Diet low in green vegetables, dairy and ruminant fats
explanation: Treatment is with a diet low in green vegetables, dairy and ruminant fats is the treatment of choice for Refsum syndrome.

question: A 45-year-old septic female develops symmetric, large ecchymotic areas with irregular borders on the extremities, ears, and nose. Laboratory testing reveals the patient has disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following is the most common underlying infection associated with this condition?
explanation: Purpura fulminans is an oftentimes dramatic presentation of large ecchymotic areas of the skin, favoring acral sites including the extremities, ears, and nose. The underlying pathophysiology is hemorrhagic infarction of the skin due to disseminated intravascular coagulation. Meningococcal infection is the leading underlying infection associated with sepsis and purpura fulminans. When children develop purpura fulminans after infection, the most common cause is group A Strep.

question: A 26-year-old man presents to the clinic with an 8-mm ulcerated papule on his left forearm. He is a recent refugee from Afghanistan and reports the lesion on his forearm has been present for a few weeks and has only slightly expanded. His past medical history is unremarkable, and there are no other lesions present elsewhere. A biopsy of the lesion is performed, and representative pathology is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the patient’s condition?
explanation: This is a patient with uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis. Recognize the classic “marquee” sign of organisms lining up at the periphery of vacuoles consistent with the history of an ulcerated lesion from an endemic country. As such, the most appropriate treatment is intralesional sodium stibogluconate, of the choices provided. Other therapies can include oral azoles or miltefosine, as well as other antimonial medications.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Keloids are dense overgrowths of fibrous tissue that generally form a response to tissue injury. Lobomycosis and dermatofibromasarcoma protuberans may mimic keloids.

question: Which of the following is more commonly associated with ulcerative colitis as compared to Crohn’s disease?
explanation: Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) may both have gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and cutaneous manifestations. CD lesions can involve any area of the GIT (from the lips to the anus), with patchy disease normally present, whereas UC is limited to the colon and rectum and tends to be continuous. Pyoderma gangrenosum and pyoderma vegetans tend to be more commonly associated with UC.

question: Drug-induced psoriasis can result from steroid withdrawal. Other medications known to cause drug-induced psoriasis are all of the following except:
explanation: Lithium, β-blockers, interferons, ACE inhibitors, and granulocyte-colony stimulating factors have all been known to cause exacerbation of drug-induced psoriasis.

question: This type of verrucous carcinoma is typically on the plantar area and is locally aggressive but rarely metastasizes:
explanation: Epithelioma cuniculatum is a plantar verrucous carcinoma that is locally aggressive but rarely metastasizes.

question: Which area of the face is associated with the highest rate of BCCs?
explanation: The most frequent site of basal cell carcinomas in one study by Heckmann et al. was the base of the nose (bordering the nasolabial fold and extending midway up the side of the nose).

question: What is the inheritance pattern of chronic granulomatous disease?

choices.E: Autosomal recessive and X linked recessive

correct_text: Autosomal recessive and X linked recessive
explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is inherited in an autosomal recessive and x-linked recessive manner. There are mutations 5 mutations total. If the mutation is present in CYBA (a cytochrome subunit), NCF1 & 2 (neutrophil cytosol factors 1 & 2 & 4) it is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The mutation in CYBB is X linked recessive.

question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of Castleman disease returns to the dermatologist with progressively worsening dyspnea of three months duration. Three months prior, she had presented with multiple painful erosions on the buccal mucosa and targetoid plaques and bullae on the dorsal hands and anterior forearms. A biopsy was performed, which showed suprabasilar acantholysis. Direct immunofluorescence showed IgG/C3 deposition in a netlike distribution in the epidermis and in a linear pattern along the dermoepidermal junction, and the patient was initiated on prednisone. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of the patient?
explanation: In this older patient with Castleman disease presenting with bullous disease involving painful oral mucositis and direct immunofluorescence showing findings consistent with paraneoplastic pemphigus who has worsening dyspnea despite treatment with prednisone, consider CT imaging for evaluation of pulmonary involvement of the disease. Many patients with paraneoplastic pemphigus can develop bronchiolitis obliterans, which is a common cause of death as it leads to respiratory failure.

question: What is the most common location of oral SCC?
explanation: Squamous cell carcinomas are the most common carcinoma of the oral cavity. The most common locations for this tumor are the lateral and ventral surfaces of the tongue, and the floor of the mouth.

question: A 70-year-old man with a history of longstanding type 1 diabetes develops restricted mobility of the joints of his hands and presents with stiff, waxy, thickened yellowed skin. This patient may also suffer from which other associated condition?
explanation: Many patients with longstanding type 1 diabetes develop diabetic cheiroarthropathy or diabetic stiff skin (digital sclerosis). This results in restricted mobility of the joints of their hands and stiff, waxy, thickened, and yellowed skin. This is thought to be due to the reaction of glucose with proteins in the skin and increased glycation end products. These patients may also suffer from Dupuytren (contracture tendon tightening, which bends the fingers).

question: A 64-year-old man presents to the office for evaluation of a slow-growing pink nodule lateral to the right eye. A biopsy is performed and is shown. The patient is most likely to need a referral to which of the following specialties for further evaluation?
explanation: The patient’s nodule and its associated pathology are most concerning for a mucinous carcinoma. In patients with mucinous carcinoma, evaluation is necessary to evaluate for a primary lesion, which is often colon cancer. As such, referral to gastroenterology is necessary for the appropriate evaluation of malignancy.

question: A patient comes into the office and states that they have been bitten by a cat. The most common organism to cause infection in the skin in this patient is:
explanation: Cat bite infections are commonly caused by pasteurella multocida. All bites should be treated with augmentin.

question: Patients with this syndrome are at increased risk for developing Lhermite-Duclos disease:
explanation: Patients with Cowden's Syndrome (multiple hamartoma syndrome) are at increased risk for Lhermite Duclos disease (dysplastic gangliocytoma of the cerebellum). They are both associated with a PTEN mutation.

question: A patient from South America develops a recurrent fever after living in crowded conditions with multiple roommates having known human body louse infestation. A diagnosis of louse-born Relapsing Fever is made. Which of the following is the implicated organism?
explanation: Louse-born relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia recurrentis. It is seen in Africa and South America, and is spread by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus). Symptoms include paroxysmal fevers, headache, myalgias, and petechial macules on trunk and extremities. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease; Borrelia duttonii and Borrelia hermsii cause tick-born Relapsing Fever; Streptobacillus moniliformis causes Rat-bite fever.

question: A 65-year-old woman presents with yellow-brown patches with an irregular outline and pinpoint petechiae within patches in successive crops. The lesions are mostly present in the lower legs and began after a long hike. Which of the following pigmented purpuric eruptions is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?

choices.A: Pigmented purpuric lichenoid dermatitis of Gougerot and Blum
choices.D: Eczematid-like purpura of Doucas and Kapetanakis

explanation: Schamberg disease is the most common orm of pigmented purpura. It can occur in children and has a peak frequency in middle-aged to older men. It is characterized by yellow-brown patches with an oval to irregular outline. There are pinpoint peteachiae within patches - likened to cayenne pepper. It occurs in successive crops and favors the lower legs.

question: What is the most common infection that can cause guttate psoriasis?
explanation: Guttate psoriasis refers to a distinctive, acute clinical presentation of an eruption characterized by small, droplike, 1-10 mm in diameter, salmon-pink papules, usually with a fine scale. It is more commonly seen in individuals younger than 30 years with a history of upper respiratory infection that precedes the eruption by 2-3 weeks. The most common organism is group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (eg, Streptococcus pyogenes). Although recurrent episodes may occur, especially those due to pharyngeal carriage of streptococci, isolated bouts are known to occur. Guttae psoriasis may also occur with other infections or in isolation without any identifiable infection.

question: The pictured plant is a member of which family?
explanation: This is a photo of ragweed, a member of the compositae (or asteraceae) family.

question: In the liver, the rate limiting step in the porphyria pathway is mediated by the enzyme:
explanation: ALA synthase mediates the first and rate-limiting step in the heme synthesis pathway. This step occurs in the mitochondria and allows for the conversion of Succinyl coA + glycine to delta aminolevilinic acid.

question: A 11 year-old female patient with hypoparathyroidism is referred to your clinic secondary to chronic mucocutanous candidiasis which is refractory to standard treatments. The patient also has malabsorption and severe chronic diarrhea. You determine that she has autoimmune polyendocrinopathy- candiasis-ectodermal dystrophy syndrome(APECED). Since only two of three major criteria are needed to make this diagnosis, this patient having demonstrated hypoparathyroidism and chronic mucocutanous candidiasis is diagnosed with APECED. What is the third major criteria that would qualify a patient to meet the diagnosis of APECED?
explanation: This patient has APECED, also know as autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1(APS type 1). Two of three major criteria are needed to make this diagnosis - chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison's disease. They usually present within the first 5 years of life with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, then before the age of ten with hypoparathyroidism, and finally in early adulthood with Addison's disease. They often present with chronic diarrhea and malabsorption. Ectodermal dysplasia usually does not present until the fifth decade. Autoimmune skin disease, such as vitiligo and alopecia areata are not uncommon.

question: A patient with scalp psoriasis has recently started a medication which results in increased levels of cyclic AMP which decreases production of TNF, IL-17, IL-23. You inform her that the most common side effect upon initially starting this medication is which of the following?
explanation: Apremilast is a phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor which results in increased levels of cyclic AMP which in turn decreases production of TNF, IL-17, IL-23. It is dosed twice daily and is titrated up over 6 days to a final dose of 30 mg PO twice daily to minimize diarrhea. It is relatively more effective for palmoplantar psoriasis and scalp psoriasis. The most common side effects are GI upset/diarrhea in 20% of cases.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is an image of monilethrix, which upon trichoscopy reveals a beaded appearance of hair due to periodic thinning of the hair shaft.

question: Which of the following hereditary skin disorders is associated with the RAS-ERK-MAPK pathway?
explanation: Skin disorders associated with the RAS-ERK-MAPK pathway include: Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome, Costello, LEOPARD, NF, and Noonan.

question: The most common cause of mortality in patients with limited systemic sclerosis is:
explanation: The most common cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with limited systemic sclerosis is pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary fibrosis is more often associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis. Mortality from renal failure has been significantly reduced by the use of ACE inhibitors.

question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Cockayne syndrome?
explanation: Patients with Cockayne syndrome do not have an increased risk of skin cancer. All the other findings are associated with Cockayne syndrome, as well as photosensitivity, deafness, cataracts, and sunken facies. Increased chromatid exchange is also seen in Bloom syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, and Fanconi's anemia.

question: Herpes-associated erythema multiforme is most commonly associated with which HLA type?
explanation: Recurrent erythema multiforme (EM minor) is usually caused by recurrent herpes simplex, most commonly HSV-1 orolabial disease. This is more correctly now called herpes-associated erythema multiforme (HAEM) and has been more commonly associated with people with HLA type B15.

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a firm, minimally elevated papule that measures 5 mm in diameter and is hyperpigmented. On palpation, the lesion seems attached to subcutaneous tissue. On dermoscopy, a central white scar-like patch surrounded by a delicate pigment network is observed. Which of the following has not been found to be associated with multiple dermatofibromas?
explanation: Melanocytic nevi is not a common cause of multiple dermatofibromas. Although some dermatofibromas are thought to arise at sites of trauma or arthropod bites, their precise etiology is not known. Multiple eruptive dermatofibromas have been observed in patients with autoimmune disorders such as lupus erythematosus and atopic dermatitis and in the setting of immunosuppression (ie, HIV infection). Clinically, dermatofibromas can be confused with cysts or melanocytic nevi, especially those with fibrosis. However, melanocytic nevi are not a common cause of multiple dermatofibromas.

question: Which of the following is true regarding this entity?

choices.A: Diabetes is present in the majority of patients with the generalized variant
choices.B: The subcutaneous variant is most common in children
choices.C: Localized lesions often ulcerate and heal with scarring
choices.D: The perforating variant classically involves the lower extremities
choices.E: 75% of localized lesions are still present 2 years after diagnosis

correct_text: The subcutaneous variant is most common in children
explanation: Granuloma annulare is the entity pictured. Subtypes include localized GA, generalized GA, macular GA, subcutaneous GA, and perforating GA. The subcutaneous variant is most common in children; there is often a history of trauma to the area.

question: The causative organism in Whitmore disease is which of the following?
explanation: Whitmore disease also known as Melioidosis is characterized by pulmonary disease, septicemia, and miliary abscesses. It is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei.

question: A 30 year old female presents with the following nail change. Which part of the nail has been affected to yield this clinical finding?
explanation: Beau's lines are transverse depressions in the nail plate that result from a temporary arrest in nail matrix activity.

question: What rare hematologic disorder can accompany varicella-zoster virus infection?
explanation: Symptomatic thrombocytopenia, while rare, has been associated with acute varicella-zoster virus infection.

question: The syndrome including mental and physical retardation, convulsions, episodic unconsciousness, liver enlargement, skin lesions, and dry and brittle hair showing trichorrhexis nodosa microscopically and fluorescing red. is:
explanation: Argininosuccinic aciduria has the features listed as well as trichorrhexis nodosa and red fluorescence of the hair.

question: A teenage female presents with the complaint of "nail fungus". On exam, she has triangular lunulae, palmoplantar hyperhidrosis, micronychia, and an absent patella. Which of the following screening tests should be ordered next to evaluate for the most severe sequelae of the patient's condition?

choices.A: X-ray of the knees, elbows, and pelvis

explanation: Patients with nail-patella syndrome can have glomerulonephritis and renal dysplasia that can lead to renal failure. Screening with urinalysis is a reasonable first test for this dangerous disease sequelae. If this is abnormal, a referral for a renal ultrasound could be useful.

question: Cicatricial pemphigoid antibodies directed against this are associated with high frequency of malignancy:
explanation: Anti-laminin 5 cicatricial pemphigoid (CP) is also known as anti-epiligrin CP. Anti-epiligrin CP is associated with an increased frequency of internal adenocarcinomas. Laminin 5 is composed of three chains (heterotrimer), alpha3, beta3, gamma2. Antibodies are frequently directed against the alpha3 chain, and so cross-reactivity can be observed with laminin 6, as laminin 6 (alpha3beta1gamma1) has the alpha3 chain as well. Beta4-integrin antibodies have been associated with ocular CP. BPAg2 antibodies are seen in CP patients that have mucosal as well as skin disease.

question: A 57-year-old male presents to the emergency department with unilateral facial swelling with areas of necrosis and hemorrhagic crust. He has an extensive underlying medical history and has been hospitalized many times over the past couple of months. A biopsy was performed bedside which reveals the findings depicted in the image. What is considered the most common risk factor for progression to disseminated disease?
explanation: Neutropenia is commonly caused by Rhizopus, Absidia, Mucor which are ubiquitous molds commonly found in the soil, decaying plants/animals, or in the air. Pathology reveals non-septate ribbon-like hyphae with 90-degree branching. There are several different clinical presentations of mucormycosis including Rhinocerebral, Pulmonary, Cutaneous, Gastrointestinal (GI), and Disseminated. The disseminated form, including hematogenous spread to the lungs, is usually observed in neutropenic patients. The rhinocerebral form is seen in diabetes and immunosuppressed states including leukemia, and the GI variant is more common in malnourished patients. Treatment includes debridement or amphotericin B depending on extent of disease.

question: A patient presents with this rash and joint pains after starting a new medication. Which of the following is the most likely medication?
explanation: Serum sickness-like reactions are thought to be due to aberrant inflammation secondary to abnormal metabolism of medication byproducts. Most reactions occur within 1-3 weeks after drug initiation. They are most likely secondary to antibiotics, particularly cefaclor.

question: Winterbottom’s sign is a characteristic feature of which of the following diseases?
explanation: Winterbottom’s sign (posterior cervical lymphadenopathy) is a clinical feature of African trypanosomiasis. Romaña’s sign (eyelid edema and conjunctivitis at site of incoculation) is a diagnostic finding in American trypanosomiasis (Chagas’ disease).

question: A healthy 50 year old man presents to your office with 3 red-brown indurated plaques on his forehead. Biopsy reveals a focal leukocytoclastic vasculitis, with a diffuse infiltration of neutrophils, eosinophils, and lymphocytes. Which of the following is a potential treatment option for this patient?
explanation: The question stem describes a case of granuloma faciale. This condition presents with red-brown papules and plaques on the face, most commonly in middle-aged Caucasian males. While traditional treatment options include intralesional steroids with or without cryotherapy, pulse dye laser (595 nm) represents another treatment option for this condition, with successful clearance in a number of case reports.

question: A patient presents with thin anterior hair and redundant, thickened skin around the neck, palms, and soles. The patient has congenital myopathy, coarse facies, facial and perianal papillomas, and cardiac and developmental disability. The mutation is in:
explanation: Patients with Costello syndrome (also known as faciocutaneoskeletal syndrome) have a mutation in the HRAS gene, which is part of the Ras- MAPK pathway. It has phenotypic overlap with Cardio-facio-cutaneous Syndrome which occurs from a KRAS mutation.

question: A 24-year-old male recently started a new medication and subsequently developed the cutaneous findings shown in the clinical image. What is the most likely medication associated with this presentation?
explanation: The clinical image demonstrates eruptive xanthomas, which present as numerous red-yellow papules clustered on extensor surfaces, buttocks, or intertriginous areas. These lesions are most often seen in the setting of severe hypertriglyceridemia (typically >3,000 mg/dL). They may occur as a primary manifestation of type I, IV, or V hyperlipidemias, or secondarily due to obesity, diabetes mellitus, alcohol abuse, or medication-induced dyslipidemia. Oral retinoids, including isotretinoin, are well-recognized causes. Other medications associated with eruptive xanthomas include protease inhibitors, olanzapine, and estrogen replacement therapy.

question: Immediate pigment darkening:

choices.A: Is caused by an increase in tyrosinase activity
choices.B: Is predominately brought on by UVB
choices.C: Is predominately brought on by UVA and visible light
choices.D: Is associated with an increase in melanocyte number

correct_text: Is predominately brought on by UVA and visible light
explanation: Immediate pigment darkening appears almost as soon as irradiation occurs. It is due to photo-oxidation of preexisting melanin by UVA light.

question: A 35-year-old male presents with painful, erosive oral lesions, accompanied by multiple flaccid bullae on his trunk. Histopathology reveals intraepidermal acantholysis, and direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits in the epidermis. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this condition?

choices.E: Topical calcineurin inhibitors ? Dapsone ? Systemic corticosteroids

correct_text: Topical calcineurin inhibitors ? Dapsone ? Systemic corticosteroids
explanation: This patient’s presentation is characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris, an autoimmune blistering disorder with intraepidermal acantholysis and IgG deposits on direct immunofluorescence. The initial treatment of choice for pemphigus vulgaris is systemic corticosteroids to rapidly control inflammation and halt disease progression.

question: A patient presents with several light blue cyst-like lesions on the eyelid. The patient also has a history of plantar hyperkeratosis, dysplastic toenails, and both upper and lower dentures since only 3 teeth grew after the patient's 'baby teeth' fell out. Which of the following syndromes is most consistent with the patient's presentation?
explanation: Schopf-Schulz-Passarge syndrome is associated with hidrocystomas of the eyelids, hypotrichosis (near complete loss of hair early in life), hypodontia, nail abnormalities, and multiple palmoplantar eccrine syringofibroadenomas.

question: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is associated with which of the following disorders?
explanation: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is associated with severe combined immunodeficiency. The most common inheritance is autosomal recessive. It is a mixed group of disorders all sharing defects in cell-mediated and humoral immunity. Skin findings include: candidal infections, mucocutaneous, bacterial pyodermas, seborrheic-like dermatitis/lichen planus-like sclerodermatous changes, aplastic thymus and pneumonias. The other listed syndromes are not associated with adenosine deaminase deficiency.

question: What is the best treatment for this infection?
explanation: The image shown is blastomycosis, indicated by the broad-based buds and the refractile wall. This is a GMS stain which highlights the walls of the blastomycosis. This is treated with itraconazole, or amphotericin B if the infection is severe.

question: The majority of naturally-occurring cases of anthrax:

choices.A: Are acquired through ingestion of spores

explanation: The majority (95%) of naturally-occurring cases of anthrax are of the cutaneous form, acquired from direct contact with the carcasses of dead sheep, cows, goats, and horses.

question: Most patients with PMLE require treatment with:

choices.A: Sunscreen and sun avoidance between 11 am and 3pm

correct_text: Sunscreen and sun avoidance between 11 am and 3pm
explanation: Most patients have mild disease that can be treated by sun avoidance, especially between 11 am and 3pm; a broad spectum sunscreen and clothing with a tight weave. In more severe cases, UV hardening, antimalarials or prednisone can be used. Cyclophosphamide is not used in PMLE.

question: Distal subungual onychomycosis is most often caused by:
explanation: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common organism involved in distal subungual onychomycosis.

question: A 71-year-old woman with recent difficulty in standing from a seated position over the last 8 weeks develops violaceous and red plaques on the dorsal hands, neck, and lateral thigh. The patient is initiated on systemic steroids with improvement. Trichoscopy of the patient’s lesions is most likely to demonstrate which of the following findings?
explanation: The patient described has dermatomyositis. In dermatomyositis, there are dilated, tortuous blood vessels found on trichoscopy.

question: The deficiency in familial multiple cutaneous leiomyomatosis is:
explanation: Fumarate hydratase is deficient in familial multiple cutaneous leiomyomatosis (Reed's syndrome). This same enzyme is deficient in familial uterine leiomyomatosis associated with renal cell cancer.

question: A patient presents with these lesions. If multiple are found, which of the following should be screened?
explanation: This photo depicts leiomyomas. They are smooth muscle tumors that present with tan to skin-colored papules/nodules. They may be agminated or arranged in a parallel array. Leiomyomas occur in familial multiple cutaneous Leiomyomatosis (Reed syndrome). It is an autosomal dominant condition due to a defect in fumarate hydratase. It presents with multiple cutaneous leiomyomas, uterine leiomyomas/leiomyosarcoma, and type II papillary renal cell carcinoma.

question: Dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata is seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation: Buschke-Ollendorf syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata (cutaneous elastomas distributed symmetrically over the buttocks, trunk and proximal extremities), and osteopoikilosis (round opacities in bones).

question: This hair disorder is used to describe end stage scarring alopecia with areas of hair growth that look like "footprints in the snow":
explanation: Pseudopelade of Brocq is an end stage scarring alopecia that presents as an oval or irregularly shaped patch of alopecia with areas of hair growth that look like footprints in the snow.

question: A patient you notice has unruly hair that looks like spun-glass hair. She is found to have uncombable hair syndrome, which is a condition with the associated hair findings of:
explanation: Uncombable hair syndrome has the characteristic findings of spun-glass hair or cheveux incoiffables. It is associated with pili trianguli et canaliculi, has a longitudinal groove and can be inherited in an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive fashion.

question: Which of the following are potential cutaneous manifestations of voriconazole therapy?
explanation: These are all potential photosensitive reactions to voriconazole. These resolve on discontinuation of voriconazole. Voriconazole can also cause photosensitivity and accelerated photoaging.

question: Which of the following is the causative organism of cat-scratch disease? B henselae B burgdorferi B bacilliformis B duttonii B quintana
explanation: B. henselae is the cause of cat-scratch disease. Humans are infected by a cat bite or scratch, while the cat flea is responsible for cat to cat transmission.

question: All of the following drugs have been reported to cause rash similar to the attached image except:
explanation: The image shows symmetrical erthematous to violaceous plaque on dorsal hands with some periungual erythema and telangiectasia. Skin biopsy was consistent with interface dermatitis and mucin. Many drugs have been reported to cause dermatomyositis-like picture, which include hydroxyurea, D-penicillamine, statins, phenytoin and alfuzosin (alpha antagonist for BPH). Captopril is not associated with DM-like rash.

question: Mastocytosis is a systemic disease that causes wheals upon rubbing a lesion (Darier's sign). Mastocytosis can be measured by examination of serum:
explanation: The most common form of cutaneous mastocytosis is urticaria pigmentosa. It is diagnosed by measuring serum tryptase levels. The new diagnostic method is measurement of tryptase in bone-marrow blood, which is a new, sensitive marker of the mast cell burden in bone marrow of patients with systemic mastocytosis.

question: Pastia's lines are seen in which condition?
explanation: Pastia's lines describes the linear petechiael streaks along body folds seen in scarlet fever, which results from pharyngitis due to erythrogenic toxin-producing strains of Group A Step. It most often affects children, who also typically have fever, sore throat, headache, a sandpaper-like eruption (tiny pink papules on erythematous background) and a strawberry tongue. Treatment is with penicillin or erythromycin for 10-14 days.

question: Which of the following is NOT caused by a dematiaceous fungus?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Hyalohyphomycosis may be caused by Penicillium marneffei, Paecilomyces, and Fusarium.

question: Eruptions caused by this plant are due to which substance?
explanation: The plant shown is poison oak, identified by its three leaves and rounded points. It contains Urushiol, which causes the associated eruption.

question: Which of the following is commony seen in seborrheic keratoses when examined with dermoscopy?
explanation: The main dermoscopic features of seborrheic keratoses include comedolike openings, fissures, milialike cysts, fingerprinting and lack of true pigment network. In fact, it is the lack of true pigment network, branched streaks, and pigment globules that differentiate SKs from melanocytic lesions.

question: Which extracutaneous organ is typically associated with this subtype of sarcoidosis?
explanation: This is an example of lupus pernio, which is often associated with chronic sarcoidosis of the lungs.

question: A 5-year-old male is diagnosed with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). NF1 is due to a mutation in the gene which encodes neurofibromin. Which of the following best describes the function of neurofibromin?

choices.E: Turns Ras to its inactive form

correct_text: Turns Ras to its inactive form
explanation: Neurofibromin is a GTPase-activating protein that negatively regulates RAS/MAPK pathway activity by accelerating the hydrolysis of Ras-bound GTP. Thus neurofibromin acts as a tumor suppressor by reducing Ras activity. In NF1, decreased neurofibromin results in unrestricted Ras activity in the RAS/MAPK and leads to the tumor growth seen in this disease.

question: Reactivation of which of the following virus(es) can lead to drug hypersensitivity?
explanation: Reactivation of latent viruses such as HHV-6, HHV-7, EBV, and CMV can increase the risk of drug hypersensitivity. Drug hypersensitivity syndrome is characterized by fever, skin eruption and internal organ involvement.

question: Dracunculiasis is typically acquired from:
explanation: Dracunculiasis, which is caused by Dracunculus medinensis, is acquired by ingestion of copepod-infested water.

question: A patient with sparse hair, a pear-shaped broad nose and cone-shaped epiphyses likely suffers which of the following conditions?
explanation: Tricho-rhino-phalangeal Syndrome is characterized by sparse hair, a pear-shaped broad nose and cone-shaped epiphyses.

question: Which bacterial disease carries a risk of mortality due to coinfection with Salmonella?
explanation: Carrion's disease, or Oroyo fever, is caused by Bartonella bacilliformis and is transmitted via the Lutzomyia sandfly. It is characterized by fevers, headache, arthralgias, and an acute eruptive stage that resembles bacillary angiomatosis. It has an untreated fatality rate of 40% often secondary to Salmonella infection; chloramphenicol is given with tetracycline for treatment. Epidemic typhus may also coexist with Salmonella.

question: The most common site for intra oral melanoma is?
explanation: Multiple case series have shown that the hard palate (and specifically the anterior hard palate/ alveolar arch) is the highest risk location for intra-oral melanoma. Prognosis is generally worse for oral melanoma, which is usually due to delay in diagnosis and presentation with more invasive disease.

question: A 25-year old man with a history of a healed genital ulcer develops a diffuse papulosquamous eruption resembling pityriasis rosea. What is the most likely time lapse between the appearance of the genital lesion and the appearance of this eruption?
explanation: The lesions of secondary syphilis are often diffusely distributed due to spirochetemia. Papulosquamous lesions are characteristic, and the presence of constitutional symptoms such as fever, fatigue, headaches, and bone pain may help distinguish secondary syphilis from pityriasis rosea. Other lesions of secondary syphilis include "moth-eaten" alopecia, mucous patches, split papules, and condyloma lata. The mucocutaneous manifestations of secondary syphilis typically occur 3-12 weeks after the appearance of the chancre and last 4-12 weeks.

question: Which of the following is true regarding culture of the organisms that cause Pityriasis versicolor?

choices.C: Difficult to grow, requires olive oil overlay
choices.D: Grow easily on Sabouraud Dextrose Agar
choices.E: Grow easily on Dermatophyte Test Media

correct_text: Difficult to grow, requires olive oil overlay
explanation: Pityriasis versicolor (Tinea versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur, M. globosa (most common cause), M. pachydermatis, M. dermatis, M. obtuse, M. restrica, M. sympodialis, and M. sloofiae. The organisms that cause Pityriasis versicolor are difficult to grow. The culture requires olive oil overlay.

question: This condition shares the same mutation as what systemic disease?
explanation: This is piebaldism, which is shown as depigmented patches. It is due to a mutation in c-KIT. It is also associated with a white forelock and heterochromia irides. There is no involvement of hearing, unlike Waardenburg which has deafness associated. Systemic mastocytosis also has a c-KIT mutation.

question: What is the underlying infection in this neonate?
explanation: This is pemphigus syphiliticus, the only blistering manifestation of syphilis. It occurs in newborns, who have severe bullous lesions.

question: Clinically this lesion appears as a small reddish-blue tender subungual tumor. An image of the histology is provided. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A glomus tumor is a small reddish-blue tender subungual tumor derived from Sucquet Hoyer Canals which allow shunting of blood from arterioles to venules and bypassing capillaries. On pathology, one can see small uniform round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm.

question: Steatocystoma multiplex and natal teeth are associated with which of the following conditions?
explanation: Jackson-Lawler pachyonychia congenita (Type 2) is characterized by thickening of the nailbed and plate, steatocystoma multiplex, and natal teeth.

question: Cat scratch disease is caused by infection with:
explanation: Cat scratch disease is caused by infection with B. henselae - a gram-negative bacillus of the genus Bartonella.

question: Currently the most common cause of photoallergic contact dermatitis is:
explanation: Sunscreen ingredients are now the most common cause Of photoallergic contact dermatitis.

question: What finding is seen on brain imaging of patients with Papillon-Lefevre Syndrome?
explanation: Papillon Lefevre Syndrome is an autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by transgredient PPK and periodontitis. There is a defect in cathepsin C. One sees dural calcification at the tentorium and choroid plexus.

question: Direct immunofluorescent studies in chronic bullous disease of childhood is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.A: Linear IgG at the basement membrane
choices.B: Linear C3 at the basement membrane
choices.C: Granular IgG at the basement membrane
choices.D: Linear IgA at the basement membrane
choices.E: Granular IgA at the basement membrane

correct_text: Linear IgA at the basement membrane
explanation: Chronic bullous disease of childhood is believed to be a variant of linear IgA bullous disease, since the two diseases are characterized by antibodies to the 97kDa antigen that is a part of BPAg2. Children present with extremely pruritic blisters in circular arrangements. Pathology shows a subepidermal bulla with neutrophils at the dermo-epidermal junction; the DIF shows IgA deposition at the basement membrane in a linear fashion.

question: The term used to describe hair shafts in anagen effluvium that are abruptly thinned, forming constrictions and breaking off at the skin surface is:
explanation: Pohl-Pinkus constriction is used to describe abruptly thinned hair shafts. This is seen in anagen effluvium, secondary to a toxic insult. The shedding of anagen hairs are always abnormal. This is analogous to Beau's lines in nails.

question: The Grzybowski type of keratoacanthoma:

choices.A: Presents in childhood on sun-exposed surfaces
choices.B: Presents with hundreds of disseminated lesions
choices.C: Is characterized by rapid growth of a single lesion reaching a diameter of 9 cm or more

correct_text: Presents with hundreds of disseminated lesions
explanation: The Grzybowski type of keratoacanthoma is typically diagnosed in adulthood, with the sudden appearance of hundreds of lesions in a disseminated fashion. The lesions are generally 2-3mm in diameter and can be found anywhere on the body including the palms, soles, larynx, and oral mucosa.

question: Lichen planus pemphigoides has been associated with an antigen to which structure?
explanation: Type XVII collagen, or BPag2 (180 kD) has been associated with LP pemphigoides.

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Morbihan's Disease?

choices.A: It is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis
choices.B: Histopathology reveals perifollicular and perivascular noncaseating epithelioid granulomas
choices.C: It occurs around the mouth and/or nose and eyes and may be triggered by topical steroid use
choices.D: It presents with blepharitis, conjunctivitis, iritis, and keratitis
choices.E: It presents with large coalescent nodules and confluent draining sinuses occupying most of the face

correct_text: It is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis
explanation: Morbihan's Disease, also known as rosacea lymphedema or persistent edema of rosacea, presents with hard, nonpitting edema. It is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis.

question: Which of the following allergens is most associated with the shown pathology in a 58-year-old woman with a recently chipped tooth?
explanation: Recognize the plaques on the tongue most consistent with oral lichen planus. Oral lichen planus has been associated with dental restorative materials, such as gold or nickel, which may be associated with oral lichen planus.

question: Characteristic eosinophilic abscesses are seen in:
explanation: Eosinophilic abscesses with minimal to no spongiosis in a hyperplastic epidermis are characteristic of pemphigus vegetans. Pemphigus vegetans is a rare, variant of pemphigus vulgaris, vegetating purulent plaques, usually in axilla, groin, or inframammary areas, with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, intraepidermal pustules filled mostly with neutrophils and eosinophils and a few hidden acantholytic keratinocytes.

question: A patient presents to your clinic after returning from vacation with painless smooth-surfaced nodules on the arm. Biopsy of one of the nodules reveals round, brownish cells attached to one another with narrow connections. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The question stem describes the typical clinico-pathologic findings of keloidal blastomycosis (Lobomycosis), which is caused by Lacazia loboi. This deep fungal organism is found in the Amazon basin and Gulf of Mexico, and is associated with dolphins. The biopsy findings are also described as "brass knuckles" or a "chain of coins." The treatment of choice is surgical excision as antifungals are ineffective.

question: A plain film showing “net-like calcification” may obviate the need for biopsy, potentially significantly increasing mortality if secondary ulceration occurs, in which of the following conditions?
explanation: The correct answer is E. Xrays of the aﬀected limb may demonstrate vascular calcification within the skin; however, this may also be seen in healthy patients with renal disease that are not aﬀected by calciphylaxis. Bone scintigraphy using technetium Tc 99m bisphosphonates in patients with calciphylaxis shows increased radiotracer uptake in soft tissues throughout the body and is specifically enhanced in indurated plaques aﬀected by calciphylaxis (but is absent in ulcers due to reduced blood flow at sites of tissue necrosis).

question: Phrynoderma is associated with deficiency of which vitamin?
explanation: Phrynoderma (toad skin) presents clinically as keratotic papules on the extremities and shoulders and results from a deficiency of Vitamin A. Vitamin A is a fat soluble vitamin. Hypovitaminosis A is often seen in diseases such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease and cystic fibrosis which manifest with fat malabsorbtion. Hypovitaminosis A is additionally associated with night blindness, xeropthalmia and keratomalacia.

question: The presence of which of the following autoantibodies is diagnostic of SLE and not reported in patients with other connective tissue diseases?
explanation: Anti-Sm is diagnostic of SLE and not reported in patients with other connective tissue diseases.

question: A 45-year-old male presents with the complaint of a red and chronically chapped lower lip. Which of the following lasers is the most appropriate to treat this condition?

choices.C: Laser treatment is not an appropriate treatment

explanation: The patient has actinic cheilitis. Actinic cheilitis is a pre-malignant condition and presents with erythema, scaling, erosions, and fissures of the lip. The CO2 laser targets water as a chromophore. This ablative laser represents a treatment option for this condition. Physical treatments for actinic cheilitis include cryotherapy, electrocautery, vermillionectomy, and laser ablation with a carbon dioxide laser or an erbium:YAG laser.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding this condition?

choices.A: Biopsy typically shows a thinned basement membrane
choices.B: 50% of patients will eventually develop systemic involvement
choices.C: Squamous cell carcinoma is a potential sequela
choices.D: C3 deficiency increases susceptibility to this condition
choices.E: UV exposure is helpful in treatment

correct_text: Squamous cell carcinoma is a potential sequela
explanation: This is an image of discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE). Squamous cell carcinoma may develop from lesions of DLE. SCCs arising from lesions of DLE are rare and aggressive tumors with greater likelihood of metastases. Cases have been reported among patients with different clinical characteristics.

question: An adolescent presents with open comedones and papules, pustules and nodules on her cheeks, forehead and chin which began after puberty. Which group of receptors recognizes bacterial patterns and is activated leading to intracellular signal transduction and upregulation of the immune response by stimulating pro-inflammatory cytokines?
explanation: Toll-like receptors are a large group of receptors that recognize certain bacterial patterns. TLR-2 activation by P. acnes leads to intracellular signal transduction and upregulation of the immune response by stimulating pro-inflammatory cytokines. Certain topical retinoids have been shown to downregulate TLR-2 expression. TLR-1 recognizes lipopeptides from gram negative bacteria and mycobacteria. TLR-4 recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from gram negative bacteria. TLR-7 serves as the ligand for Imiquimod activating interfon gamma production. TLR-9 recognizes unmethylated bacterial DNA and has also been implicated the interactions between smoking and hydroxychloroquine.

question: Which of the following causes tinea imbricata?
explanation: Tinea imbricata is characterized by concentric, annular, scaly rings resembling erythema annulare centrifugum. The causative agent is T. concentricum, which is endemic to the South Pacific, South and Central America and Asia. The infection is usually chronic.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding coccidiomycosis?

choices.A: Droplet transmission is the most common method of acquisition of disease
choices.B: Erythema nodosum is associated with a poor prognosis
choices.C: First line treatment in pregnancy is itraconazole
choices.D: Approximately 75% of those contracting the disease will be symptomatic
choices.E: Southeast Asians are at a higher risk of disseminated disease

correct_text: Southeast Asians are at a higher risk of disseminated disease
explanation: Southeast Asians and African Americans are at a higher risk for disseminated cocci, as are pregnant women and the immunocompromised.

question: A patient with Refsum syndrome with ocular anomalies such as nystagmus and night blindness has which of the following?
explanation: Patients with Refusum syndrome have a deficiency in phytanic acid oxidase. The ocular abnormalities seen are pigmentary retinopathy, cataracts, nystagmus, and night blindness.

question: Which of the following concomitant conditions or exposures increase the risk of squamous cell carcinoma?
explanation: All of the above conditions have been linked to an increased risk of developing SCC.

question: Ananas comosus causes an irritant dermatitis attributed to which irritant?
explanation: Ananas comosus is the pineapple. Pineapples contain the irritants bromelin (a proteolytic enzyme) and calcium oxalate (which causes fissures that grant bromelin access to dermal vessels).

question: Ultraviolet light spectrum most completely encompasses which of the following spectrums?
explanation: The ultraviolet spectrum encompasses Vacuum UV from 10-200nm, UV-C from 200-290nm, UV-B from 290-320nm and UV-A from 320- 400nm.

question: Ecthyma contagiosum or infectious pustular dermatitis is transmitted from animal to humans by fomites. The host is:
explanation: Ecthyma contagiosum, also known as orf, is caused by parapoxvirus and the host is sheep, goat, or reindeer. It is transmitted to humans by direct contact or fomites. Animal and meat handlers are the most susceptible to getting orf.

question: A patient in your occupational dermatology clinic presents with mottled hyperpigmentation with areas of hypopigmentation and hair loss. She has a history of numerous SCCis (squamous cell carcinomas in situ). Upon further examination, she has many symmetric, yellow, punctate corn- like papules on both palms (shown in image). The patient likely was chronically exposed to which of the following?
explanation: Chronic arsenic exposure can occur through contaminated drinking water or occupational exposure. It is characterized by mottled hyperpigmentation with areas of hypopigmentation, keratoses on the palms and soles and other sites, alopecia, and multiple non-melanoma skin cancers, particularly Bowen’s disease (SCCis). Arsenical keratoses are precancerous papules on the palms and soles that are symmetric, yellow and punctate. They measure 2-10 mm in size and favor the thenar and hypothenar eminences, distal palms, lateral fingers, dorsal aspect of the interphalangeal joints, and weight-bearing plantar surfaces. They rarely occur on the trunk, proximal extremities, eyelids and genitalia and may coalesce into plaques.

question: Follicular atrophoderma is a feature of which of the following conditions?
explanation: Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome is a rare genodermatosis that manifests with the classical triad of basal cell carcinoma, follicular atrophoderma, and hypotrichosis; yet it may be accompanied by milia, ichthyosis, neurological symptoms, and visceral malignancies. Symptom onset is nonsimultaneous, and hence the diagnosis is often made late and the opportunity of counseling and following up is missed. Though the gene responsible for this syndrome is yet nonspecified, it is confirmed to be localized to the long arm of chromosome X.

question: The National Psoriasis Foundation Consensus recommends that patients with latent TB should be treated with a TB treatment:

choices.C: 1-2 months prior to starting anti-TNF therapy

correct_text: 1-2 months prior to starting anti-TNF therapy
explanation: The National Psoriasis Foundation Consensus states that patients with a positive TB, treat latent TB for at least 1-2 month prior to starting TNF therapy. After 1-2 months of appropriate TB treatment, psoriasis therapy may begin is necessary.

question: This is a term used to describe the thin epithelium immediately beneath the nail plate, with an absent granular layer:
explanation: The nail bed is described as the thin epithelium immediate beneath the nail plate. It does not have a granular layer.

question: The portion of the electromagnetic spectrum that produces a particular biologic effect is called the:
explanation: The action spectrum is the wavelengths that produce a certain biologic effect. The action spectrum for photosensitivity from exogenous chemicals is usually in the UVA range. The radiation that is absorbed by those chemicals is called their absorption spectrum.

question: A patient is diagnosed having Menke's kinky's hair syndrome with a deficiency in:
explanation: Patients with Menke's Kinky Hair syndrome have a X-linked recessive disorder in the ATP7A gene. This gene is responsible for the copper translocating membrane ATPase. They have brittle "steel wool" hair with a cupid's bow lips, pale and lax skin.

question: A 46-year-old man presents with abrupt-onset, well-demarcated red target-shaped macules on the bilateral dorsal hands and forearms. One week prior, the patient reports taking medication for an infection. A biopsy of a lesion is performed, which shows vacuolar interface change without eosinophils. Which of the following is likely to prevent the recurrence of the lesions?
explanation: Most cases of erythema multiforme are related to prior herpes simplex virus infection. Therefore, antiviral prophylaxis for herpes labialis infection, for instance, is most likely to prevent the recurrence of the lesions of erythema multiforme.

question: The most common location of the lesions in nephrogenic fibrosing dermopathy is:
explanation: The most common location for lesions of nephrogenic fibrosis dermopathy is the lower extremities.

question: This term describes transverse white lines that affect all the nails and can be from arsenic poisoning, leprosy, and systemic disease. This nail defect is called:
explanation: Transverse white lines that affect ALL the nails and grow out with nail growth are called Mee's lines. They are caused by parakeratosis of the ventral nail plate. They are associated with arsenic poisoning, rheumatic fever, congenital heart failure, leprosy, and systemic disease.

question: A patient that has Darier's disease typically has skin findings of hyperkeratotic papules in the seborrheic areas and nail findings of:

choices.A: Alternating red and white longitudinal bands

correct_text: Alternating red and white longitudinal bands
explanation: Patients with Darier's disease typically have alternating red and white longitudinal bands with a V- shaped distal nicking of the nail plate, subungual hyperkeratosis, and skin findings of hyperkeratotic papules in the seborrheic areas.

question: Which of the following forms of angioedema is mediated by kinin release?
explanation: Types of angioedema mediated through kinin buildup include hereditary angioedema, acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency, and ACE inhibitor associated angioedema. These conditions are not associated with concurrent urticaria.

question: The changes that occur on the nose in patients with rosacea is due to:
explanation: In patients with rosacea, patients experience rhinophyma that is from the sebaceous hyperplasia. Initially the nose becomes swollen with prominent pores followed by fibrosis in the later stages.

question: What is the antigen in this disease?
explanation: This is bullous pemphigoid which is due to antibodies to BPAg1 and BPAg 2. It is a subepidermal blister.

question: Clinically, a nondescript hyperkeratotic papule on the ulnar side of the base of the fifth finger is most likely:
explanation: Accessory digits (supernumerary digits) are usually found at the base of the fifth finger, often bilaterally.

question: A 35-year-old male presents for follow-up of chronic hand dermatitis. Statistically, patch testing would most likely show:
explanation: Hand dermatitis affects up to 10% of the population and has multiple potential causes. Irritant contact dermatitis is the most common subtype, resulting in negative patch test results. However, several large consensus recommendations support patch testing for all patients with chronic hand dermatitis lasting longer than three months to evaluate for allergic contact dermatitis.

question: The usual culture medium for mycobacteria is:

choices.D: Agar supplemented with heme and nicotinamide

explanation: The Lowenstein-Jensen medium is used to culture mycobacteria most commonly.

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding pseudoporphyria?

choices.A: It has not been associated with naproxen
choices.C: Clinically it is easily distinguishable from porphyria cutanea tarda
choices.D: It has not been associated with furosemide
choices.E: UV protection is not helpful for treatment

explanation: Pseudoporphyria is a phototoxic reaction that clinically and histologically resembles porphyria cutanea tarda. In pseudoporphyria, however, there is typically no porphyrin abnormality.

question: The most common finding in patients with systemic sclerosis is:
explanation: Esophageal dysfunction is the most common systemic finding in systemic sclerosis.

question: A patient with a pulmonary infection and cervical adenopathy has vesicles, papules and ulcerations on the oral and nasal mucosa. Tissue culture reveals yeast with multiple buds giving a mariner's wheel appearance. The organism is:
explanation: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis causes a chronic progressive infection that is most commonly seen in rural areas of South America. Patients may have constitutional symptoms, lung involvement, ulcers of the upper respiratory and digestive tract, and verrucous/ulcerated cutaneous lesions. Classically, Paracoccidioides brasiliensis has a mariner's wheel appearance.

question: Stroking or scratching the skin, tight clothing, or towel drying after a hot shower, inducing wheals and flares, would all be seen in which of the following underlying conditions?
explanation: Dermographism is an exaggerated tendency to develop both wheal and flare when the skin is stroked. It is the most common form of physical or chronic inducible urticaria. It is also called dermatographism, dermatographia, and dermatographic urticaria. Stroking or scratching the skin, tight clothing, and towel drying are examples of stimuli inducing whealing and symptomatic dermatographism (a type of inducible urticaria).

question: A young man presents with explosive onset of severe cystic acne with acute, suppurative nodules and plaques that ulcerate and form a blackish eschar on the trunk as well as the face. Which of the following is true regarding this entity?

choices.A: High-dose isotretinoin monotherapy is the treatment of choice
choices.B: Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated given risk of sepsis
choices.C: P. acnes osteomyelitis presents with lytic changes on x-rays and bone scans
choices.D: The sternoclavicular joint is often involved in this entity
choices.E: Women are more often affected than men

correct_text: The sternoclavicular joint is often involved in this entity
explanation: Acne fulminans is a rare, explosive form of severe cystic acne affecting young males. Patients may be systemically ill, with leukocytosis, fever, arthralgias, and myalgias. Lytic changes, indicative of a sterile osteomyelitis, can be seen on x-ray and bone scans. The sternoclavicular joint and chest wall are most frequently affected. Treatment is with oral prednisone, intralesional steroids, antibiotics, and isotretinoin.

question: Patients of which HLA type are more prone to drug-induced lupus erythematosus when exposed to hydralazine?
explanation: Drug-induced lupus erythematous has been associated with exposure to hydralazine, procainamide, sulfonamides, penicillin, anticonvulsants, minocycline, and INH. It generally has a benign course. The presence of anti-histone antibodies are closely associated with symptomatic disease. Hydralazine and procainamide are common culprits, with slow acetylators of hydralazine (HLA-DR4) more prone.

question: You are consulted to evaluate this patient with tender, warm plaques on his shins. A chest radiograph demonstrates hilar adenopathy, and patient is febrile. What other symptom may the patient have?
explanation: Erythema nodosum (EN) is represented by tender, warm nodules, and plaques, often but not exclusively located on the anterior shin. It represents reactive panniculitis. Causes include infections (streptococcal, tuberculosis, Yersinia, Mycoplasma, Campylobacter, Salmonella, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis), drugs (sulfonamides, gold, and estrogen/ OCPs), inflammatory bowel disease, pregnancy, Hodgkin disease and lymphoma, and sarcoidosis. Löfgren syndrome is a variant of sarcoidosis with erythema nodosum, hilar adenopathy, fever, and arthritis. This patient is demonstrating EN and hilar adenopathy, which makes you concerned for sarcoidosis and possible Löfgren syndrome.

question: A 47-year-old patient with psoriasis, chronic venous insufficiency and venous ulcers presents with one week's history of purpuric papules with some vesiculobullous lesions affecting the lower extremities and distal forearms. The distal lesions have central necrosis with scattered erosions. The patient says the lesions itch and complains of mild abdominal pain. How should the patient be managed?
explanation: The correct answer is U/A. The clinical presentation is most consistent with a small vessel vasculitis. Palpable purpura of the lower extremities, arthralgias and abdominal pain suggest IgA vasculitis (IgAV). According to the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) criteria, purpura or petechiae with lower limb predominance not related to thrombocytopenia is mandatory for IgAV diagnosis; the additional finding of abdominal pain or arthralgia yields a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 87%. Compared to pediatric IgAV, adult IgAV patients are more likely to experience relapses and recalcitrant disease, especially those with renal manifestations. Adults tend to have more severe IgA nephropathy (IgAN) with lower remission rates. Therefore, in adults with suspected IgAV, U/A should be ordered to evaluate for hematuria and proteinuria.

question: "Mousy" odor of urine is characteristic of which of the following syndromes?
explanation: Phenylketonuria will cause a "mousy" odor in the urine.

question: Secondary systemic amyloidosis:

choices.A: Classically involves the tongue and periorbital skin
choices.C: Can be noted on biopsy of normal skin
choices.D: Can involve deposition of beta 2-microglobulin in the setting of rheumatoid arthritis

correct_text: Can be noted on biopsy of normal skin
explanation: Secondary systemic amyloidosis presents with deposition of amyloid in the adrenals, liver, spleen, and kidney as a result of some chronic disease, such as TB, leprosy, Hodgkin's, Behcet's, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, schistosomiasis, or syphilis. The skin is not involved. AA amyloid fibrils, derived from SAA protein (an acute phase reactant) are deposited. AA is also seen in Muckle-Wells and familial mediterranean fever. Biopsy of normal skin may be positive for perivascular amyloid. Dialysis-related amyloidosis occurs via deposition of beta 2-microglobulin component altered by uremia, and resuls in carpal tunnel syndrome, bone cysts, and spondyloarthropathy.

question: Which of the following disorders is primarily associated with a monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type?
explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum is an destructive, inflammatory disease of the skin characterized by a painful nodule or pustule that later forms a progressively enlarging ulcer. On pathology, there is a neutrophilic infiltrate with leukocytoclasia. Diseases that have been associated with pyoderma gangrenosum include inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis, an IgA monoclonal gammopathy (primarily), and myelodysplasia.

question: Lindsay's nails (distal nail normal, proximal nail white) is characteristic of:
explanation: Lindsay's nails are characteristic of chronic renal failure and indicate nailbed edema.

question: Non-bullous icthyosiform erythroderma can be caused all of the following mutations except:
explanation: Non-bullous congenital erythroderma (NCIE)is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a collodion baby presentation at birth, and generalized erythroderma with fine white scale, palmoplantar keratoderma, and heat intolerance. NCIE may be caused by mutations in transglutaminase-1 gene (TGM1), the 12R-lipoxygenase gene (ALOX12B), and the lipoxygenase-3 gene (ALOXE3). Mutations in the keratinocyte TGM1 gene interferes with normal cross-linking of structural proteins and the lipid envelope, leading to defective cornification and desquamation. ALOXE3 functions as an epoxy alcohol synthase using the product of ALOX12B as the preferred substrate; either gene can be the site of mutations causing NCIE. Deficiency in steroid sulfatase results in X-linked ichthyosis.

question: Leishmania donovani is transmitted by:
explanation: Leishmania donovani is transmitted by Phlebotomid sandflies.

question: Patients with Werner’s syndrome typically experience which of the following types of cardiac disease?
explanation: Werner syndrome or adult progeria is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in WRN (Recql2) gene, which encodes DNA helicase. This defect leads to defects in DNA repair and replication. Patients prematurely age and essentially experience many diseases of aging early in childhood and teen years. They exhibit tight atrophic skin, relatively large heads for body size, leg ulcers and cannities. Patients experience early, accelerated atherosclerosis leading to death by myocardial infarction. In addition, type II diabetes, cataracts, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and hypogonadism are features.

question: What was this patient most likely doing that caused this condition?
explanation: This photo depicts cutaneous larva migrans, which is characterized by tortuous pruritic tracks moving slowly, 2 mm-2cm/day. It lacks collagenase so it is unable to penetrate the basement membrane. Lesions will usually appear on the buttock or feet where contact is made with infested beach sand. Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by larvae of hookworms from dogs and cats (Ancylostoma braziliense or Bunostomum phlebotomum).

question: The main cause of nutritional disease in high-resource nations is:
explanation: Alcoholism is the main cause of nutritional disease in high-resource nations. Other conditions that cause nutritional disease include: unusual diets, postoperative state, psychiatric illness, inflammatory bowel disease, cystic fibrosis, surgical bowel dysfunction, and inborn errors of metabolism.

question: Carrion's disease is characterized by fevers, headaches and arthralgias and is accompanied by severe hemolytic anemia. Superinfection with which organism is the most frequent cause of death?
explanation: Carrion's disease (Oroya fever) is characterized by fevers, headaches and arthralgias and is accompanied by severe hemolytic anemia. Superinfection with Salmonella is the most frequent cause of death. Protection from sandfly bites is all-important.

question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the lesion shown, which has sarcoidal granulomas on histopathology and colorless, birifrigent crystals on polarized light?
explanation: The image shows a foreign body reaction with sarcoidal granulomas consistent with such a reaction. The presence of colorless, birifrigent crystals is most characteristic of silicosis.

question: The female Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis mite can lay up to 100 eggs. It has an ovoid, flat body and how many short legs?
explanation: The female Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis mite has an ovoid, flat body and 8 short legs.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of lichen planus pigmentosus inversus?
explanation: Occasionally epidermotropic T-cells are seen in the lichenoid reaction and thus may raise concern for mycosis fungoides. Lichen planus pigmentosus inversus, in particular, presents in classic sites of mycosis fungoides, including the axilla, inguinal, and inframammary areas. The individual lesions of lichen planus pigmentosis are typically smaller than those encountered in mycosis fungoides, thus helping with the differential. Lesions of lichen planus pigmentosus are hyperpigmented, with most cases presenting in skin of color. Oral involvement is rare and the trunk can be involved. Ashy dermatosis presents with blue-gray or gray-brown (ashy) macules and patches most commonly on the trunk, neck, and proximal extremities in a symmetric distribution. Histologic analysis will demonstrate vacuolar degeneration of the basal layer with pigmentary incontinence and dermal macrophages laden with melanin.

question: A 63-year-old male develops small, non-tender, violaceous papules on his dorsal hands, face, ears, and trunk. The patient also develops a destructive arthropathy with finger deformities. What percentage of patients with this condition has an associated malignancy?
explanation: This patient has developed multicentric reticulohistiocytosis. Histopathology of the skin lesions will display multinucleated oncocytic giant cells with eosinophilic ground glass cytoplasm. Half of these patients will develop a mutilating arthritis. 20-25% of patients with multicentric reticulohistiocytosis will develop an associated malignancy. The malignancy is usually a carcinoma, but there is no predominant type.

question: In alkaptonuria there is a blue-black discoloration in the sclera near the insertion of the rectus muscles. This sign is referred to as which of the following?
explanation: Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disease with a deficiency in homogentisate 1,2- dioxygenase. The osler sign is a blue black discoloration in the sclera near the insertion of the rectus muscles, oil droplet opacities in the cornea, pigmented pingucela, and granules in the episclera.

question: Which of the following contains active furocoumarins?
explanation: The fig tree contains active furocoumarins, which may cause a phytophotodermatitis.

question: What is the most common cutaneous finding in POEMS syndrome?
explanation: Hyperpigmentation. POEMS syndrome, also known as Crow-Fukase syndrome, is an acronym for polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy (most common being hypogonadism), M-protein (IgG and IgA light chains), and skin changes. Of the cutaneous signs, hyperpigmentation is the most common, occurring in up to 90% of affected patients.

question: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is associated with mutations in collagen VII. Trauma or friction induced blistering in these patients have a plane a splitting in the:

choices.B: None of these answers are correct

explanation: The split in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is found in the sublamina densa, where the collagen VII anchors the epidermis to the anchoring plaques in the dermis.

question: Pineapples contain which of the following proteolytic enzymes?

choices.D: All of these answers are correct
choices.E: None of these answers are correct

explanation: Bromelin is a proteolytic enzyme found in pineapples. It is granted access to dermal vessels by calcium oxalate-induced fissures.

question: Which of the following are true regarding actinic reticuloid?

choices.A: CD4+ T cells in lesional skin
choices.E: Positive photo patch testing is rare

explanation: Actinic reticuloid is a type of chronic actinic dermatitis. Ive et al. introduced the disease as a severe dermatosis with no apparent photoallergen. It generally affects elderly males and is characterized by infiltrated erythematous plaques on an eczematous background in exposed sites with lymphadenopathy.

question: A 52-year-old, previously healthy patient presents with sudden onset painful violaceous papules and plaques on the arms and legs. Denied preceding illness, including upper respiratory or gastrointestinal complaints. Other pertinent positive reviews of system findings included fever (Tmax of 102F), myalgias, arthralgias, lethargy, and painful skin lesions. The patient is not hypotensive, diaphoretic, or tachycardic. No family history of similar illness, and the patient denied recent travel or sick contacts. Blood cultures are no growth to date. Based on the history and clinical photos, which of the following treatments is most appropriate?
explanation: C) The correct answer is systemic corticosteroids. The patient has Sweet syndrome (SS, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis). SS is characterized by the abrupt onset tender erythematous papulonodules or plaques with predominantly dermal neutrophilic infiltrates. SS may be categorized into 3 categories: classic, malignancy-associated, and drug-induced subtypes. The differential diagnosis includes infections, inflammatory, and neoplastic processes. Although SS is a diagnosis of exclusion, proper work-up should include sterile tissue biopsies for tissue culture and histology. The diagnostic criteria for SS is abrupt onset of typical cutaneous lesions, histopathology consistent with SS, and two of the four minor criteria (fever and constitutional signs and symptoms; preceding associated infections, vaccinations or associated malignancies, inflammatory disorders, drug exposure or pregnancy; leukocytosis; excellent response to systemic steroids). This patient’s histopathology showed dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrates and tissue culture was negative for bacteria, atypical mycobacteria, and fungi. Systemic corticosteroids are considered first-line therapy with excellent response bring a minor diagnostic criterion. For patients in whom systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated or a steroid-sparing agent is preferred, colchicine (1.5 mg/day), dapsone (100-200 mg/day), and potassium iodide (900 mg/day) are reasonable options. This patient responded quickly to systemic prednisone (1 mg/kg tapered over 6 weeks) with no disease recurrence at six-month follow-up.

question: A 13-year-old boy presents with skin lesions that flare during the spring and summer, especially in temperate climates. Phototesting to both UVA and UVB is abnormal, suggesting that his skin lesions can be provoked by UVB and UVA. This example of phototesting to UVB or UVA is abnormal in approximately two-thirds of patients with which condition?

choices.E: Actinic prurigo ? Photorecall reaction to methotrexate

explanation: Photoaggravated dermatoses are conditions in which the primary underlying disease is not caused, but rather exacerbated, by sun exposure, sometimes severely. Phototesting is usually normal, with lupus erythematosus being the exception. Photoaggravated dermatoses include: Hartnup disease, reticular erythematous mucinosis, and Grover disease. Actinic prurigo is triggered by UVR exposure and therefore typically flares during spring and summer, especially in temperate climates. In actinic prurigo, phototesting results are abnormal in approximately two-thirds of patients and cutaneous lesions can be provoked by UVB or UVA. Phototesting in patients taking methotrexate is normal.

incorrect_rationales.D:
Hartnup disease

?. Photorecall reaction to methotrexate

question: You are evaluating a 44-year-old man who presents with a new rash. He takes off his shirt and raises his arms to show you. In the left axilla, you see a hyperpigmented velvety plaque. Which one of the following medical conditions should consider?
explanation: The patient likely has acanthosis nigricans associated with diabetes mellitus and insulin resistance.

question: A patient presents with a focal absence of epidermis on the scalp. This can be associated with:
explanation: Patients that are diagnosed with Adams-Oliver syndrome have aplasia cutis congenita (ACC) over the posterior scalp, terminal transverse defects of the limbs, and small toenails. Most aplasia cutis congenita cases are on the scalp and present as single lesions. ACC can also be associated with Trisomy 13.

question: Which of the following is the best treatment for this condition?
explanation: This is peri-oral dermatitis, which is best treated with doxycycline of these choices. Several therapies, including oral antibiotics (e.g., tetracyclines), topical antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, clindamycin), topical metronidazole, topical azelaic acid, topical sulfacetamide-sulfur, and topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus), have been used with some success to treat peri-oral dermatitis.

question: The Gorlin syndrome is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Mesothelioma is a feature of the BAP1-cancer syndrome; it is not associated with Gorlin syndrome.

question: What is the average time between a basal cell carcinoma primary tumor and its metastasis?
explanation: The size of a basal cell carcinoma is directly related to its metastasis risk. Invasion of bone, cartilage, and muscle is not common, however, spread does occur along the perichondrium, periosteum, fascia, or tarsal plate. The most common site of metastasis is the to lymph nodes.

question: This variant of amyloidosis is derived from degenerated tonofilaments of keratinocytes:
explanation: Lichen amyloidosis and macular amyloidosis are derived from degenerated tonofilaments of keratinocytes.

question: Palmoplantar keratoderma with deafness is caused by a defect in which gene?
explanation: Palmoplantar keratoderma with deafness is caused by a defect connexin 26 encoded by GJB2.

question: Variants of xeroderma pigmentosum are due to all of the following defects except:
explanation: The photosensitivity of xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by defect in DNA repair mechanisms. Helicase is involved with DNA unwinding and is mutated in XP-B and XP-D. XP-F and XP-G involves a mutation in an endonuclease that incises damaged DNA for repair. Thymidine kinase is not affected.

question: An 8 year-old child comes into the dermatology office for a linear, psoriasiform plaque on the right upper leg. The lesion is biopsied and is consistent with an inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus. However, on histology, there is also granular degeneration of the upper layrs of the epidermis with large, clumped, keratohyalin granules, and compact orthokeratosis. What condition could the offspring of this patient be at risk for?
explanation: Epidermolytic ichthyosis. Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis is associated with mutations in keratins 1 and 10, and ILVEN with EHK are thought to occur because of mosaic mutations in these genes. Patients with ILVEN revealing EHK histology may transmit the mutated gene to their offspring resulting in widespread cutaneous involvement known as epidermolytic ichthyosis or bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma and must be counseled about this possibility.

question: A 52-year-old man is hospitalized for chronic pancreatitis.
