Reactive arthritis, formerly called Reiter's syndrome, is a chronic inflammatory disease similar to psoriasis with psoriatic arthritis, and is thought to be a variant form. The classic triad consists of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis. Few patients present with the classic triad, and thus the syndrome can be diagnosed with peripheral arthritis >1 month duration and associated urethritis (or cervicitis). It occurs in young men with the HLA-B27 genotype and rarely occurs in women. Skin findings include keratoderma blennorrhagicum and circinate balanitis (in men), as well as oral erosions, severe stomatitis, and nail changes. The course of disease is marked by exacerbation and remission; a chronic deforming arthritis occurs in 20%. Treatment includes topical steroids, NSAIDs, methotrexate, acitretin, cyclosporine, and TNF-inhibiting biologics, such as etanercept. The condition is no longer referred to as Reiter's syndrome, after it was discovered that Hans Reiter committed war crimes as a Nazi at the Buchenwald concentration camp during World War II.

question: Which of the following is a progestin used in oral contraceptives with low intrinsic androgenic properties?
explanation: Desogestrel, norgestimate and gestodone are progestins with low intrinsic androgenic properties. Antiandrogenic progestins include drospirenone and cyproterone.

question: Transmission of this eruption is primarily via which route?
explanation: Varicella is primarily spread via respiratory droplets, and less frequently, direct contact.

question: Patients with Chondrodysplasia punctata can have findings of stippled epiphyses on X-ray examination. Which other x-linked dominant condition can have stippled epiphyses?
explanation: All of the syndromes listed have X-linked dominant inheritance. CHILD syndome also has findings of stippled epiphyses.

question: The most likely organism to cause this infection is:
explanation: The organism that causes erosio interdigitalis blastomycetica is candida albicans.

question: Which HLA type is more commonly associated with this clinical finding?
explanation: The condition shown is balnitis circinata which is part of the constellation of findings in Reiter's syndrome in addition to arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. There is a higher incidence of this condition people with HLA-B27.

question: A teenage patient with several weeks of fatigue, fever, and pharyngitis develops a morbilliform eruption after receiving amoxicillin. The causative organism of his systemic symptoms may cause all of the following diseases EXCEPT:

choices.A: Non-sexually related acute genital ulcers (Lipschutz ulcers)

explanation: The correct answer is E. The question describes the ampicillin/amoxicillin rash associated with infectious mononucleosis and EBV infection. EBV causes all of the following except for E; JC virus causes PML.

question: The patient demonstrated with these cutaneous findings would most likely also have which of the following?
explanation: This patient has eruptive xanthomas, a condition which is classically associated with elevated serum triglycerides.

question: Hepatitis C infection is associated with:
explanation: Cutaneous manifestation associated with hepatitis C include necrolytic acral erythema, porphyria cutanea tarda, lichen planus, polyarteritis nodosa and mixed cryoglobulinemia. Mixed cryoglobulinemias is a systemic vasculitis with variable manifestations including palpable purpura, arthralgias and weakness.

question: What is the most appropriate action in this otherwise healthy patient based on the image in the photograph?

choices.D: Magnetic resonance imaging of the foot

explanation: The image depicts piezogenic papules, a benign entity associated with fatty connective tissue protrusion (most commonly) of the heel. Plain film of the foot will not reveal anything. Magnetic resonance imaging of the foot may provide additional detail particularly if the foot were under pressure - revealing areas of slight protrusion of fatty connective tissue - but imaging is not necessary to make this diagnosis.

question: An HIV positive male presents with psoriasis over 8% of his body (not face or scalp), he has not tried any prescription medications. He is not using moisturizers. What is the correct initial approach?

choices.A: Begin acitretin 25 mg PO daily after checking CBC, CMP, lipid panel
choices.B: Begin Otezla (apremilast) starter pack by mouth as directed with goal to titrate up to 30 mg two times a day
choices.C: Start mometasone 0.1 ointment BID to affected areas on body, advise face to feet moisturizer at least BID
choices.D: Test the patient for tuberculosis and if negative start Humira (adalimumab) subcu injection 80 mg initial dose on day 1 followed by 40 mg subcu
choices.E: injection on day 8 and 40 mg subcu every two weeks thereafter ? Start cyclosporine and monitor renal function and blood pressure

correct_text:
Start mometasone 0.1 ointment BID to affected areas on body, advise face to
feet moisturizer at least BID
explanation: The correct answer is to begin topical steroid two times a day to the rash and use emollient at least two times a day to the body in patient with 8% BSA psoriasis who has not tried any prescription treatments.

question: Spastic diplegia is associated with which of the following disorders?
explanation: Sjogren-Larsson syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ALDH3A2 gene that encodes the enzyme fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase. This disorder is characterized by ichthyosis with pruritus, spastic diplegia or quadriplegia, mental retardation, epilepsy, glistening dot retinal pigmentation, and dental enamel dysplasia.

question: What is the most likely causative organism of this eruption?
explanation: The erythematous serpiginous eruption across the foot shown here is a classic presentation for larva migrans. These lesions are the result of the hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense penetrating the intact epidermis and migrating at the rate of 1-3 cm/day.

question: A rancher in Central America is seen for a well-circumscribed and necrotic ulcer on the hand with an overlying eschar. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Anthrax, also known as woolsorter’s disease or malignant pustule is caused by Bacillus anthracis, a gram-positive rod. It is primarily caused by contact with infected wild or domestic animals including sheep, cattle, horses, goats, or their products such as wool. This organism has 3 clinical forms: inhalation, gastrointestinal and cutaneous. The primary lesion is a “malignant pustule” which begins as a painless papule that evolves into a hemorrhagic bulla. Ultimately, a black eschar forms. The lack of pain is helpful in distinguishing between anthrax and other infections of the skin which are painful, such as ecthyma. The other listed organisms are not causes of this disease. file:///tmp/Quiz_Questions_1778874819.html Page 1,514 of 1,559

question: Which of the following is TRUE about the patient with this finding?

choices.A: Oral cephalexin should provide significant improvement in this lesion.
choices.B: This patient likely has an underlying immunodeficiency.
choices.C: Excision is the most definitive treatment for this lesion.
choices.D: Histologically, numerous neutrophils are seen at the edge of the ulcer.
choices.E: This patient likely has an underlying psychiatric disorder.

correct_text: This patient likely has an underlying psychiatric disorder
explanation: This patient likely has an underlying psychiatric disorder. This is a factitial lesion, which is evidenced by the irregular, sharp, geometric borders, and lack of surrounding inflammation.

question: A 24-year-old female patient presents with groups of itchy and tender small red papules around the eyes, nostrils, and mouth. Which of the following treatments is the first-line treatment used to treat severe cases of this condition?
explanation: Periorificial dermatitis is a common facial skin problem characterized by groups of itchy or tender small red papules. It is given this name because the papules occur around the eyes, the nostrils, the mouth, and occasionally, the genitals. In more severe cases, a course of anti-inflammatory oral antibiotics may be prescribed for 6–12 weeks as the first-line treatment. This also helps to reduce the rebound flare seen after stopping the topical steroid.

question: A 30 year old pregnant woman presents with a red lesion near her nail that has rapidly appeared. She is in her third trimester, and has had a normal pregnancy course to date. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A pyogenic granuloma is one of several vascular lesions that can present on the skin during pregnancy, and they often develop rapidly in a peri-ungual location. At present, the pathogenesis of pyogenic granuloma is unknown. In addition to pregnancy, reported triggers include antecedent trauma and certain drugs, including acitretin, HIV protease inhibitors, EGFR inhibitors, docetaxel, capecitabine and rituximab. In the case of pyogenic granulomas arising during pregnancy, they often regress after delivery and treatment is not usually required unless they cause excessive bleeding.

question: Which form of BCC is the most common form in patients with HIV infection?
explanation: Superficial BCC is the most common form of BCC seen in patients with HIV.

question: A 31-year-old male is admitted for fever, weight loss, malaise and mild shortness of breath. Dermatology is consulted for a widespread eruption of the lesoins pictured scattered on the arms, legs, trunk, nose, cheeks, chin, and oral mucosa. The oral mucosa also demonstrates white patches that can be removed with gentle pressure to reveal underlying erythema. Which of the following herpes viruses is implicated in the pathogenesis of the growths in this patient?
explanation: The case describes AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma (KS), an angioproliferative tumor involving the skin and other organs. The oral muscoal finding of thrush and Kaposi sarcoma are both AIDS- defining illnesses. HHV-8 is found in classic, AIDS-associated and immunosuppression-associated KS. It is the inciting factor in KS pathogenesis, and it infects lymphatic and vascular endothelial cells. Although HHV-9 infection is necessary for the development of KS, it is not sufficient. Transmission is not fully understood, but has been reported through sexual contact, saliva contact and blood transfusion. HHV-8 can be detected in KS through immunohistochemical staining.

question: The causative organism of epidemic typhus is:
explanation: Epidemic typhus is caused by infection with R. prowazekii, usually transmitted by the body louse.

question: A 2 year old female patient has linear atrophy in a Blasckoid distribution, alopecia, nail dystrophy, abnormal teeth, and colobomas. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
explanation: Focal dermal hypoplasia, or Goltz syndrome, is an x-linked dominant condition with a defect in the PORCN gene. It is characterized by linear atrophy in a Blasckoid distribution, alopecia, nail dystrophy, abnormal teeth, and colobomas. file:///tmp/Quiz_Questions_1778874819.html Page 1,519 of 1,559

question: Pernio or Chilblains is an inflammatory skin condition which is triggered by cold, wet, non- freezing environmental conditions. Acral skin has violaceous discoloration accompanied by burning or itching. While avoidance and prevention is best, the most effective pharmacologic treatment is:
explanation: Nifedipine is effective in about 70% of patients with pernio in prevention of the development of new skin lesions. The other options listed, other than aspirin, are anecdotally suggested to be helpful.

question: Solar urticaria:

choices.A: Can present with nausea, wheezing dyspnea and syncope
choices.B: Usually occurs to only UVB radiation
choices.D: Is an idiopathic, type IV photosensitivity disorder
choices.E: Rarely lasts for more than 6 months to 1 year

correct_text: Can present with nausea, wheezing dyspnea and syncope
explanation: Mediator release during widespread whealing from solar urticaria may result in nausea, wheezing, faintness, and syncope.

question: LEMD3 is mutated in which of the following syndromes?
explanation: LEMD3 or MAN1 is mutated in Buschke-Ollendorf syndrome. Common skin findings include dermatofibrofibrosis lenticularis disseminata. The radiographic finding commonly seen is osteopoikilosis. The gene defect was recently described as MAN1/LEMD3, a gene encoding for a nuclear membrane protein.

question: The most common cutaneous association with monilethrix is:
explanation: Monilethrix is an autosomal dominant condition which, by definition, presents with beaded hair. Clinically, patients present with short, sparse lusterless hair. Keratosis pilaris is the most common associated feature.

question: On dermoscopy, which of the following findings most strongly supports the correct diagnosis?
explanation: Maple leaf structures on dermoscopy support the diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

question: This patient has less than three lesions which are anesthetic and anhidrotic. What cytokine profile does this condition have?
explanation: This is tuberculoid leprosy which classically has a low concentration of organisms because the body is reacting to the M. leprae. Thus the patients get anesthesia and anhidrosis. There are typically less than three hypopigmented patches. Tuberculoid leprosy is associated with a Th1 cytokine profile including IFN-gamma, IL-2 and IL-12. Lepromatous leprosy is Th2.

question: A patient is given a single dose of diethylcarbamazine and soon after develops edema, itching, fever, arthralgias, and exacerbation of pruritus. The patient most likely has which of the following underlying infections?
explanation: This patient developed an acute reaction to diethylcarbamazine, indicating a Mazzotti reaction. This reaction is seen with onchocerciasis. The appropriate treatment for onchocerciasis, caused by Onchocerca volvulus, is ivermectin. These patients may demonstrate pruritus, dermatitis, leopard skin, onchocercomas (nodules with microfilariae), and blindness.

question: Common drugs causing SJS/TEN include all except:
explanation: NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, and sulfa drugs are common inciting agents of SJS/TEN. The drugs that most commonly cause SJS/TEN are: Sulfonamides: cotrimoxizole Beta-lactam: penicillins, cephalosporins Anti-convulsants: lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone Allopurinol Paracetamol/acetominophen Nevirapine (non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (oxicam type mainly).

question: A 72 year old male patient presents with mucosal lesions as well as skin lesions that blister. The DIF has a fine linear deposition along the DEJ. What is the target antigen of cicatricial pemphigoid?
explanation: This is cicatricial pemphigoid which can affect the mucosa and the skin. The antigen is the C- terminus of BPAg2.

question: Contagious pustular dermatitis (Orf) is caused by a:
explanation: Orf is caused by orf virus (OV), a poxvirus of the genus Parapoxvirus.

question: Rare cases of which photosensitivity disorder have been associated with erythropoietic protoporphyria?
explanation: Rare cases of solar urticaria have been associated with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), lupus erythematosus (LE), and with certain drugs. Blood tests for LE and EPP should be performed in patients with this diagnosis.

question: A 77-year-old male with a past medical history consistent with HIV/AIDS presents to the dermatology clinic with a tender, ulcerated abscess on his neck. Biopsy is performed, which reveals the findings depicted in the histologic image. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation: The image, along with the vignette, describes Cryptococcossis in setting of HIV/AIDS. Histopathology can reveal a gelatinous pattern with many organisms or a granulomatous pattern with fewer organisms. In addition, inflammation and necrosis can also be noted. PAS will stain the central yeast forms, and other stains that can be used include mucicarmine, Alcian blue, and India ink. The causative agents are usually Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii, and immunosuppressed states (as described in this case) can increase risk of acquiring this infection, especially if exposed to soil or pigeon droppings. Most infections remain within the lungs (90%), but 10% of cases can disseminate. Treatments include amphotericin B, Fluconazole, and Voriconazole.

question: A 55-year-old White woman presents for evaluation of hair loss. Examination reveals decreased frontal scalp hair density with perifollicular erythema and scale. A punch biopsy is performed to confirm the diagnosis. Which of the following represents the most likely histologic findings from this patient?

choices.A: Peribulbar mononuclear cell infiltrate (with occasional eosinophils), with an increased number of miniaturized hairs
choices.B: Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate obscuring the interface between follicular epithelium and dermis
choices.C: Incomplete, disrupted follicular anatomy with pigment casts noted
choices.D: Decreased total number of hairs, with loss of the sebaceous glands and residual hair shafts surrounded by mild, granulomatous inflammation
choices.E: Vacuolar interface alteration of the epidermis with increased mucin

correct_text:
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate obscuring the interface between follicular
epithelium and dermis
explanation: The correct answer represents the findings seen in frontal fibrosing alopecia (a subset of lichen planopilaris), which is the condition described. Lichen planopilaris manifests histologically with similar findings to lichen planus, with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate found at the dermal-epidermal junction. The infiltrate is more superficial than that of alopecia areata.

question: A 36-year-old woman presents with multiple pale pink papules on the bilateral cheeks and lower eyelids over the last week. There is no erythema or telangiectasias on exam. A biopsy of one of the lesions is performed, showing periadnexal granulomas with central caseating necrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the treatment of the patient?
explanation: The patient’s pale pink papules with involvement of the lower eyelids and pathology showing caseating periadnexal granulomas is most consistent with lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei. There is limited evidence for treatment, however existing studies show benefit from oral dapsone, used with or without prednisolone for treatment of this condition.

question: A 38-year-old man with psoriasis complicated by arthritis presents for treatment of nail pitting. He has previously used triamcinolone 0.1% ointment to control his psoriasis, including on his nails; however, he has been unable to see improvement in his nails, which has been bothersome and extensive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of the patient’s disease?
explanation: In a patient with psoriatic arthritis and extensive nail involvement who has previously trialed topical corticosteroids, a trial of a systemic biologic agent is likely the most appropriate choice. There is some evidence of including tazarotene or tacrolimus ointments, though given the extensive involvement a biologic agent may be best. Prior studies have shown efficacy in a variety of biologic agents for both psoriatic arthritis and nail involvement—which can be related to poor quality of life.

question: A patient with Bloom Syndrome is most likely to have which laboratory abnormalities:
explanation: Bloom syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder due to a mutation in the BLM gene which codes for a DNA helicase. Patients have impaired DNA repair after UV exposure and increased photosensitivity. Clinical features include photodistributed erythema, cheilitis, high-pitched voice, hypogonadism, and increased risk for leukemia, lymphoma and GI adenocarcinoma. Laboratory evaluation reveals decreased IgA, IgM and IgG leading to increased risk of respiratory infections.

question: Which of the following skin manifestations of M. tuberculosis infection is a tuberculid?
explanation: A tuberculid is a cutaneous immunologic reaction to tuberculosis elsewhere in the body. By definition, cultures and stains for M. tuberculosis are negative. Erythema induratum of Bazin/ Nodular vasculitis present as erythematous or cyanotic nodules on the posterior calves. 85% of cases occur in women.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of diabetic skin?

choices.A: There is a well-established association between deep granuloma annulare (GA) and diabetes
choices.B: Candida tropicalis is the most common cause of angular cheilitis
choices.C: Yellow skin may occur in up to 10% of diabetics
choices.D: Approximately 20% of diabetics have necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum (NLD)
choices.E: The level of cleavage in bullous diabeticorum is subcorneal

correct_text: Yellow skin may occur in up to 10% of diabetics
explanation: Perhaps 0.3 to 3% of diabetics have NLD, whereas approximately 20% of NLD patients have diabetes or glucose intolerance. The split in bullous diabeticorum is normally either intraepidermal or subepidermal. C. albicans is the most common cause of diabetes-related yeast infections. The association between GA and diabetes is controversial, but if the two are related, generalized and perforating GA have been implicated. Yellow skin may occur in up to 10% of diabetic patients and is characterized by diffuse yellow-orange skin. Half of these patients have elevated serum carotene levels. The suggested is cause is elevated consumption of yellow fruits and vegetables in the setting of impaired hepatic metabolism of carotene and subsequent non-enzymatic glycosylation of dermal collagen.

question: The most effective treatment for symptomatic ocular rosacea is:

choices.E: Combination topical antibiotic and corticosteroid eye drops

explanation: Gentle lid washes, warm compresses, eye drops and topical antibiotics may quell mild lif inflammation. For those with moderate to severe ocular rosacea, short courses of oral tetracyclines prove to be the most effective treatment.

question: Which of the following is true regarding immediate pigment darkening?

choices.C: Requires the synthesis of new melanin

explanation: Tanning develops in two phases, early (transitory) and late (stable). The immediate darkening is in response to UVA and is related to photo-oxidation of pre-existing melanin.

question: Which of the following is not a tick-borne disease?
explanation: Yaws is caused by Treponema palladium, subspecies pertunue, which is transmitted nonsexually by contact with infectious lesions.

question: Scrofuloderma is most commonly associated with an underlying infection of what organ system?
explanation: Scrofuloderma is a tuberculous or nontuberculous mycobacterial infection affecting children and young adults, representing direct extension of tuberculosis into the skin from underlying structures such as lymph nodes, bone, or lung. It most commonly presents as a neck abscess secondary to a tuberculosis infection of the cervical lymph nodes. It is manifested by the development of painless subcutaneous swellings that evolve into cold abscesses, multiple ulcers, and draining sinus tracts. The diagnosis is based on positive Mantoux test/PPD test, histologic features of caseating granulomatous inflammation, culture, and favorable response to anti-tuberculosis therapy.

question: A florist presents with painful, red, thickened, and fissured fingertips involving both hands, along with throat tightness and lip swelling after handling the flowers shown. She reports similar reactions in the past when arranging bouquets. What is this plant, associated with "tulip fingers" and allergic contact dermatitis due to tulipalin A?
explanation: Alstroemeria (Peruvian lily) is shown. It is a well-recognized cause of fingertip allergic contact dermatitis in florists, known as "tulip fingers." The allergen is tulipalin A (a hydrolyzed tuliposide), a potent sensitizer that causes painful, fissured, thickened fingertips. Florists and horticulture workers are at highest risk. Airborne symptoms such as allergic conjunctivitis, throat tightness, urticaria, and facial angioedema may also occur. Alstroemeria belongs to the Alstroemeriaceae family (formerly grouped with Liliaceae). Tulipalin A is also found in true tulips (Liliaceae), leading to cross-reactivity.

question: Inhibition of which of the following enzymes is most likely to improve the patient’s condition, as shown in the images?
explanation: Note the lesions on the abdomen, for which histopathology shows findings confirming a diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis. The treatment of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis is dapsone. Dapsone works by inhibition of myeloperoxidase, leading to decreased neutrophilic oxidative damage.

question: Crusted scabies is a risk factor for all the follow patients except:
explanation: Farmers are not at increased risk of crusted scabies.

question: Papillary dermal deposits of IgA and a papillary dermal infiltrate of neutrophils is diagnostic of:
explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an uncommon chronic, pruritic papulovesicular dermatitis occurring most commonly in young to middle-aged adults. Common sites of predilection include the buttocks, elbows, knees, scapula and scalp. Typical histologic features include accumulation of neutrophils at the tips of dermal papillae sometimes admixed with eosinophils. Direct immunoflorescence (DIF) reveals granular deposits of IgA within the dermal papillae.

question: Which of the following is most closely associated with Staphylococcus aureus?
explanation: Bullous impetigo is caused by phage group II Staphylococcus aureus.

question: Which contact allergen is found in Krazy glue?
explanation: Ethyl cyanoacrylate is a chemical found in Krazy Glue. It can also be found in nail adhesives causing a dermatitis on the face and fingers, nail dystrophy, and a generalized rash. Formaldehyde is a widely used chemical found in a variety of applications and is a common allergen. It can be found in paper, skin and hair products, cosmetics, and permanent press textiles.

question: The term used to describe the thinning of the hair shaft, which forms constrictions along the hair, due to the disruption of the anagen cycle is:
explanation: Pohl Pinkus constriction is due to a toxic insult. This causes the disruption of the anagen cycle with thinning of the hair shaft, forming constrictions along the hair. This is analogous to Beau's lines in nails.

question: The development of which malignancy is most commonly associated with lymphomatoid papulosis?
explanation: Lymphomatoid papulosis is a recurrant eruption of unclear etiology characterized by the appearance of red-brown papules and nodules which spontaneously disappear in 3 to 8 weeks. It is notable for histologic features which suggest a CD30 positive malignant lymphoma. There is controversy regarding whether lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) is a malignant, premalignant or benign condition. The disease may last from months to years and in up to 20% of patients, it may be preceded by, followed by, or associated with another type of cutaneous malignancy. Generally, this is mycosis fungoides, a CD30-positive large T-cell lymphoma or Hodgkin's disease. Because of this potential risk, long-term follow-up of these patients is required.

question: Patients with hemochromatosis are at increased risk for which of the following?

choices.E: All of these options are correct

correct_text: All of these options are correct
explanation: Patients with hemochromatosis have increased intestinal iron absorption leading to systemic iron overload. Signs include a generalized metallic-grey to brown hyperpigmentation, koilonychia, alopecia (especially pubic/axillary hair), cardiac failure/arrhythmias/heart block, hepatomegaly with cirrhosis, diabetes (bronze diabetes), polyarthritis with chondrocalcinosis and are susceptible to Vibrio vulnificus and Yersinia infections.

question: What organism produces round thick walled spiny macroconidia and pear shaped microconidia?
explanation: At room temperature Histoplasma capsulatum produces round thick walled spiny macroconidia and pear shaped microconidia.

question: A 35-year-old male presents with painful ulceration on his left lower leg which appeared four days ago and has been growing larger. He has no other skin lesions. He denies any trauma to the area, has no personal or family history of autoimmune disease, and has not traveled out of the country in many years. He does not take any medications. He smokes cigarettes and endorses cocaine use about 2 weeks ago. Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause his leg ulcer?
explanation: Levamisole is a synthetic antihelminthic medication that is a common bulking agent in cocaine, present in up to 70% of the US supply of cocaine. Levamisole-associated vasculopathy can occur several days to weeks after using contaminated cocaine. The classic skin finding is tender purpura, commonly on the external ears and cheeks. However, pyoderma gangrenosum has also been reported with cocaine tainted with levamisole. These ulcerations occur on the lower or upper extremities, lacking the arthralgias or ear purpura involvement of classic levamisole toxicity. Levamisole-associated pyoderma gangrenosum has been reported to respond to brief courses of systemic steroids.

question: A child is brought to your clinic for evaluation. Upon examination of his nails, you notice triangular lunulae. Which of the following do you also expect to find on exam?
explanation: The finding of triangular lunulae should alert one to the diagnosis of Nail-Patella syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition due to a LMX1B mutation. Absent or hypoplastic patellae is characteristic of this condition.

question: A 56-year-old woman presents with an expanding ulceration on her lower extremities, which have grown over the last several months. Dermoscopy of the lesion reveals a yellow, structureless background with linear vessels with branching. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for the patient?
explanation: Recognize the depressed ulcerations on the lower extremities with the dermoscopic findings consistent with necrobiosis lipoidica. Treatment of this condition should include intralesional or topical corticosteroids or topical tacrolimus.

question: Which genetic defect could explain cutaneous findings in addition to abnormal immunoglobulin levels, recurrent respiratory infections, hypogonadism, and an increased risk of leukemia and lymphoma?
explanation: Bloom's syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the RecQL3 gene encoding a DNA helicase. Clinically, individuals with Bloom's syndrome have a photodistributed erythema with telangectasia on the malar eminences. The may also have decreased IgM and IgA levels, hypogonadism, and an increased risk for leukemia and lymphoma.

question: What phenotype results from a low activity of double stranded RNA adenosine deaminase?
explanation: Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (or acropigmentation symmetrica of Dohi) is an autosomal dominant disease with hypo and hyper pigmented macules and patches on the dorsal hands and feet associated with a low activity of double stranded RNA adenosine deaminase.

question: Acute intermittent porphyria has an enzyme defect in:
explanation: Acute intermittent porphyria has a defect in porphobilinogen deaminase. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare autosomal dominant metabolic disorder affecting the production of heme, the oxygen-binding prosthetic group of hemoglobin. They present with periodic attacks of colic, paralyses (motor neuropathy), and psychiatric disorders, but no skin lesions.

question: Which of the following is a feature of microcystic adnexal carcinoma that DOES NOT help distinguish it from a desmoplastic trichoepithelioma?
explanation: Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma is one of the differential diagnoses for microcystic adnexal carcinoma. Both MAC and desmoplastic trichoepithelioma commonly arise on the face.

question: Which two characteristics combined form a significant risk for acquiring sporotrichosis? 1. Animal handler 2. Male gender 3. Alcoholism 4. Filipino or African decent 5. Genetic predisposition
explanation: A variety of domestic animals can carry Sporotrichosis. Alcoholism increases the risk for this cutaneous infection.

question: A 35 year-old dentist presents with tingling in his fingertips. What allergen is most likely to cause this dermatitis?
explanation: Methyl methacrylate is found in synthetic resins, dentures, artificial, nail adhesives, and acrylic bone cement. This allergen may penetrate through the gloves to the fingertips and most often affects the first three fingers. In addition to dermatitis, it also causes a peripheral neuropathy.

question: A woman with no known past medical history comes into your dermatology office with several small, firm, skin-colored papules in the periorbital area, especially the eyelids. You biopsy one of the lesions, and the histology is below. What test should you order next for the patient?
explanation: Histology features a clear cell syringoma. Clear cell syringomas are associated with diabetes mellitus. Therefore, screening for diabetes with an HbA1c may be performed.

question: A 7 year old girl with abnormally short hair has progressive seizures, lethargy, ataxia, and mental retardation. A blood test reveals elevated levels of ammonia. What is the affected gene?
explanation: Argininosuccinic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in argininosuccinase. It is characterized by trichorrhexis nodosa, hyperammonemia, hepatomegaly and vomiting, seizures, lethargy, coma, ataxia, and mental retardation.

question: A patient has a granulomatous plaque that is diagnosed as swimming pool granuloma. The treatment for this is:
explanation: Swimming pool granuloma or fish tank granuloma is caused by M. marinum and begins as a small plaque at the site of inoculation and evolves to a granulomatous plaque. It occurs as a sporotrichoid spread. The treatment is minocycline.

question: This type of syphilis has the clinical characteristic of widespread cutaneous eruptions, ham- colored macules on the palms and soles, moth eaten alopecia and condyloma lata.
explanation: This is an example of secondary syphilis. It involves the skin and mucous membranes. It also lasts for 4 to 12 weeks. It involved widespread cutaneous eruptions, ham-colored macules on the palms and soles, mucous patches, condyloma lata, split papules and moth eaten alopecia.

question: Blueberry Muffin Baby can be a feature of all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Blueberry muffin lesions can be seen in the setting of prenatal infections (e.g. TORCH), severe anemia (e.g. Hemolytic Disease of the newborn) and neoplastic diseases (e.g. rhabdomyosarcoma). It has also been reported with LCH.

question: Which of the following are characteristics of Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome?

choices.A: Shortened phalanges, sparse hair, bulbous nose
choices.B: Brittle hair, short stature, cerebellar ataxia
choices.C: Palmoplantar keratoderma, trichorrhexis nodosa, sinus infections
choices.D: Sparse fine hair, Short extremities, Immunodeficiency
choices.E: Kinky hair, frontal bossing, small widely spaced teeth with poor enamel

correct_text: Shortened phalanges, sparse hair, bulbous nose
explanation: Characteristic features of trichorhinophalangeal syndrome are shortened phalanges, sparse hair, and bulbous nose.

question: Lumisterol is an inactive epidermal reservoir of which vitamin?
explanation: Lumisterol and tachysterol are inert byproducts created during the biosynthesis of vitamin D. When Previtamin D3 is exposed to light, it can result in photoisomerization of previtamin D3 to lumisterol and tachysterol. If previatmin D3 is depleted, lumisterol and tachysterol can become converted back to previtamin D3.

question: A patient has Conradi-Hunermann-Happle syndrome with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, ventricular septal defect, and asymmetric limb shortening. The bone finding for the disease is:
explanation: Patients with Conradi-Hunermann-Happle syndrome has chondrodysplasia punctata that is X- linked dominant. They have ventricular septal defects and asymmetric limb shortening.

question: In a well-designed study, the impact of psoriasis on health-related quality of life was found to be similar to which of the following conditions?
explanation: The emotional and physical burden of psoriasis is easily underestimated. Rapp et al found that patients with psoriasis report reduced physical and mental functioning (“heath related quality of life”) similar to that seen in patients with cancer, hypertension, arthritis, heart disease, diabetes, and depression.

question: This disorder is linked to an abnormality in which of the following intercellular proteins?
explanation: In staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), phage group II Staphyloccocus aureus produces toxins that cleave desmoglein 1.

question: Phytophotodermatitis is caused by which of the following wavelengths of light?
explanation: UVA rays are responsible for the phototoxic reaction which occurs with phytophotodermatitis.

question: Which of the following is caused by a mutation in a gene that leads to defective NF-KB activation?
explanation: Incontinential pigmenti is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by a mutation in the NEMO gene located at Xq28. NEMO is an NF-KB modulator. A genetic defect in NEMO leads to defective activation of NF-KB (a transcription factor).

question: A 24 year-old man from New York City develops fever, chills, malaise, and a severe headache. His apartment has a mouse problem. On examination, multiple, discrete papulovesicles and a single eschar are found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical description is that of rickettsialpox, which is caused by R. akari and spread by liponyssoides sanguineus - the house mouse mite.

question: Coxsackievirus A16 is implicated in the pathogenesis of which of the following dieases?
explanation: Hand-Foot-and-Mouth disease may be caused by coxsackievirus A16. Group A coxsackievirus infection is also associated with herpangina.

question: Hypopigmented mycosis fungoides:

choices.A: Does not differ from classic mycosis fungoides in terms of those affected
choices.B: Is more likely to occur in patients with skin types V and VI
choices.C: Is more likely to occur on the face
choices.D: Occurs in older patient populations in comparison to classic mycosis fungoides
choices.E: Occurs in women more commonly than men

correct_text: Is more likely to occur in patients with skin types V and VI
explanation: Hypopigmented mycosis fungoides occurs more commonly in younger patients and patients with darker skin types.

question: Common cause(s) of drug-induced pemphigus foliaceus:
explanation: Penicillamine and captopril are common causes of drug-induced pemphigus. Thiol drugs cause pemphigus foliaceus Pemphigus foliaceus presents with erythematous, scaly or crusted plaques. Vesicles, bullae and erosions may or may not be present. It most commonly affects the trunk. The oral mucosa is not involved.

question: Which of the following is not true of this condition?

choices.C: Associated with third trimester of pregnancy

explanation: The figure illustrates polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PUPPP) with erythematous papules within striae, sparing the umbilicus. There is no associated maternal or fetal risk.

question: Which of the following melanoma subtypes is more likely to be seen in patients with darker skin types?
explanation: Acral lentiginous melanoma is the predominant type of melanoma in dark-skinned individuals. It is usually located on the soles, palms, and subungual regions of patients in their fifth to sixth decade of life.

question: A patient with coarse facies, broad nasal bridge, and extensive eczema might be expected to have which abnormal laboratory value?
explanation: Patients with Hyper IgE Syndrome (Job syndrome) have impaired regulation of the IgE function and increased susceptibility to infections. In addition to recurrent cutaneous infections including cold abscesses, patients have widespread eczematous dermatitis, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and typically have coarse facies with broad nasal bridge and a prominent nose.

question: A 30-year old male presents with clustered, painful plaques on his shoulder. Histopathology showed interlacing bundles of cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and no mitoses. Desmin and SMA stains were positive. What gene defect is associated with the development of these lesions?
explanation: The patient has multiple cutaneous leiomyomas. Hereditary leiomyomatosis is an inherited defect of fumarate hydratase. These patients develop multiple cutaneous leiomyomas and have an increased incidence of renal cell carcinoma. Female patients will usually also develop significant uterine leiomyomatosis resulting in hysterectomy.

question: You are evaluating a 1-year-old female with a crusted perioral and perianal eruption and diarrhea after weaning off breastmilk. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
explanation: Acrodermatitis enteropathica occurs from genetic or acquired zinc deficiency. It presents in newborn infants at 4 to 10 weeks of age when breastmilk is weaned. There is an acral, perianal, and perioral crusted psoriasiform eruption with associated diarrhea and alopecia.

question: A newborn has a mottled pinkish blue appearance to the skin that does not change with temperature. Multiple rewarming attempts are futile. What is the most likely associated finding?
explanation: The vignettes describes a newborn with cutis mamorata telangiectasia congenita. It is distinct from cutis mamorata which is physiologic. Patients with CMTC may have no associated abnormalities but the most common of the choices here is mild ipsilateral limb hypoplasia.

question: Which of the following extracutaneous findings is most likely to be found in this 7-year-old boy?
explanation: A review of cases in the United Kingdom showed that 1 in 10 patients who are carriers of a gene mutated in X-linked ichthyosis, as shown here, have atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.

question: Which of the following underlying conditions is least likely to be associated with the finding depicted in the image?
explanation: The image shows Aplasia cutis. This condition can rarely be associated with bony abnormalities, skeletal abnormalities, brain malformations, cleft lip, and syndactyly. Liver abnormalities are not a known association with aplasia cutis

question: An infant presents with yellowish-brown, crusted papules with petechiae in a seborrheic distribution. Which of the following statements about this entity is likely to be true?

choices.A: Maternal-fetal transmission most likely occured in the peripartum period
choices.B: CD1+, S100+ cells with comma-shaped nuclei should be seen on biopsy
choices.C: This presentation is consistent with Jacquet's dermatitis
choices.D: An autosomal recessive defect in holocarboxylase synthetase is the cause
choices.E: This presentation occurs when the infant is weaned off of breast milk

correct_text: CD1+, S100+ cells with comma-shaped nuclei should be seen on biopsy
explanation: This infant has Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease). Multisystem involvement may be present.

question: You see a 3-year-old child with an asymptomatic nodule pictured below. You rub the lesion for 15 minutes and the spot urticates. Otherwise, the child is in good health. What would the next step in management be?

choices.A: Reassurance and avoidance of prevocational factors

correct_text: Reassurance and avoidance of prevocational factors
explanation: Reassurance and avoidance of prevocational factors. The patient appears to have a solitary mastocytoma with a positive Darier sign. Solitary cutaneous mastocytomas are most commonly seen in infancy. The majority of these lesions improve spontaneously over several years duration and resolve before puberty. Treatment is mainly symptomatic. Reassurance and avoidance of triggering factors suffice in most cases.1

question: The most common location of cutaneous lesions in neonatal lupus erythrematosus is:
explanation: Neonatal lupus erythrematosus(NLE) is a form of subacute cutaneous lupus erythrematosus(SCLE) that occur in infants whose mothers have anti-Ro autoantibodies. Unlike SCLE in adults, lesions of NLE have a predilection for the face especially periorbital region.

question: Which of the following is a sign of EARLY postnatal congenital syphilis?
explanation: Wimberger's sign is a sign of early postnatal congenital syphilis (occurs < 2 years old). Wimberger's sign is a radiographic sign showing a sawtooth appearance of the proximal tibia.

question: You are consulted by a pediatrician about an otherwise healthy baby born with a "wound" on the scalp with no apparent bony abnormalities on palpation. What is the next best step in management?

choices.A: Place a referral for surgical excision
choices.B: Daily dressing changes with petroleum jelly

explanation: The pictured condition is aplasia cutis congenita, a uncommon but not rare condition in neonates. It is thought to be caused by vascular insults or incomplete closure of tissues. In this child, there is no surrounding hypertrichosis or vascular stain on exam. However, the lesion does appear to be midline, which should also raise suspicion for underlying abnormalities. Therefore, the next best step would be to order an MRI to assess for central nervous system involvement.

question: A healthy 13-year-old boy presents to the pediatrician with this eruption on the hands, feet, and oral mucosa. The mother states that he also has had a fever for the last day with malaise. Which type of virus is responsible for this condition depicted in the image?
explanation: The image, along with the vignette, describes Hand-foot-and-mouth (HFM) disease. The causative agent is coxsackievirus A16, A6 which is a ssRNA picornavirus. This rash starts out as macules that progress to vesicles/pustules on the hands, feet, groin, and mucosa. Other symptoms include fever, anorexia, malaise, abdominal pain, myocarditis, pneumonia, and encephalitis. This condition usually resolves in 1 week, but the A6 variant can present with more severe blistering and widespread disease.

question: A 2 year-old has a high fever for three days, as the fever breaks, a generalized rash appears on the trunk. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Roseola (also known as exanthem subitum or Sixth disease) typically appears in toddlers. A high fever followed by a generalized maculopapular rash is characteristic for this HHV6 infection.

question: A 1-year-old female presents to the pediatrician with this eruption that started on the face and progressed to a more diffuse distribution. The mother endorses that the infant also has a cough, irritated eyes, and runny nose. Which of the following vitamins can aid in treatment of this condition?
explanation: The image, along with the vignette, describes Measles (Rubeola) or First disease. The causative agent is single stranded RNA paramyxovirus that is spread via airborne transmission. This rash starts out as erythematous macules and papules on that face, usually behind the ears, that progress to a more diffuse distribution. Koplik spots, gray-white papules on the buccal mucosa, usually appear before the rash and fade 2- 3 days after the rash onset. There is usually an associated high fever, cough, coryza (rhinitis), and conjunctivitis. Complications can be severe and include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, otitis, pneumonia, myocarditis, and delayed neurodegenerative disorder. Treatment with vitamin A can reduce morbidity.

question: A 4-month-old febrile child presents with the findings shown on the upper trunk. Obstruction of which of the following structures is most associated with the patient’s condition?
explanation: The presence of multiple vesicles on the trunk of a febrile infant or neonate should raise suspicion for miliaria. This is due to obstruction of the eccrine ducts, which reduces normal thermoregulation they provide.

question: What is the best treatment of this condition?
explanation: This is perianal strep which occurs in kids. It presents with sharply demarcated tender brightly erythematous plaques in the perianal region in children. Treatment is Penicillin or Amoxicillin for 10 days to three weeks. It can recur, and if it does it requires retreatment with antibiotics.

question: A four-year-old is seen in opthalmology by referral of neurology. He was premature at birth and has a history of seizures, learning disability, and fine scale diffusely on the body with areas of thickened skin. Eye exam notes perifoveal crystalline inclusions in the macula of the retina. Which of the following correctly highlights the pathology in this disease?

choices.A: Impaired transport of very long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes
choices.B: Impaired lipid metabolism leading to an accumulation of fatty alcohols
choices.C: Impaired lipid droplet breakdown leading to intracellular triglyceride accumulation
choices.E: Impaired lipase leading to triglyceride accumulation in muscles

correct_text: Impaired lipid metabolism leading to an accumulation of fatty alcohols
explanation: Sjogren-Larsson syndrome is caused by a deficiency of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH3A2), leading to abnormal lipid metabolism affecting the skin, brain, and retina, and is correct because it uniquely presents with ichthyosis, spastic neurological impairment, and perifoveal crystalline inclusions (glistening white dots), matching the case description.

question: A 7-year-old male returns from a camping trip to Tennessee and develops fever, headache, malaise and myalgias. He then develops a macular rash on his ankles and wrists. Given the high concern for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, what is the appropriate treatment?
explanation: The preferred treatment for all patients with Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever is doxycycline. Although tetracyclines can cause dental staining when administered to children younger than eight years old, the risk of staining is minimal if a short course is prescribed. In a study of 53 children who received doxycycline for RMSF, none developed dental staining.

question: What is the most common cause of neonatal purpura fulminans?
explanation: In children, purpura fulminans may have several causes. It is a highly characteristic feature of meningococcal septicemia and may occur as a sequelae to a number of infections, including streptococcal infections, varicella, and measles. In the neonate, however, its occurrence is highly suggestive of homozygous protein C deficiency.

question: Hereditary coproporphyria is characterized with photosensitivity and the defect is:
explanation: Hereditary coproporphyria is characterized by photosensitivity and can also present with neuropsychiatric issues. They also have skin fragility and blistering is common. It is caused by a defect in Coproporphyrinogen oxidase.

question: You are consulted to evaluate a full-term neonate in the newborn nursery and find widespread blotchy erythematous macules, papules, and pustules. Which of the following is most likely to be found upon evaluation of a smear of one of the pustules?
explanation: The stem describes the classic presentation of erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN), which occurs in nearly half of all full term neonates. The pustules are sterile and a smear shows eosinophils.

question: Posterior auricular adenopathy is a common feature of which of the following infectious exanthems?
explanation: Lymphadenopathy with 1-7 days of malaise is commonly described in rubella infection. A rose-pink macular rash follows the prodrome.

question: Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria is one of the cutaneous porphyrias. The defect in this disease is:
explanation: Patients with hepatoerythropoietic porphyria have a defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. This is a cutaneous prophyria characterized by attacks.

question: A 10 year old girl presents with a lacy reticular rash on the bilateral extremities. About 1 week prior she notes she had a fever and myalgias. Which of the following virus is the most likely culprit?
explanation: The clinical presentation of a lacy reticular rash on the bilateral extremities in a child, following a febrile illness with myalgias, is characteristic of erythema infectiosum, also known as fifth disease. This condition is caused by parvovirus B19, which is a single-stranded DNA virus.

question: A 4 month-old with diffuse blisters and erosions has a skin biopsy diagnostic of generalized mastocytosis. Which topical agent should be avoided in this patient?
explanation: Mastocytosis comprises a group of diseases characterized by increased number of mast cells in the skin and other organs. Seventy-five percent of cases occur before the age of 2. Patients with mastocytosis should avoid potential mast degranulators including aspirin, codeine, opiates, procaine, spicy foods, cheese, alcohol, polymyxin B.

question: A 14-year-old child is brought to the dermatologist for evaluation of facial skin lesions, as shown. The child has a history of developmental disability and seizure disorder. A mutation in a protein that results in modification of which of the following processes is implicated in the patient’s condition?
explanation: The presence of facial angiofibromas, developmental disability, and seizure disorder is consistent with a syndrome—most notably tuberous sclerosis. This disease is based on a mutation in the TSC1 and TSC2 genes that encode hamartin and tuberin. These two tumor suppressor genes function to control cellular proliferation and growth; thus once mutated, there is proliferation to lead to many of the sequelae of tuberous sclerosis, such as hamartomas.

question: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic disorder characterized by a facial port-wine stain associated with ocular and neurologic abnormalities. It can occur in the first year of life and is more common in patients with bilateral forehead port-wine stains. Which of the following is the most common neurologic abnormality in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome?
explanation: Of the answer choices listed, the most common neurologic abnormality that patients with Sturge- Weber syndrome develop is seizures.

question: A 1-week full-term newborn presents to the office with circumscribed, erythematous, indurated subcutaneous nodules on the back and buttocks. A biopsy is performed, and the histology is below. Which specific lab needs to be monitored for the next several months in this newborn?
explanation: Calcium. The diagnosis is subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn. Some patients develop hypercalcemia or thrombocytopenia, and the former may appear 1–4 months after the onset of the skin lesions. Severe hypercalcemia may be associated with fever, eosinophilia, and persistent nephrocalcinosis.

question: An 8 year old boy with seasonal allergies presents with red brown macules on the trunk present for several months. Parent mentions that when these lesions are scratched they form an irritated, red wheal. Which of the following sign is likely described?
explanation: Darier's sign is seen in patients with urticarial pigmentosa, a common form of mastocytosis. Erythema and wheals are commonly elicited with stroking or rubbing secondary to mast cell degranulation. Symptoms can range from very mild (flushing, hives, no treatment needed) to life-threatening (vascular collapse).

question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The bullous lesions represented are nonscarring and are associated with obvious nail dystrophy. Epidermolysis bullosa simplex, Dowling-Meara type (generalized severe) is the best option.

question: A teenager presents to your surgery clinic for removal of a cyst, which often drains fluid, in the suprasternal notch. Upon examining the excision on histology, you notice thick ciliated epithelium. The most likely developmental defect in this case is:
explanation: Bronchogenic cysts are midline lesions that are most commonly found in the suprasternal notch. They often drain fluid. The lining of the cyst is typically ciliated pseudostratified respiratory-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Squamous metaplasia is common. In the wall, it is very common to find smooth muscle and cartilage.

question: A father brings in his child who has a history of atopic dermatitis. He reports a one-week history of blisters on the extremities and states this looks different than his usual eczema. The child is appearing well and happily cooperative with your exam. What is the next step in management?
explanation: The patient's arm shows a superficial erosion with serous crust, which is consistent with bullous impetigo. Caused by exfoliative toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus, the primary lesion is a bulla; however, often only erosions and a collarette of scale are noted on exam. A wound culture will readily grow S. aureus to confirm the diagnosis. Cutaneous bacterial infections are more common in patients with atopic dermatitis due to impaired barrier function. Treatment: Limited disease can be treated with topical mupiricin ointment twice daily for 5 days. Patients with widespread disease or systemic symptoms can be treated with oral antibiotics such as cephalexin, erythromycin, or clindamycin (if MRSA is suspected).

question: The muscle that is affected in a patient with a fibromatosis colli is:
explanation: Fibromatosis colli affects the lower sternocleidomastoid muscle that my arise from birth trauma. These occur in the pediatric patients and can spontaneous remit.

question: Which of the following may be associated?
explanation: Nevus sebaceus can very rarely be associated with multiple anomalies. Schimmelpenning syndrome can include seizure disorder, mental retardation, coloboma, as well as skeletal, cardiac and genitourinary abnormalities.

question: Juvenile self-healing papular mucinosis is associated with which of the findings?
explanation: Self-healing papular mucinosis is a rare disorder characterized by small, nontender, flesh-colored papules commonly seen on the head, neck, trunk, and periarticular areas of children. Self-healing papular mucinosis is associated with systemic findings during acute stages, including fever, arthralgias, weakness, and often carpal tunnel syndrome. A handful of cases have been reported in adults, although systemic symptoms are not typically found in this population.

question: This syndrome has aplasia cutis congenita, cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, limb defects and cardiac abnormalities:
explanation: Adams-Oliver syndrome is characterized by aplasia cutis congenita on the scalp (with skull ossification defect), cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, limb defects and cardiac abnormalities. Aplasia cutis congenital (ACC) is characterized by an absence of skin and subcutaneous tissue.

question: The ocular complication associated with this condition is also seen in which of the following?
explanation: The lesion shown here is a Nevus of Ota. This is associated with a ~10% risk of developing glaucoma. Of the answer choices, Port Wine stains (capillary malformations) are also associated with increased risk of glaucoma. Bilateral lesions, lower eyelid lesions, and choroidal hemangiomas have a higher risk of glaucoma.

question: A 10-year-old male presents with recurrent crops of hypopigmented macules and crusted papules on the trunk and extremities. What is the hypothesized pathogenesis of this disorder?
explanation: The image shows pityriasis lichenoides chronica (PLC), a rare, chronic cutaneous disorder most commonly seen in children and young adults with a slight male predominance. PLC presents with a widespread eruption comprised of scaly, red-brown papules and plaques that resolve with hypopigmentation. Both pityriasis lichenoides at varioliformis acute (PLEVA) and PLC contain lesional T cell infiltrates, with a general predominance of CD8+ T cells in PLEVA and CD4+ cells in PLC (Choice 1).

question: The dermatologist on call is requested to visit the NICU to evaluate an infant born 12 hours earlier with a disseminated rash. Two punch biopsies are performed and a c-KIT positive infiltrate is noted in the dermis of each sample. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The patient presents with likely systemic mastocytosis, but definitively with diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis based on the appearance of the skin lesions and the c-KIT positive staining pattern.

question: Which of the following lab abnormalities is most common in patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) is associated with mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott- Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASp). The classic triad of WAS is immunodeficiency, eczema, and thrombocytopenia. Thrombocytopenia is also seen in the milder variant of this condition, X-linked thrombocytopenia (XLT).

question: The treatment for acrodermatitis enteropathica is:
explanation: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is due to a defect in zinc absorption and will respond to zinc supplementation. Findings include periorificial, scalp, and acral dermatitis, scaling, vesicles/bullae, erosions, alopecia, diarrhea and stomatitis.

question: A 20-year-old male presents with jaundice, hepatomegaly, blue lunulae, and the ocular finding as shown. What is the genetic mutation in this condition?
explanation: The correct answer is the ATP7B gene (Choice 3), which is mutated in Wilson's disease. In this condition, there is a defect in copper metabolism leading to deposition in the liver and subsequent liver failure. Cutaneous findings include Kayser-Fleischer rings (due to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane), blue lunulae, and pretibial hyperpigmentation.

question: A healthy, full-term infant develops a pustular, erythematous eruption on her face and trunk on the third day of life. A smear taken from one of these pustules would show:
explanation: This baby has developed erythema toxicum neonatorum, a benign, self-limited eruption that occurs in the majority of healthy, full-term infants. Erythema toxicum usually develops on the second or third day of life and resolves by day 10. A smear taken from one of the pustules will demonstrate eosinophils, which is sufficient to make the diagnosis.

question: Hemangiomas of infancy are more likely to occur:

choices.B: In children who are large for gestational age

explanation: Infantile hemangiomas are more likely to occur in multiple gestation.

question: A 17 year old male presents for a routine skin check. Mom notes a family history of melanoma in the child’s aunt and basal cell in the child’s father. Upon routine exam you notice the following lesion. What is the most likely next best step?
explanation: Supernumerary nipples, also known as accessory nipples, are benign congenital anomalies that are typically asymptomatic and do not require treatment. They are often discovered incidentally during routine physical examinations and do not pose any health risks. Given that the patient is asymptomatic and has no associated complications, reassurance is the most appropriate next step.

question: Which of followings syndromes characterized by Seborrheic-like or exfoliative dermatitis:
explanation: Immunodeficiency disorders may be associated with a variety of cutaneous abnormalities, and recognition of these clinical features may allow an early diagnosis of primary immunodeficiency. Cutaneous abnormalities may include cutaneous infections, atopic-or seborrheic-like dermatitis, macular erythemas, alopecia, poor wound healing, purpura, petechiae, telangiectasias, pigmentary dilution, cutaneous granulomas, extensive warts, angioedema, and lupus-like changes. Leiner's disease or erythroderma desquamativum is a complication of seborrheic dermatitis in infants (dermatitis seborrhoides infantum) There is usually a sudden confluence of lesions, leading to a universal scaling redness of the skin (erythroderma). The young patients are severely ill with anemia, diarrhea, and vomiting.The disease is both a familial and a nonfamilial form. The former is noted for having a functional deficiency of C5 complement, resulting in defective opsonization. These patients respond to antibiotics and infusions of fresh frozen plasma or whole blood. The other choices in the questions can all be associated with atopic-like dermatitis.

question: A mitten deformity is most characteristic of what inherited disease?
explanation: Recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is characterized by pseudosyndactyly and mitten deformities of the hands and feet.

question: A newborn presents to clinic with an erythematous semi-blanchable patch involving the forehead that becomes prominent with crying. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Nevus simplex, also known as salmon patches, nevus flammeus neonatorum, stork bites, are common vascular malformations seen at birth. Common locations are seen on the forehead, and nuchal region. They can be accentuated with increased activity, such as crying.

question: What is the most appropriate initial treatment for an infant with atopic dermatitis?
explanation: Topical corticosteroids are the first-line treatment for atopic dermatitis in infants. They help reduce inflammation and manage flare-ups.

question: What is the genetic mutation in hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED)?
explanation: Clouston syndrome (HED) is caused by mutations in the GJB6 gene (13q12), encoding the gap junction protein connexin 30 (Cx30).

question: What is the diagnosis for this skin condition?
explanation: Eczema herpeticum is a secondary infection that occurs in patients with atopic dermatitis. It is readily identified by monomorphic punched out erosions occuring within areas of eczema. Intact vesicles are less commonly seen. The treatment involves systemic antivirals as well as continuation of topical steroids.

question: What syndrome is most strongly associated with the findings shown in the image provided?
explanation: The photo shows keratosis pilaris atrophicans faceii and surgically corrected ptosis. Both of these findings are associated with Noonan syndrome. Noonan syndrome is a condition most commonly occurring sporadically and is due to a mutation in PTPN11. This condition is allelic with LEOPARD syndrome. Noonan syndrome is characterized by lower extremity lymphedema, multiple cafe au lait macules, hypertelorism, a webbed neck with a low posterior hairline, and pulmonic stenosis.

question: Which of the following virus families is responsible for the lesions shown on this 3-year-old male's chest?
explanation: The image shows molluscum contagiosum, which is a member of the Poxvirus family.

question: An 18-month-old boy with a history of eczema was brought into the clinic by his mother for concerns over his worsening eczema. His mother has been unable to bring him into the dermatology clinic for a follow-up due to lack of transportation. She recently ran out of topical corticosteroids and his eczema has been slowly worsening. His mother also noted decreased oral intake and new onset low grade fevers. Physical examination reveals the skin findings in the image. Which of the following nail findings can be seen as a complication of this disease?
explanation: The child is presenting with eczema coxsackium, a self-limited viral illness due to the coxsackie virus, the cause of Hand-Foot-and-Mouth disease. It presents with widespread monomorphous vesicles with a predilection for areas affected by eczema. A benign delayed manifestation of eczema coxsackium is nail change, such as onychomadesis or Beau's lines.

question: A child presents with nodular venous malformations and multiple benign bony tumors in the cartilage. Which of the following is most likely to be defective?
explanation: Maffucci syndrome is characterized by the progressive growth of vascular hamartomas and enchondromas. Approximately a third of patients develop malignancies including chondrosarcomas, fibrosarcomas, angiosarcomas, gliomas, and teratomas. The syndrome is caused by a sporadic mutation in isocitrate dehydrogenase.

question: A 3-month-old infant presents with the physical exam findings shown here along with ipsilateral leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI. Upon further questioning, the mom notes A that occasionally the baby seems to jerk rhythmically and close their eyes and be B unresponsive for a few seconds to minutes. Ophthalmologic examination reveals increased C intraocular pressure. Which of the following is the most likely associated systemic D complication in this patient? E Renal artery stenosis

choices.B: Elevated episcleral venous pressure leading to glaucoma

explanation: This question stem describes Sturge-Weber syndrome characterized by: ○ Port-wine stain (capillary malformation) in V1/V2 distribution (CN V trigeminal nerve). ○ Leptomeningeal angiomatosis (seizures, neurologic deficits). ○ Glaucoma (due to elevated episcleral venous pressure).

incorrect_rationales.A: that occasionally the baby seems to jerk rhythmically and close their eyes and be
incorrect_rationales.B: unresponsive for a few seconds to minutes. Ophthalmologic examination reveals increased
incorrect_rationales.C: intraocular pressure. Which of the following is the most likely associated systemic
incorrect_rationales.D: complication in this patient?

question: A 3 month old presents with a diffuse vesiculobullous rash with copper colored macules on the palms and soles. You ascertain from the history that his mother had a nonpainful erosion on her labia during pregnancy which spontaneously resolved. What other symptoms would you expect this infant to have?
explanation: Pseudoparalysis of Parrot is a sign of early congenital syphilis. Early congenital syphilis occurs before 2 years of age, whereas late congenital syphilis generally occurs after 2 years of age.

question: Which of the following vascular lesions is most likely to proiferate after birth and later, spontaneously involute?
explanation: Infantile hemangiomas will typically appear within weeks after birth, proliferate over the first 3-9 months (up to 18 months), and involute over several years. Most are resoved at age 10.

question: Which of the following lesions demonstrates a pseudo-Darier’s sign?
explanation: Smooth muscle hamartomas are benign tumors which arise from smooth muscle of the dermis. Pseudo-Darier's sign may be elicited due to transient piloerection after rubbing. Histologically, red-orange bundles and fascicles are present with blunt-ended nuclei.

question: Koplik spots typically appear:

choices.E: At the same time as the exanthem

explanation: The enanthem of measles typically precedes the morbilliform eruption by 48 hours. They generally last 12-72 hours. However, this enanthem does not appear in all patients with measles.

question: A 10 year-old male presents with new pink-red papules distributed on his bilateral cheeks, elbows, knees, and buttocks. The lesions are not pruritic. His mother notes he has suffered from low grade fevers over the past few days, but is otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Papular acrodermatitis of childhood (Gianotti-Crosti syndrome) typically affects children 6 months to 10 years of age and is characterized by symmetric papules (and sometimes papulovesicles) involving the face and buttocks (“four cheeks”) and extensor surfaces of the upper and lower extremities. Lesions tend to be asymptomatic. Multiple infectious etiologies have been implicated, including Epstein- Barr virus (most common in the U.S.) and hepatitis B (most common in Europe). However, the eruption is most often self-limited, resolving in 4 to 8 weeks, and thus further work-up (e.g., testing for hepatitis) is indicated only if additional clinical symptoms are present.

question: A 17-year-old boy presents with a changing lesion on his scalp. On examination, there is a firm, dome-shaped nodule overlying a hairless, yellow-orange, verrucous plaque. Biopsy of the nodule reveals a well-circumscribed dermal tumor composed of basaloid cells with papillary mesenchymal bodies and mucin within the tumor islands. No retraction artifact, cytologic atypia, or mitotic activity is noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Trichoblastoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm that can arise within a nevus sebaceous during adolescence. Histopathology demonstrates basaloid cells, papillary mesenchymal bodies, and mucin deposition without atypia or mitotic activity.

question: An 8 year-old boy presents with pink, flushed cheeks and a low-grade fever. One week later, a lacy eruption appears. What is the most likely etiology?
explanation: Fifth disease is caused by Parvovirus B19. Most cases start with prodrome of fever, malaise, headache and rhinorrhea. Cutaneous reaction follows approximately 5-7 days later with erythema of the cheeks ("slapped cheeks") and reticulate rash of the trunk and extremities.

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with a unilateral, irregularly bordered, tan-brown patch on the right chest and shoulder with increased terminal hair growth, consistent with Becker’s nevus as seen in the clinical image. Which of the following extracutaneous findings is most likely to be associated with Becker’s nevus syndrome?
explanation: Becker’s nevus is a cutaneous hamartoma of ectodermal and mesodermal tissues that typically arises around puberty, most often in males. When Becker’s nevus occurs in association with extracutaneous abnormalities, the condition is termed Becker’s nevus syndrome. The most commonly reported extracutaneous finding is ipsilateral breast or chest hypoplasia, which may be subtle or pronounced. Other reported associations include asymmetric limb hypoplasia or hypertrophy, scoliosis, spina bifida occulta, and supernumerary nipples.

question: A 4 year-old boy has a single circular alopecic atrophic patch on the vertex of the scalp. This most likely is due to which of the following conditions?
explanation: Aplasia cutis congenita often affects the vertex of the scalp and heals with a circular atrophic alopecic scar.

question: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of urticarial plaques, conjunctivitis, and joint pain triggered by cold exposure. Genetic testing identifies an NLRP3 mutation. Which treatment would be most effective in preventing future flares?
explanation: This is familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS), an NLRP3-mediated CAPS disorder. First line treatment is IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab, rilonacept).

question: You are called to the NICU to evaluate a newborn. Upon examination, you see that the neonate has large, yellow, adherent plates separated by broad, deep, intensely red fissures. You immediately suspect a genetic syndrome. In which of the following conditions is the early initiation of systemic retinoids considered part of first-line therapy and can reduce mortality?
explanation: Harlequin ichthyosis. Over the past two decades, improved postnatal care and oral retinoid therapy have led to prolonged survival in an increasing number of harlequin ichthyosis patients. Early administration of systemic retinoids, in particular acitretin, usually with an initial dose of 1 mg/kg/ day, has been shown to result in shedding of the large, keratotic plates within weeks as well as improvement of the ectropion and eclabium.1

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of brownish macules and papules on his trunk and extremities. Physical examination reveals positive Darier's sign, and laboratory tests show elevated serum tryptase levels. Which of the following systemic findings is most commonly associated with the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Urticaria pigmentosa is a form of cutaneous mastocytosis that can present with systemic symptoms due to mast cell degranulation and histamine release. This includes recurrent diarrhea caused by histamine-induced hypersecretion.

question: The disorder caused by a defect in intestinal zinc-specific transporter SLC39A4 is most likely to present:
explanation: In acrodermatitis enteropathica, there is decreased absorption of zinc from the infant's gastrointestinal tract. The zinc in breast milk has greater availability than nonmaternal sources thus protecting the child from disease expression until weaning.

question: A 4-year-old male presents with lesions on the hands, and feet with small papulovesicles with surrounding mild erythema. Mom reports he has not been eating well, and you see a few small gray-white vesicles and shallow erosions on the hard and soft palate as well. Mom is concerned about the course and complications. What is true regarding counseling of sequelae of this entity?

choices.A: There is a very high association with recurrent EBV and viral titers must be followed
choices.B: Nail shedding, onychomadesis, can occur but results in normal nail plate growth
choices.C: Brittle hair often results 2-3 weeks after the eruption subsides
choices.D: Risk of testicular involvement is high and close monitoring is recommended
choices.E: Severe birth defects have been seen when women are exposed in early pregnancy so ? contact and respiratory isolation is needed

correct_text:
Nail shedding, onychomadesis, can occur but results in normal nail plate
growth
explanation: This vignette describes hand-foot-mouth syndrome. A common finding after the viral illness is to have shedding of the fingernails, onychomadesis. Afterwards the nails grow back normally and reassurance is important for patients and parents.

question: A 14-year-old child is brought to the dermatologist for evaluation of facial skin lesions, as shown. The child has a history of developmental disability and seizure disorder. Which of

choices.A: the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding skin screening in this
choices.E: Every 1 year ? Every 3 months ? Every 5 years

explanation: The patient’s skin lesions are consistent with facial angiofibromas; combined with the history of developmental disability and seizure disorder, these raise significant concerns for tuberous sclerosis. A joint committee on this disease recommends an annual examination with dermatology for the inspection and management of related skin lesions.

incorrect_rationales.D:
Every 3 years

?. Every 3 months

?. Every 5 years

question: A 3-month-old infant presents with the findings seen in the photo in the first week of life. The mother reports the infant was born with a membrane encasing it that later "peeled off". History is also notable for poor weight gain and multiple rounds of antibiotics since birth. On physical exam there is diffuse erythema, scaling, and sparse eyebrow hair. Laboratory studies show eosinophilia (1,500/µL) and markedly elevated IgE (2,500 IU/mL). A biopsy demonstrates spongiosis, parakeratosis, and a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis, and the next diagnostic step?

choices.A: Netherton syndrome; genetic testing for SPINK5 mutation
choices.C: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; blood cultures and anti-staphylococcal
