choices.E: Omenn syndrome; flow cytometry and lymphocyte subset analysis ? Lamellar ichthyosis; genetic testing for TGM1 mutation

correct_text: Omenn syndrome; flow cytometry and lymphocyte subset analysis
explanation: B) Omenn syndrome. Key features of Omenn syndrome include neonatal onset erythroderma with generalized scaling and sparse hair (including eyebrows). Patients have elevated IgE and eosinophilia with failure to thrive and recurrent bacterial infections. Mutations in either RAG1/RAG2 will result in defective T-cell production.

incorrect_rationales.D:
antibiotics

?. Lamellar ichthyosis; genetic testing for TGM1 mutation

question: A male infant presents to the office with his mother, who notes he has a ring of hair loss on his scalp. She says she had a prolonged labor and that this is her first child. Their pediatrician referred him to you for further evaluation and management. On examination, you note annular alopecia. What condition is this associated with?
explanation: Caput succedaneum presents as localized edema of the scalp due to labor and occurs most frequently in the setting of prolonged labor and primigravidas. On examination, annular alopecia, also known as “halo scalp ring,” can be seen due to pressure necrosis.

question: A 12-year-old boy with a history of multiple basal cell carcinomas is brought to the office for evaluation of pits on his palms and lateral fingers. Which of the following is most likely also seen in the patient's condition?
explanation: Basal cell nevus syndrome is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the PTCH1 gene. Clinically, patients may have numerous basal cell carcinomas, palmoplantar pits, jaw cysts, frontal bossing, bifid ribs, calcification of the falx cerebri, medulloblastoma, ovarian fibromas, and fibrosarcomas.

question: An eight year-old boy presents with pink, flushed cheeks and a low-grade fever. A lacy skin eruption then appeared. What is the most likely etiology?
explanation: Fifths Disease or erythema infectiosum, is caused by parvovirus B19, a single-stranded DNA virus. There are a few clinical presentations including slapped cheeks, a diffuse lacy rash on the trunk that spreads gradually toward the distal extremities, papular-pruritic "gloves-and-socks" syndrome and aplastic crisis which does not have concomitant rash.

question: A 24-month-old infant presents with red-brown, crusted papules with petechiae in a seborrheic distribution. A biopsy is done to confirm a diagnosis. Which histologic picture is most likely?

choices.A: Mixed cellular infiltrate in a “ball and claw” pattern
choices.B: CD1a-, S100- cells with reniform nuclei
choices.C: Superficial perivascular infiltrate with mild spongiosis and neutrophil containing scale
choices.E: Foamy histiocytes with Touton giant cells ? CD1a+, S100+ cells with reniform nuclei

correct_text: CD1a+, S100+ cells with reniform nuclei
explanation: This patient most likely has Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Langerhans cells are CD1a and S100 positive. The nuclei are described as kidney-shaped, or reniform.

incorrect_rationales.E: Foamy histiocytes with Touton giant cells

question: What is the most common tumor associated with this condition?
explanation: Recent reviews have identified trichoblastoma as the most common tumor arising within nevus sebaceous, even more frequent than syringocystadenoma papilliferum.

question: A full term neonate is noted to have small pustules with no underlying erythema present at delivery. The pustules are easily removed with clearing of the vernix and a collarette appears. A gram stain is done showing predominately neutrophils without bacteria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis typically begins with sterile pustules that leave a characteristic collarette when ruptured. The lesions heal with hyperpigmented macules. Gram stain shows a predominance of neutrophils.

question: Which of the following laboratory abnormalities are most associated with a worse prognosis in neonatal lupus erythematosus?
explanation: Thrombocytopenia and transaminitis are associated with neonatal lupus and may indicate a worse prognosis.

question: A 6 month-old has a verrucous plaque on the mucosal surface of the lower lip. Skin biopsy is consistent with Riga-Fede disease (an eosinophilic ulceration). You should refer the patient to:
explanation: Riga-Fede disease is a benign ulcerative granulomatous process that occurs in reaction to chronic, repetitive trauma of the oral mucosa by the teeth. Clinically, it appears as firm, verrucous plaques. It may be associated with an underlying developmental anomaly or underlying neurologic disorder in up to 25% of cases.

question: A healthy neonate presents with discrete, scattered, 1-3mm yellowish papules on the face, trunk, arms, and legs. An erythematous flare surrounds the papules. Palms and soles are spared. Papules started on the second day of life, and some initial papules have already resolved. Which of the following would you recommend?
explanation: This case describes erythema toxicum neonatorum, a benign, self-limited neonatal eruption that spares the self-limited neonatal eruption that spares the palms and soles that affects 7-45% of newborns. The condition typically presents on the second or third day of life and resolves by approximately 1 week. No treatment is indicated.

question: A child presents with a 1 cm yellow-red nodule on the face. Pathology shows Touton giant cells. What is the most frequent site of extracutaneous involvement in this disease?
explanation: The eye is the most frequent site of extracutaneous juvenile xamthogranuloma. Ocular involvement is typically unilateral.

question: A five year old male presents with lifelong mild to moderate asymptomatic enlargement of the right nipple compared to the left nipple; no gynecomastia present. What is the best approach to this situation?

choices.D: Magnetic resonance imaging with and without contrast of the chest

explanation: Reassurance is all that is necessary for benign nipple enlargement. Patient can be referred to plastic surgery for revision if he chooses to do so in the future on his own accord.

question: What is the most common associated mutation with the condition shown here?
explanation: The condition shown is a Nevus of Ota. This presents with facial dermal melanocytosis due to mosaic mutations in genes including GNAQ.

question: A 9-year-old girl presents with an acute eruption of multiple erythematous, 5- to 10-mm inflammatory papules and papulovesicles, some of which form hemorrhagic or necrotic on her trunk and proximal extremities. Lesions have been self-resolving after a few weeks with no treatment. She denies systemic symptoms. You suspect pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA). A biopsy of one of these lesions is performed. What is the phenotype of cells that supports the diagnosis of PLEVA?
explanation: Immunohistochemical studies can help confirm the diagnosis of pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA). The inflammatory infiltrate is primarily composed of CD8+ T lymphocytes. CD30 stains are usually negative, unlike lymphomatoid papulosis.

question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the dermatologist with a firm bluish nodule on the right lateral forehead, about 1 cm superior to the lateral edge of the eyebrow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The location on the lateral forehead near the eyebrow of a firm, blue-colored nodule is most characteristic of a dermoid cyst. These lesions should be surgically excised and may need imaging when it appears midline.

question: This healthy 2-year-old female presents with a 2-day history of the pruritic rash seen here. She had mild edema of the dorsal hands and feet and positive dermatographism on exam. All lesions were transient, lasting less than 24 hours in the same location. She was otherwise well and her parents denied any fever or systemic symptoms. What is the best diagnosis?
explanation: The physical exam and findings suggest urticaria multiforme. The patient expresses pruritus, acral edema, positive dermatographism, and transient lesions and importnatly she is otherwise well.

question: Which type of porphyria manifests with peripheral neuropathy, colicky abdominal pain, but NO cutaneous symptoms?
explanation: Acute intermittent pophyria is caused by a defect in the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase. Patients present with peripheral neuropathy and occasionally seizures, abdominal pain, and tachycardia. There are no skin changes as no dermal porphyrins are found.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the image?
explanation: The bright red erythema of perianal streptococcal disease can also involve the creases of the groin and axillae.

question: A 9-year-old child comes to your office for resistant eczema. On examination, you note circinate scaling erythematous plaques bordered by a double-edged scale. You suspect a genetic syndrome and perform light microscopy of hairs from the patient. Which of the following is a particularly high-yield area to obtain hairs from to increase the chance of a positive diagnosis?
explanation: Eyebrows. Light microscopic examination of clipped hair from the scalp and (of particularly high yield) the eyebrows often reveals trichorrhexis invaginata (bamboo hair) with a ball-and-socket appearance or nodular thickening of the distal end of broken hair shafts (“golf tee,” “matchstick”). Multiple additional abnormalities may be observed, including pili torti, trichorrhexis nodosa, and “helical” hair.1,2

question: A 2-year-old boy is brought by his mother for evaluation of a rash. Exam shows large annular, targetoid, edematous, violaceous plaques on the upper extremities and face. He is well- appearing and afebrile. Parents report a recent upper respiratory infection. Skin biopsy reveals leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
explanation: The findings are classic for acute hemorrhagic edema of infancy, a benign, self-limited small vessel vasculitis that resolves within 1–3 weeks. Supportive care is the treatment of choice.

question: A patient presents with recurrent infections, non-blanching purpuric macules on the legs and arms, and eczematous lesions over the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder, affecting almost exclusively males, caused by mutations in WAS gene. Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich may have unstable sialoglycoprotein CD 43 on the surface of lymphocytes. It is characterized by thrombocytopenia with resultant bleeding / bruising, immunodeficiencies including both B-cell and T-cell abnormalities with resultant fungal, viral, and bacterial infections, and severe atopic dermatitis (usually begins in the first few months of life). There is an increased risk for lymphoreticular malignancy (20%).

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with multiple pigmented macules on his trunk and extremities. He has a history of pulmonic stenosis surgically corrected at birth. Physical examination reveals low-set ears and mild ocular hypertelorism. Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following specialist evaluations is most important in the ongoing care of this patient?
explanation: This presentation is consistent with LEOPARD syndrome (Lentigines, Electrocardiographic conduction abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonic stenosis, Abnormal genitalia, Retarded growth, Deafness), which is also known as Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines. Sensorineural hearing loss is a hallmark, so audiology evaluation is essential.

question: A 4-month-old African-American male presents for the rash shown. The rash has been

choices.A: present for the past two months. The mother describes that the baby tends to be bothered
choices.B: by this rash and can be seen trying to rub his feet together.
choices.C: Which of the following tests should be performed next?
choices.E: KOH ? Skin biopsy ? Mineral oil prep ? Bacterial culture

correct_text: KOH ? Skin biopsy ? Mineral oil prep ? Bacterial culture
explanation: This clinical image and scenario most likely represents Infantile acropustulosis (IA), which is a benign vesiculopustular condition with an often chronic course in infants. The etiology is unknown. Some studies suggest that African-American male infants are more commonly affected. IA is characterized by recurrent crops of intensely pruritic vesiculopustules on the palms and soles. The diagnosis is based on clinical features and given the similar appearance, scabies should be ruled-out with a mineral oil prep.

question: A 4-year-old boy presents for a well-child check. His mother notes some changes to his hair and skin, including dry scaly skin and brittle hair, as shown. The patient is at the 6th percentile for height and 38th percentile for weight. A hair mount reveals alternating light and dark banding. Abnormalities in which of the following amino acids is most associated with the patient’s condition?
explanation: Recognize the constellation of dry and scaly skin, brittle hair, short stature, and “tiger tail” banding on a hair mount as consistent with trichothiodystrophy. The short brittle hair is the result of a deficiency of sulfur-containing amino acids, like cysteine.

question: A 15-year-old male with mild intellectual impairment presents with multiple hyperpigmented lesions on the trunk and axillary freckling. Family history was positive for similar lesions in his mother. No ocular findings or cutaneous findings consistent with neurofibromas or plexiform neurofibromas were present. Genetic testing was negative for Neurofibromatosis Type 1. What gene mutation accounts for this patient’s condition?
explanation: This case represents Legius syndrome (Choice 4), which is due to an autosomal dominant mutation in SPRED-1. This syndrome accounts for up to 2% of all patients meeting criteria for NF1. The clinical presentation is similar to that of NF1 with multiple CALMs, axillary or inguinal freckling. Mild intellectual disability, macrocephaly are also commone features. Other NF1-associated features such as Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, NF1-specific bone lesions, optic pathway gliomas, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors are absent.

question: Pachyonychia congenita type 2 is most commonly associated with which of the following:
explanation: Pachyonychia congenita type 2 may be associated with natal teeth and steatocystoma. Pachyonychia congenita type 1 is associated with benign leukoplakia.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis in this 16 year old patient who developed this generalized eruption 2 weeks after onset of sore throat due to strep infection?
explanation: Although the exact mechanism is not understood, there is a well-known correlation between a history of upper respiratory infection secondary to group A beta-hemolytic streptococci and the subsequent development of guttate psoriasis. The eruption may resolve spontaneously or with treatment (topical steroids or ultraviolet therapy). A portion of these patients eventually develop chronic, plaque-type psoriasis.

question: Which of the following encompasses the most common extracutaneous manifestation of PHACE syndrome?
explanation: Haggstrom et al. observed that the most common extracutaneous findings in PHACE syndrome were abnormalities in the cerebrovasculature (91%) followed by cardiac anomalies (67%).

question: This syndrome is characterized by a nevus sebaceous associated with ocular malformations, mental retardation, seizures, and skeletal and cardiovascular abnormalities:
explanation: Schimmelpenning syndrome (aka organoid nevus syndrome) involves a mostly linear nevus sebaceous associated with ocular malformations, mental retardation, seizures, and skeletal and cardiovascular abnormalities. Nevus sebaceous is a congenital hairless, yellow to orange plaque on the scalp.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with the findings seen in the image. He also has thrombocytopenia with purpura and a history of recurrent pyogenic bacterial infections. What is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
explanation: The findings described are consistent with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. The characteristic triad can be simplified to the three Ps: Pruritus (atopic dermatitis), Purpura (thrombocytopenia leading to purpura and other bleeding), and Pyogenic infections.

question: POEMS syndrome is associated with which of the following:
explanation: The acronym POEMS stands for polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M- protein, and skin changes.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with chronic, serpiginous, erythematous plaques with a double- edged scale. His hair is brittle and beaded with intermittent nodes and constrictions. His history is notable for recurrent eczematous plaques since infancy. Which topical medication requires particular caution in this patient due to risk of systemic absorption and toxicity?
explanation: This child has Netherton syndrome, characterized by ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, trichorrhexis invaginata, and atopic dermatitis. Barrier dysfunction can lead to systemic absorption of medications. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are especially risky due to potential systemic immunosuppression and toxicity.

question: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn is usually treated with:
explanation: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn is rare and self-limited. It is thought to result from perinatal stress and resolves in 3-6 months. Treatment is usually not necessary unless hypercalcemia develops.

question: Which of the following diseases with immunodeficiency has an increased risk of lymphoreticular malignancy?
explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in WAS gene. Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich have atopic dermatitis with increased risks for secondary infection, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent bacterial infections. They are also at an increased risk for lymphoreticular malignancy (20%).

question: A Wright stain of the contents of a pustule of a neonate with erythema toxicum is likely to show what type of cells?
explanation: Erythema toxicum presents with papules & pustules that start within 48 hours of birth and last 2-3 days. They affect the face, trunk, and proximal extremities but spare the palms and soles. These pustules in erythema toxicum are filled with eosinophils.

question: A neonate is examined in the NICU after being born to a mother with the below findings on her hands. Which of the following are most likely to be seen in the neonate?
explanation: This patient's mother has an exam consistent with secondary syphilis. Syphilis, part of the "other" category in the TORCHes infection, can be passed down from mother to fetus during pregnancy. Of all the listed complications, pseudoparalysis is associated with congenital syphilis. Pseudoparalysis of Parrot, named after Jules Marie Parrot, is a manifestation of early congenital syphilis where infants are unwilling to move their upper extremities due to immense pain from syphilis affecting the bone and joints. As syphilis is on the rise in the US, it is important to know the many signs of congenital syphilis.

question: Which of the following is more common in the juvenile variant of the skin disease depicted here?
explanation: Calcinosis cutis is more common in juvenile dermatomyosits (compared to the adult population).

question: A 3-week-old infant is brought to the office with subcutaneous nodules on his shoulders and upper back. A biopsy of one of the lesions is performed and is shown below. Which of the following laboratory tests is the most appropriate to monitor to evaluate for resolution of the patient’s condition?
explanation: Recognize the vignette and pathology showing inflammatory cells and fat necrosis as consistent with subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn. As such, calcium levels should be monitored for the resolution of the disease. Hypercalcemia can be noted with the resolution of the disease.

question: What should this patient be evaluated for?
explanation: This is a giant congenital melanocytic nevus (GCMN), which is associated with neurocutaneous melanosis. GCMN overlying the spinal column and skull or multiple satellite lesions can be associated with neurocutaneous melanosis (symptoms of increased cranial pressure, spinal cord compression or leptomeningeal melanoma) Symptomatic neurocutaneous melanosis has a poor prognosis (50% develop leptomeningeal melanoma). These children need an MRI to rule-out CNS involvement.

question: A 5-year-old boy presents with recurrent “cold” abscesses on the trunk, chronic eczematous dermatitis, and a history of recurrent pneumonias. His IgE level is markedly elevated. Genetic testing is most likely to reveal a mutation in which of the following genes?
explanation: Autosomal dominant Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome) is caused by STAT3 mutations and presents with "cold" abscesses, eczema-like dermatitis, recurrent pneumonias, retained primary teeth, and elevated IgE levels.

question: Patients with congenital syphilis may have dental findings called:
explanation: The dental findings that may be found in patients with late congenital syphilis are called Hutchinson's teeth, which refers to enamel hypoplasia of maxillary central incisors and semi-lunar notching on the incisal edge of mandibular incisors.

question: A 30-year-old male presents with grouped reddish papules in a circular pattern on the posterior neck, both arms, trunk, and legs. A biopsy of a representative lesion demonstrates transepidermal elimination of elastic tissue. This is most characteristic of which dermatologic condition?
explanation: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS): a rare skin disorder in which abnormal elastic tissue fiber passes from the papillary dermis (inner layer of skin) to the epidermis (outer layer of skin), described as transepidermal elimination. EPS presents as a cluster of small reddish bumps 2-5 mm in diameter, often grouped in linear, circular or serpiginous (snake-like) patterns. Each lesion may have a central pit, which is sometimes filled by a crusty or scaly plug. Usually, there are no symptoms, but sometimes elastosis perforans serpiginosa is pruritic (itchy). EPS usually arises on the back of the neck (70%) and less frequently on one or both arms (20%), face (11%), legs (6%) and trunk (3%).

question: A patient presents for Mohs surgery of this lesion. Upon further questioning, he notes his

choices.A: father was diagnosed with colon cancer at the age of 40. What is the most appropriate
choices.E: Check TSH/T4 ? Urinary cytology ? PET scan

correct_text: Check TSH/T4 ? Urinary cytology ? PET scan
explanation: This pathologic image is consistent with sebaceous carcinoma. This, in conjunction with a first degree relative with a history of colon cancer, causes concern for Muir- Torre syndrome. This is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutations in MLH1, MSH2, and MSH6 (DNA mismatch repair proteins). Patients can present with sebaceous gland tumors, such as sebaceous adenomas and carcinomas as well as keratoacanthomas. Furthermore, patients are at risk for several internal malignancies, most commonly gastrointestinal followed by genitourinary. Therefore, a workup including colonoscopy, endoscopy, urinary cytology, and CBC should be undertaken.

question: What is the best therapeutic option to treat the condition in the image shown?
explanation: The condition shown is eczema herpeticum. The most appropriate treatment is acyclovir. Eczema herpeticum is considered as one of the few dermatological emergencies. Prompt treatment with antiviral medication should eliminate the need for hospital admission. Oral acyclovir 400–800 mg 5 times daily, or, if available, valaciclovir 1g twice daily, for 10–14 days or until lesions heal. Intravenous aciclovir is prescribed if the patient is too sick to take tablets, if the eye is involved, or if the infection is deteriorating despite treatment. Secondary bacterial skin infection is treated with systemic antibiotics. Topical steroids are not generally recommended but may be necessary to treat active atopic dermatitis. Consult an ophthalmologist when eyelid or eye involvement is seen or suspected.

question: A Wright stain of the contents of a pustule from a neonate with transient neonatal pustular melanosis will likely show what type of cells in abundance?
explanation: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis presents at birth as small pustules with no underlying erythema. They have a collarette when ruptured and heals with hyperpigmented macules. They occur more commonly in darkly pigmented neonates. Pustules of transient neonatal pustular melanosis are filled with neutrophils.

question: A 31-year-old male with history of recurrent febrile episodes presents with the following skin findings. The gene that is mutated in this condition encodes for what type of protein?
explanation: The correct answer is the telomerase complex (Choice C), as this case represents dyskeratosis congenita. Dyskeratosis congenita occurs due to mutations in TERT (AD/AR), TERC (AD), DKC1 (XLR), or TINF2 (AD) genes which encode for proteins involved in telomere maintenance. Affected patients manifest reduced telomerase activity and abnormally shortened telomeres leading to chromosomal instability and cellular replication dysfunction. Clinical features include bone marrow failure and the triad of abnormal reticulated hyperpigmentation on the face/neck/upper trunk, oral leukoplakia (premalignant), and onychodystrophy (pterygium, anonychia, longitudinal ridging/ splitting).

question: A middle-aged man who had not previously seen a healthcare provider dies suddenly from gastrointestinal hemorrhage. His spouse reports he had multiple blue spots on his skin that would occasionally be painful at night. Post-mortem examination reveals multiple soft blue compressible tumors on the trunk, arms, and tongue. Which of the following is the most likely associated mutation?
explanation: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome, also known as Bean syndrome, is a rare sporadic or sometimes autosomal dominant disorder with soft compressible blue tumors on the trunk and arms. Nocturnal pain is characteristic. Gastrointestinal hemangiomas can cause hemorrhage or intussusception. Mutations in the TIE2 gene have been reported.

question: An 11-month-old boy presents with the following rash. What gene mutation could you test for that would aid in treatment of the pictured disease?
explanation: The pictured condition is Langerhans cell histiocytosis, with cutaneous involvement characterized by the pink to skin colored papules in the flexural axilla. BRAF mutations, usually V600E, have been reported in 40%-70% of cases. Case series and early clinical trials have shown promise for targeting the BRAF V600E mutation with vemurafenib and other BRAF inhibitors.

question: Which of the following conditions shares a mutation with mucosal and acral lentiginous melanomas?
explanation: Piebaldism involves mutations in the c-KIT proto-oncogene, which is the same gene commonly mutated in mucosal and acral lentiginous melanomas. Piebaldism an autosomal dominant disorder and results in defective migration of melanoblasts. It presents clinically with patterned areas of depigmentation.

question: A 6-year-old non-toxic-appearing child with no past medical history presents with pruritic, maroon, polycyclic papules and plaques favoring the trunk and extremities; edema of the extremities could be appreciated. Pertinent history and review of systems include recently resolved rhinorrhea of unknown etiology; no recent medication and vaccine exposures. Physical exam was notable for dermographism and individual lesions lasted less than 24

choices.A: hours. Laboratory findings were negative for elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP,
choices.B: ferritin) of clinical significance. Based on the history and clinical photos, which of the
choices.C: following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices.E: Serum-sickness reaction ? Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) ? Urticaria multiforme (UM) ? Still disease (SD)

correct_text:
Serum-sickness reaction ? Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE) ? Urticaria
multiforme (UM) ? Still disease (SD)
explanation: The correct answer is UM. UM is a common, benign hypersensitivity reaction mediated by histamine. This entity often presents after a preceding illness, medication exposure, or vaccination. Patients are usually non-toxic-appearing and skin findings include polycyclic, annular erythematous wheals on the face, trunk, and extremities. Dermographism can be elicited in many patients because UM is mediated by histamine; moreover, the lesions are usually pruritic, not painful, and last less than 24 hours.

question: A 1-year-old child with a history of seizures is referred to a pediatric dermatologist for evaluation of skin lesions. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the gene encoding hamartin. Which of the following cutaneous findings is most likely to be present in this patient at this time?
explanation: This patient with a history of seizures and a mutation in the gene encoding hamartin most likely has tuberous sclerosis complex due to a TSC1 gene mutation. The most common skin findings in infancy and early childhood include hypomelanotic macules (ash leaf spots) and confetti-like hypopigmented lesions.

question: The dermoscopic findings depicted in this image are most consistent with what diagnosis?
explanation: The image shows a Spitz nevus. A classic starburst pattern can be seen under dermoscopy for this melanocytic lesion.

question: An 18-year-old presents with multiple thin, yellowish papules on the neck and axillae. Skin biopsy shows fragmented, basophilic, calcified elastic fibers in the mid-dermis. The ocular findings seen in this condition are also associated with which of the following disorders?
explanation: The findings are consistent with pseudoxanthoma elasticum, which is associated with angioid streaks. Angioid streaks are also seen in sickle cell anemia, Paget disease of bone, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and lead poisoning.

question: A 1-month-old child is brought by her father to the office for evaluation of a rash in the diaper region, as shown. The father reports appropriate feeding and no change in the

choices.A: number of wet diapers daily. The child is fussy during diaper changes, but otherwise, she is
choices.B: in good health. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation: The bright red patches with intertriginous involvement in the diaper area along with satellite lesions in this infant are consistent most with diaper dermatitis with candidiasis.

question: A 6 year old presents with dome shaped, flesh colored papules with central umbilication on the trunk. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: Reassurance and observation: The stem is describing molluscum contagiosum. This is a self limited viral eruption in immunocompetent children. Treatment is not necessary. However, if treated, modalities such as liquid nitrogen or imiquimod.

question: What deficiency is responsible for this condition?
explanation: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare inherited disorder transmitted in an autosomal recessive fashion. The disorder is caused by an inability to absorb zinc. the clinical syndrome is characterized by acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. Zinc deficiency from other causes (including chronic wasting, poor oral intake, lack of supplementation in total parenteral nutrition) can cause similar clinical changes.

question: An infant is referred by their pediatrician for further evaluation of seborrheic dermatitis refractory to standard therapy. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: In infants, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) can mimic severe seborrheic dermatitis. A skin biopsy should be performed to make the diagnosis.

question: A patient with this autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in helicase is at increased risk for which malignancy?

choices.E: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation: Bloom syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in DNA helicase. It is characterized by photo-distributed erythema in a butterfly distribution, malar hypoplasia with a prominent nose, high-pitched voice, and an increased risk for malignancy (acute leukemia, lymphoma, and GI adenocarcinoma.)

question: A mutation in which of the following has been associated with both Sturge-Weber Syndrome and port-wine stains?
explanation: The Sturge–Weber syndrome and port-wine stains are caused by a somatic activating mutation in GNAQ.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient based on this image?
explanation: In neonatal cephalic pustulosis (neonatal acne), papules and pustules are present but comedones are absent. Spontaneous remission occurs.

question: A newborn presents with a pustular rash, joint swelling, oral mucosal lesions, and pain with movement. Over time, cutaneous pustulosis, ranging from discrete crops of pustules to generalized severe pustulosis and ichthyosiform lesions develop. In addition the newborn develops sterile multifocal osteomyelitis and periostitis. What is this condition?
explanation: This condition is deficiency of the interleukin-1-receptor antagonist (DIRA) and due to a mutation in the IL1RN gene. Muckle-Wells syndrome is due to a mutation in the CIAS1 gene and presents with sensorineural deafness, recurrent hives, and amyloidosis. Familial Mediterranean fever is most often due to a mutation in the MEFV gene. Hyper-IgD syndrome is a rare periodic fever syndrome characterised by attacks of fever, arthralgia, skin lesions including cyclical mouth ulcers, and diarrhea due to mutations in the mevalonate kinase gene. PAPA syndrome presents with pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum and acne and is associated with mutations in the CD2 binding protein 1 (CD2BP1).

question: The standard of care of patients with acute Kawasaki disease is:
explanation: Kawasaki disease, also called mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, is an acute febrile disorder based on the clinical criteria of changes in peripheral extremities, polymorphous exanthema, conjunctival injection without exudates, changes in the lips or oral cavity, acute cervical lymphadenopathy. Fever must be present, lasting more than 5 days. Treatment is aimed to prevent coronary aneurysms and myocardial infarction. Treatment for acute Kawasaki disease is intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours and aspirin therapy.

question: What is the most common tumor associated with this condition?
explanation: Recent reviews have identified trichoblastoma as the most common tumor arising within nevus sebaceous, even more frequent than syringocystadenoma papilliferum.

question: You are called to the NICU to evaluate this patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.D: Reassure and follow up in 3 months

explanation: This kodachrome is of aplasia cutis congenita. This is a localized developmental defect involving variable skin thickness. It typically occurs along developmental suture lines on the scalp. It can rarely be associated with underlying bony abnormalities, skeletal abnormalities, brain malformations, cleft lip, and syndactyly. The hair collar sign is a ring of dark, long hair at the periphery of aplasia cutis congenita. An MRI should be performed prior to any biopsy given the potential for underlying connection to the CNS.

question: Rhinorrhea, condylomata lata, and mucous patches are all seen with which congenital disorder?
explanation: Signs of congenital syphilis include rhinorrhea, snuffles, rhagades, condylomata lata, and mucous patches. Condylomata lata or a generalized papulosquamous eruption of secondary syphilis may be present in diaper area.

question: What imaging study is best to confirm PHACE syndrome?
explanation: The best imaging test looking for associated cerebral anomalies in patients with PHACE syndrome is MRI/MRA.

question: A concerned couple presents to your pediatric dermatology clinic with their newborn infant who has a non-inflamed superficial ulceration on the dorsal hand, present since birth. The patient is otherwise healthy. Based on the clinical description and age of the patient, you tell the parents:

choices.A: The ulceration will resolve in months to years
choices.B: This condition is usually associated with many genetic abnormalities
choices.C: This lesion may be caused by vigorous sucking of the affected region in utero
choices.E: Common locations include the head and neck

correct_text:
This lesion may be caused by vigorous sucking of the affected region in
utero
explanation: A sucking blister is caused by vigorous sucking of the affected region in utero. Common locations include the radial forearm, wrists, hands, and fingers. It may present with an intact bulla, erosion, callus or superficial ulceration on a non-inflamed base. It is usually an isolated finding without associated abnormalities. It resolves over days to weeks and therapy is usually supportive.

question: What the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Ichythosis vulgaris and hyperlinear palms are both independent minor criteria for the diagnosis of atopic dermatitis in both children and infants.

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple small brown macules around his lips, eyes, and genitals. He also has several blue-gray papules on his trunk and extremities. His medical history is notable for a left atrial myxoma. Skin biopsy of one of the pigmented papules reveals an epithelioid blue nevus. Which of the following additional findings is most likely associated with this patient’s condition?
explanation: This patient has Carney complex, which is characterized by periorificial lentigines, epithelioid blue nevi, and cutaneous and cardiac myxomas. Endocrine abnormalities are also common, particularly Cushing disease due to primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease.

question: The causative agent of Roseola is:
explanation: Roseola is caused by Human Herpesvirus 6, a double stranded DNA virus.

question: Multiple cylindromas are associated with:
explanation: The Brooke-Spigler syndrome (BRSS) is defined by the presence of multiple trichoepitheliomas, cylindromas and spiradenomas. Patients with BRSS may rarely develop extracutaneous tumors in the parotid or minor salivary glands. It is caused by mutatinos within CYLD, a tumor suppressor gene encoding an enzyme that interacts with multiple substrates of NF-kappa B.

question: A 1-year-old child comes to the office with concerns from the pediatrician for a genetic syndrome. The patient has a history of epilepsy, subependymal nodules, and cardiac rhabdomyomas. You examine the child’s skin for any cutaneous stigmata of the disorder you suspect. Which of the following cutaneous manifestations occurs the earliest in this genetic syndrome?
explanation: Hypomelanotic macules. The child most likely has tuberous sclerosis. The first cutaneous lesions are typically the white patches that are oval and shaped like an “ash leaf.” These congenital white, leaf-shaped macules, also called hypomelanotic macules, are found in 85% of patients with tuberous sclerosis and range in number from 1 to 100, although 3 lesions greater than 5 mm must be present to satisfy the criteria. Occasional patients may not develop the macules until 6–8 years of age.

question: A 3-year-old male presents with yellow, pruritic crusted papules on his scalp. On physical examination, a bilateral petechial rash overlies the axillary region. X-ray of the skull reveals lytic lesions. He has recently started complaining about excessive thirst, and his mother has noticed an increase in his urinary frequency. Histopathology reveals mononuclear cells with reniform nuclei and pale cytoplasm in the dermis with an edematous background, and eosinophils. Cells staining positively for CD1a and S100. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: This patient has Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) given the rash in a seborrheic distribution, petechiae, and Langerhans cells seen on histology with positive CD1a and S100 staining with eosinophils. Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a common complication if the malignancy affects the skull, with children presenting with polyuria and excessive thirst. A urine osmolality test can help diagnose DI. Other complications of LCH include alveolar bone loss and pulmonary disease.

question: A 6 month-old presents with the follwing lesions around the mouth and groin. Several bullae are also present on the fingers and toes. Which of the following laboratory values is likely to be abnormal?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is acrodermatitis enteropathica. Alkaline phosphatase is a zinc dependant enzyme that is decreased in response to low serum zinc levels.

question: A 2 day-old full term neonate develops blotchy erythematous macules with small central pustules over the upper trunk and extremities. A gram stain reveals predominantly eosinophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a very common eruption in healthy newborns. A gram stain reveals sterile pustules containing eosinophils.

question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the dermatologist with multiple seborrheic crusted papules on the frontal scalp and anterior arms with surrounding petechiae. A biopsy reveals a dense deposition of CD207-positive cells with eosinophils. Further evaluation with an x-ray reveals osteolytic bone lesions of the skull. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation: This is a patient with Hand-Schuller-Christian disease. This disease presents like Letterer-Siwe with seborrheic papules; however, it notably has diabetes insipidus with osteolytic bone lesions, which often require treatment with vasopressin.

question: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents with the shown lesion. He has a

choices.A: history of seizures and developmental delay. Which of the following evaluations is most
choices.B: appropriate to identify associated conditions in this disease?
choices.E: Vascular imaging ? Liver ultrasound ? Thyroid scintigraphy scan

explanation: In patients with nevus sebaceous where it is believed to be related to a syndrome, such as Schimmelpenning syndrome, additional evaluation may be necessary. This can include studies around the brain or skull in particular. Given the patient’s other neurologic symptoms, evaluation of possible skull defects should be essential, thus skeletal radiography is the next appropriate step for this patient.

question: A 75-year-old man presents with the following lesion on the right anterior neck. He states it has been present since birth or early infancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is a example of a verruous somewhat linear plaque present since birth or early infancy, which is most consistent with an epidermal nevus.

question: You are called to the NICU to evaluate this lesion, what is the next best step?
explanation: This kodachrome shows a child with an accessory tragus. These typically occur on the preauricular cheek but can also occur on the lateral cheeks and neck. They can be associated with branchial arch syndromes (Goldenhar, oculo-auriculo-vertebral). They can be associated with hearing or genitourinary defects and therefore acoustic testing should be pursued.

question: A 3-year-old girl presents with linear areas of atrophy following the lines of Blaschko on the trunk and extremities. She also has red papillomatous growths on the lips and perianal region, as well as soft nodular outpouchings on the abdomen. Similar skin findings are present in her mother. What was the most likely inheritance pattern for this patient’s condition?
explanation: This patient has focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome), caused by mutations in the PORCN gene on the X chromosome. In familial cases, the condition most commonly follows an X-linked dominant inheritance pattern. It is usually lethal in males, so most affected individuals are heterozygous females.

question: A full-term newborn presents at 2 weeks of age with firm, erythematous to violaceous subcutaneous nodules on the back and upper arms. A punch biopsy reveals lobular panniculitis with histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells, necrosis, and needle-shaped clefts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Obtain serum calcium level and monitor periodically
choices.D: Reassure parents and discharge with no follow-up

correct_text: Obtain serum calcium level and monitor periodically
explanation: This patient likely has subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn (SCFN), which can lead to delayed-onset hypercalcemia. Monitoring serum calcium is essential for early detection and management.

question: A newborn patient presents with linear hypopigmentation along Blaschko’s lines on the left maxillary face and left trunk. A diagnosis of Hypomelanosis of Ito is suspected. What is the next appropriate step in management?

choices.A: Reassurance that this is a benign lesion
choices.C: Punch biopsy of the hypopigmented region

explanation: Up to 30% of patients with Hypomelanosis of Ito may have CNS, ocular or MSK findings. An ophthalmology exam would be appropriate.

question: What syndrome can accessory tragi be associated with?
explanation: Accessory tragus is the most common congenital defect of the external ear and linked to maldevelopment of the first branchial arch. It can be associated with several syndromes including Goldenhar syndrome, in which epibulbar dermoid and vertebral defects are also common. An accessory tragus usually it appears as a small skin-colored tag or nodule arising near the tragus; it is composed of normal epidermis with dermal adipose tissue, pilosebaceous units, eccrine glands, elastic fibers, and cartilage.

question: A child presents with high fever, strawberry tongue, lymphadenopathy, and a polymorphous exanthem. Approximately how many of these patients will have coronary artery aneurysms if left untreated?
explanation: This child has Kawasaki's disease, or mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. Other features include conjunctival injection and extremity erythema and edema. Twenty-five percent of untreated patients go on to develop coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment is with IVIG and aspirin.

question: A 4-week-old female presents to the pediatric emergency department with a rapidly expanding, vascular-appearing growth on the left shoulder. Laboratory studies reveal severe thrombocytopenia and an elevated D-dimer. Which of the following skin conditions is most likely implicated in this patient’s presentation?
explanation: A rapidly expanding vascular lesion in an infant accompanied by severe thrombocytopenia and elevated D-dimer is most consistent with Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, a consumptive coagulopathy that occurs in association with kaposiform hemangioendothelioma or, less commonly, tufted angioma.

question: A patient has soft, compressible, painful blue tumors that are seen in the trunk and arms. A mutation in the TIE2 gene is identified in the patient. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has all the clinical signs of blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome (due to TIE2 mutation). These patients can also have melena that occurs with gastrointestinal hemangioma rupture. Other involvement of the condition may be in the lung, eye, and CNS.

question: What type of virus can present with the typical clinical presentation of “slapped cheeks” followed by a lacy eruption on extremities?
explanation: The erythematous eruption on the cheeks precedes the generalized lacy rash of erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease). The causative agent is parvovirus B19, a single stranded DNA virus.

question: What is the function of the gene which is defective in ataxia-telangiectasia?

choices.B: Cross-linking of structural proteins in the protein and lipid envelope of the upper
choices.E: Pathway of cholesterol biosynthesis ? Tumor supressor protein

explanation: The defective gene is ataxia-telangiectasia (Louis-Bar syndrome) is the ATM gene, which is responsible for DNA repair, especially after ionizing radiation. Ataxia telangiectasia (A-T) is an autosomal recessive disorder primarily characterized by cerebellar degeneration, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, cancer susceptibility and radiation sensitivity.

question: A patient undergoes duplex ultrasound of the left leg which demonstrates fast-flow arteriovenous shunts. They have a history of heart failure that has worsened since puberty and a number of capillary and lymphatic malformations. Which gene is implicated in this condition?
explanation: Parkes-Weber is a capillary malformation-arteriovneous malformation syndrome secondary to a somatic mutation in the RASA1 gene. It typically presents with capillary malformations, venous malformations, lymphatic malformations, and multiple fast-flow arteriovenous malformations/ shunts. There is often a poor prognosis after puberty.

question: A newborn infant presents with ring of long, dark, coarse hair surrounding a midline scalp patch of alopecia. What is associated with this finding?
explanation: The "hair collar sign" is associated with ectopic brain tissue and is thought to arise from a congenital herniation through the skull. Caution must be used in evaluation as biopsy or needle aspiration may lead to retrograde infection.

question: What disorder is associated with a defect in LMX1B?
explanation: Nail–patella syndrome is an autosomal dominantly inherited condition due to mutations in LMX1B, which encodes a transcription factor that regulates collagen synthesis. The condition most frequently involves the thumb and may also involve the other fingers but to a lesser extent. The nails are absent or hypoplastic, and the dystrophy is usually more marked on the radial side of the digit. A triangle-shaped lunula is commonly observed. The nail changes are typically associated with bony abnormalities, including absent or hypoplastic patellae, radial head dysplasia, and iliac crest exostoses (“horns”). In children, the diagnosis is best confirmed by the presence of iliac horns on pelvic X-ray.

question: A premature infant who is being weaned off breast milk develops vesicobullous and eczematous skin lesions and diarrhea. Which of the following is NOT another classic precipitant for this condition?
explanation: Zinc deficiency can be seen in premature or term infants being weaned off breast milk, which is usually high in zinc content, as well as in parenteral nutrition use, alcoholism because of poor nutritional intake, malabsorption, IBD, diets high in grains containing phytate which binds zinc, and metabolic stress.

question: In patients with diffuse congenital hemangiomatosis, the most common site for extracutaneous involvement is the:
explanation: Diffuse congenital hemangiomatosis is characterized by multiple hemangiomas with the liver being the most common extracutaneous site, followed by the lungs. Liver hemangioma may be complicated by hepatomegaly, obstructive jaundice, and portal hypertension.

question: A 4-hour-old newborn is being evaluated for swelling on the scalp. The newborn was born via a prolonged spontaneous vaginal delivery to a G1P1 28-year-old woman with no significant medical history. The newborn’s vitals are within normal limits. On physical exam, the newborn is crying appropriately and has a firm, nonpitting swelling over the right and left posterior scalp with surrounding ecchymoses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: A firm, nonpitting swelling on the head in a newborn after a prolonged delivery is most consistent with caput succedaneum, a self-resolving condition that is the result of fluid accumulation above the periosteum that crosses suture lines. Thus, reassurance and observation is most appropriate.

question: A 5-year-old girl presents to the pediatric dermatologist with her parents for evaluation of this lesion in her scalp. The lesion was present at birth, but it is becoming more noticeable as she gets older. The parents are concerned about the prognosis of this lesion. What is the most common malignant neoplasm associated with the lesion depicted in the image?
explanation: The image, along with the vignette, describes a Nevus Sebaceus. These are described as waxy plaques with an orange hue on the head/neck which are usually present from birth. There are several neoplasms associated with this lesion including trichoblastoma, SCP, and BCC. Although BCC is seen in <1% of cases, it is the most common malignant neoplasm observed in this lesion.

question: Which of the following types of pityriasis rubra pilaris is the most common in children?
explanation: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is classically categorized into 5 types (although it should be noted that a sixth type is increasingly-recognized). Type IV (circumscribed juvenile form) is the most common type to occur in children.

question: The Carney complex is associated with a defect in:
explanation: A PRKAR1A gene defect is associated with the Carney complex.

question: The infant shown in this image is at risk for which of the following complications?
explanation: This patient has a segmental infantile hemangioma on the face and should be evaluated for PHACES syndrome: posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects and coarctation of the aorta (Choice 5), eye anomalies, sternal defects and supraumbilical raphe. Work-up includes MRI/MRA of the head and neck, referral to a cardiologist, and referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist.

question: How are these lesions typically distributed?

choices.B: On the palmar surface of the hand

explanation: This is an epidermal nevus. Epidermal nevi are a heterogenous group of mosaic lesions that are typically distributed along the lines of blaschko and can be located anywhere on the body (trunk, extremities, face and scalp). Clinically they can appear smooth, warty or barely palpable. Even the color of epidermal nevi can vary from being flesh colored to tan, brown or pink.

question: Which presentation of psoriasis is more common in children:
explanation: The majority of cases of guttate psoriasis occur in persons under the age of 30.

question: A 2-year-old child comes to your office for resistant eczema. On examination, you note circinate scaling erythematous plaques bordered by a double-edged scale. Light microscopic examination of clipped hair from the eyebrows reveals hair shaft abnormalities. You suspect a genetic syndrome. Which medication has been described in patients with this genetic syndrome as having dramatically increased percutaneous absorption?
explanation: Topical calcineurin inhibitors. The child in the vignette has Netherton syndrome (NTS). The hair abnormality seen in Netherton syndrome is trichorrhexis invaginata. The characteristic lesions present on exam are known as ichthyosis linearis circumflexa. Although the skin lesions of NTS may respond to topical tacrolimus, dramatically increased percutaneous absorption of this medication has been described in NTS patients, due to their severe skin barrier dysfunction. Use of topical tacrolimus therefore requires monitoring of plasma drug levels. Topical pimecrolimus has also been successfully used, with considerably less systemic absorption.

question: A 10-year-old girl presents with multiple ill-defined hypo pigmented macules and patches, ranging from 0.5 to 2 cm in diameter with fine scaling. Her lesions are located on both cheeks. Which of the following conditions describes this clinical picture, which is thought to result from a low-grade eczematous dermatitis that disrupts the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes?
explanation: Pityriasis alba frequently affects children and adolescents with AD. It is characterized by multiple ill-defined hypopigmented macules and patches, usually 0.5 to 2 cm in diameter, with fine scaling; the lesions are typically located on the face, especially the cheeks, but occasionally appear on the shoulders and arms. Pityriasis alba is most obvious in individuals with darkly pigmented skin and/ or following sun exposure. It is thought to result from a low-grade eczematous dermatitis that disrupts the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes.

question: A 4-year-old patient presents with the pictured findings here that arose after playing outside. What antihistamine would be the most appropriate to help reduce symptoms while also being the least sedating?
explanation: Fexofenadine is widely regarded as the least sedating of the second-generation antihistamines. These oral agents are available over the counter and are FDA- approved for use in patients as young as 6 months for urticaria, making them a useful option to help reduce itching and localized skin reactions from hives or insect bites.

question: A 2-year-old male with recurrent flares of the pictured findings developed non-tender nodules on his bilateral thighs. What would likely establish the diagnosis?

choices.C: Flow cytometry to evaluate CD18 expression
choices.D: Genetic testing for STAT3 and DOCK8 mutations

correct_text: Genetic testing for STAT3 and DOCK8 mutations
explanation: This presentation is most consistent with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), which is characterized by severe eczema, recurrent staphylococcal and viral skin infections, and the development of “cold” (non-tender) abscesses and subcutaneous nodules due to impaired inflammation. Facial eczema with crusted papulopustules in early childhood plus deep, painless thigh nodules strongly raises suspicion for HIES. Genetic testing for STAT3 and DOCK8 mutations would establish the diagnosis, as STAT3 deficiency (autosomal dominant) and DOCK8 deficiency (autosomal recessive) account for most cases. STAT3-HIES is more commonly associated with skeletal abnormalities and “cold abscesses,” while DOCK8-HIES more prominently features recurrent viral infections, food allergies, and higher malignancy risk.

question: A 3 year old patient presents to your clinic with the following lesion. Mom notes that the child is unbothered by this, is otherwise healthy and has been meeting appropriate developmental milestones. Which of the following is the next best step?
explanation: Lymphangioma circumscriptum (LC) is a benign lymphatic malformation that often presents as clusters of hemorrhagic or translucent vesicles on the skin (also referred to as having a frogspawn appearance). Reassurance is the most appropriate next step; the child is asymptomatic, otherwise healthy, and meeting developmental milestones.

question: A patient presents with multiple juvenile xanthogranulomas, axillary freckling, multiple café-au-lait macules, three neurofibromas and a family history of NF-1. Historically, what other condition has been associated with this presentation?
explanation: The association of NF-1, juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG), and juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia has been described in the literature. However, a recent study concluded that juvenile xanthogranulomas do not appear to confer an increased risk for malignancy in children with NF-1, although this study had several limitations: retrospective design, small number of cases, and inconsistent documentation of clinical findings, including age at disappearance of JXG.

question: A 3 month-old girl with multiple hemangiomas along her right jaw is most at increased risk for:
explanation: Hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors which have proliferating phase and then a spontaneous involution phase. Depending upon the location, some hemangiomas may have more long term sequelae such as scarring or structural malformation, and rarely, consumptive coagulopathy. Infants with hemangiomas of the beard distribution should be evaluated for subglottic hemangiomas which may lead to airway obstruction.

question: GLUT-1 stains placental tissue. What other tissue shows positive GLUT-1 staining?
explanation: The correct answer is infantile hemangioma, which reliably displays GLUT-1 positivity. GLUT-1 stains infantile hemangioma with high sensitivity and specificity. Glomus tumor, capillary vascular malformation (also called port-wine stain), salmon patch, and angel's kiss are other vascular lesions that do not stain with GLUT-1.

question: What is the most common tumor associated with this condition?
explanation: Recent reviews have identified trichoblastoma as the most common tumor arising within nevus sebaceous, even more frequent than syringocystadenoma papilliferum.

question: A 15 year old boy is brought to the office for hair loss. As an infant he was especially sensitive to the sun and frequently developed erythema, edema, and blisters on his cheeks. He is short for his age with diffuse telangiectasias and hyperpigmentation on his face. You notice that his thumbs are short and he is missing eyebrows and eyelashes. Genetic testing highlights a mutation in RECQL4.

choices.A: In addition to counseling the family on the development of non-melanoma skin cancers,
choices.B: which non-dermatologic condition most commonly associated with this disorder should

explanation: Sarcomas, specifically osteosarcoma and fibrosarcoma are pathopnemonic for Rothmund- Thompson, also called poikiloderma congenita, which has a genetic mutation in RECQL4. 30% of patients with Rothmund-Thompson will develop osteosarcomas, making this highly important to counsel patients and parents on. Later in life, these patients may also develop a number of verrucous keratoses on their palms and non-melanoma skin cancers.

question: Rapp-Hodgkin is caused by a defect in the following gene:
explanation: Rapp-Hodgkin, along with the other ectodermal dysplasia-clefting syndromes, is reportedly caused by a defect in the p63 gene.

question: Of the Waardenburg syndrome types, which of the following is a unique feature of Shah- Waardenburg syndrome (WS4)?
explanation: Hirschsprung disease. In WS4, the characteristic findings of WS occur in association with Hirschsprung disease. In many patients, a white forelock, amelanotic macules, and heterochromia irides are present. Deafness is fairly common, but dystopia canthorum and a broad nasal root are uncommon. Additional rare manifestations (associated with SOX10 mutations) include central nervous system dysfunction, neonatal hypotonia, and arthrogryposis.

question: Which finding is associated with Pachydermoperiostosis:
explanation: The scalp change seen in pachydermoperiostosis is cutis verticis gyrata.

question: A 4-year-old girl presents with a fever that lasted about 5 days. Afterward, she developed the skin findings pictures along with injection of the conjunctiva, strawberry tongue, and a widespread morbilliform eruption of erythematous macules and papules. Mom reports swelling of the hands and feet that has improved, with desquamation present now. On physical exam you note an enlarged cervical lymph node. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation: The case describes the classic findings in Kawasaki disease. Treatment of choice is IVIG plus high-dose aspirin. IVIG should be administered as soon as possible, a single dose of 2 g/kg over 8-12 hours is superior to multiple daily doses in preventing coronary artery aneurysms. IVIG decreased the mortality from 2% to 0.3% and the incidence of aneurysm from 25% to 5-10%. Aspirin is recommended at 30-100 mg/kg/day for 14 days or until afebrile for 48-72 hours, then continued at 3-5 mg/kg daily for 6-8 weeks.

question: A 2 week old infant presents with greasy yellow scale on the scalp and erythematous patches on the face and diaper area. The infant is otherwise well and not pruritic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Seborrheic dermatitis in infants typically presents in the first weeks of life. Clinical findings can be consistent with adult seborrheic dermatitis-greasy scale, erythema. However, distribution can involve the scalp, face, as well as the intertriginous areas (diaper area).

question: A 2-day-old infant is being seen in the hospital for the following rash. Which of the following is not true about the infant’s disease?

choices.A: Lesions have a predilection for the face
choices.B: Skin lesions typically resolve without scarring
choices.C: Heart block often develops after birth
choices.D: There is a strong association with anti-SSA/Ro antibodies
choices.E: There are also reports of the presence of U1RNP antibodies

correct_text: Heart block often develops after birth
explanation: Heart block often develops after birth. This baby has neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE). Heart block is almost always present by birth, but on rare occasions has developed after birth.1

question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Aplasia cutis congenita is characterized by the absence of a portion of skin, most commonly presenting as a solitary defect on the scalp, but sometimes it may occur as multiple lesions. The lesions are non-inflammatory, well-demarcated ones that appear as an atrophic, membranous, ulcerated area with alopecia. The condition may be associated with other physical anomalies.

question: A 6-year-old girl is taken to the emergency department by her parents for a fever, which the patient has had for a 5 day duration. She has bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, edema of the feet, and no lymphadenopathy. Her skin exam reveals scattered, dusky erythematous macules and patches, many of which were targetoid, on the torso and extremities. She also has the pictured oral finding. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The pictured oral finding is that of "strawberry" tongue. This patient fulfills the clinical criteria for Kawasaki disease with fever for 5 days, bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, strawberry tongue, edema of feet, and polymorphous exanthem.

question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The well-defined erythematous plaque is an example of psorisis in the diaper area. The moist nature of the diaper environment results in a loss of the classic silvery scale.

question: In a child with zinc deficiency, yet normal or near normal zinc levels, which test could be a valuable adjunctive test?
explanation: The diagnosis of zinc deficiency should be consideredi in at-risk individuals with acral or periorificial dermatitis. Chronic diaper dermatitis in an infant should lead to the evaluation for zinc deficiency. A low serum zinc level can usually confirm the diagnosis. If normal or near normal a low serum alkaline phosphatase, a zinc-dependent enzyme, may be a valuable adjunctive test.

question: An infant presents with red-purple, granulomatous nodules occurring in the diaper area. The etiology is secondary to local irritation, maceration, and Candida albicans. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The etiology of granuloma gluteale infantum is multifactorial, resulting from the unique environment of the diaper area. It presents as red-purple, granulomatous nodules occurring in the diaper area. Treatment consists of topical antifungal agents, barrier creams, and anti-inflammatory agents as needed.

question: What is the first-line treatment for the condition pictured?
explanation: The condition shown is erythrokeratodermia variabilis (EKV), a genetic skin disorder characterized by the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern of mutations in GJB3, GJB4, and GJA1 genes, which encode connexins, the component parts of gap junctions. Patients present with stable hyperkeratosis and transient patches of erythema. Goals of treatment are to attenuate hyperkeratosis and minimize discomfort. First-line treatment involves emollients, keratolytics such as urea and salicyclic acid, and topical retinoids such as tretinoin or tazarotene. Systemic retinoids may be used for more severe or generalized disease.

question: The most common age group for papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome is:
explanation: This unique presentation of parvovirus B19 infection typically occurs in adolescents and young adults. It usually occurs in the spring and summer.

question: What is this often misdiagnosed as?
explanation: This is lichen sclerosus et atrophicus in a child. Onset of LS&A occurs in childhood in about 10% of the cases. Girls outnumber boys 10:1. It is frequently misdiagnosed as child abuse as there can be hemorrhagic bullae as part of the disease. The porcelain white and hemorrhagic bullae are clues to think of LS and A. There is an increased risk of genital SCC in both men and women.

question: Which of the following forms of epidermolysis bullosa is autosomal recessive?
explanation: The forms of junctional epidermolysis bullosa are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. These include Herlitz, non-Herlitz, JEB with pyloric atresia, JEB inversa, and GABEB.

question: What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Lichen striatus is a benign and self limited inflammatory condition, most commonly affecting pediatric patients. The flat topped papules form Blashko's lines. The dermatitis is usually asymptomatic and treatment is not necessary. When an extremity is involved, there may be associated nail dystrophy.

question: Psammomatous melanotic schwannomas are associated with:
explanation: Psammomatous melanotic schwannomas have been described in the Carney complex, a defect in the tumor suppressor gene, PRKAR1A.

question: A 10-year-old boy presents with severe, painful photosensitivity and a history of non- blistering phototoxic reactions after minimal sun exposure. Laboratory tests reveal elevated levels of protoporphyrin IX in red blood cells. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
explanation: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is caused by partial ferrochelatase deficiency, leading to accumulation of protoporphyrin IX and non-blistering, painful photosensitivity.

question: What is the most likely condition associated with this lesion?

choices.A: This lesion is not associated with any of the above listed conditions

correct_text: This lesion is not associated with any of the above listed conditions
explanation: The image is that of a Becker's nevus, which is an acquired unilateral hamartomatous lesion found in adolescent males typically on the shoulder, upper chest, or back. It can be distinguished from a cafe-au-lait macule (particularly the "Coast of Maine" cafe-au-lait macule seen in McCune-Albright syndrome) by the hypertrichosis that is not present in a cafe-au-lait. It is not associated with the listed conditions.

question: A 7-year-old male patient comes into the office for "resistant eczema" his whole life, as pictured below. His mother also states that she was in labor for a very long time and had to have a cesarean section. You suspect a genetic syndrome. Which doctor should you refer this patient to who may be able to help decrease morbidity in this patient and the referral can most likely result in an actionable finding?
explanation: Urology. The patient has X-linked ichthyosis. This condition results from a deficiency of steroid sulfatase (arylsulfatase C) and occurs in 1 : 2000 to 1 : 5000 male births. Onset is usually before age 3 months. Cesarean birth is typical, with failure in progression of labor because of a placental sulfatase deficiency. There is a 12%-15% incidence of cryptorchidism (undescended testicle) and an independently increased risk of testicular cancer. If cryptorchidism is present, an orchiopexy may be performed and monitoring for testicular cancer can be performed throughout the patient's life. 1

question: The most common enzyme abnormality in congenital adrenal hyperplasia is:
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is present in 95% of cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. This defect in adrenal steroidogenesis can occur at any point in life, but affected girls will generally present around puberty with hirsutism and mentsrual irregularity/primary amenorrhea. The key feature is excess androgen production. The other listed enzymes are not the most common mutations in congenital adrenal hyperplasia

question: This 8-year-old patient is brought in by his father for the lesions pictured on the lips. The father tells you that the patient is healthy aside from an episode of intestinal intussuusception several months ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome results from an autosomal-dominant mutation in the STK11 gene (serine threonine kinase). Clinical manifestations may include: mucocutaneous (oral/acral) lentigines, intestinal polyposis +/- intussusception, and various malignancies. The remaining answer choices may produce multiple lentigines, but are not typically associated with intussusception.

question: Which of the following conditions is NOT found in Von-Hippel Lindau syndrome?
explanation: Connective tissue nevi are not a feature of Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is characterized by all the options listed except connective tissue nevi. Other findings include pancreatic cysts/carcinoma and cutaneous capillary malformations of the head and neck and polycythemia.

question: Patients with Cornelia de Lange syndrome have a low set hair line, trichomegaly, hirsutism, and synophrys. The skin finding is:
explanation: Patients with Cornelia de Lange syndrome have cutis marmorata with low set hair line, trichomegaly, synophrys, hirsutism, and heart defects. The associated gene is NIPBL and SMC1L1.Poikiloderma occurs in Rothmund-Thomson and Werner syndrome. Scleroderma occurs in Werner syndrome.

question: Retention of primary teeth is a prominent dental finding of which of the following conditions?
explanation: Hyper-Immunoglobulin E syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition with impaired regulation of IgE function and deficient neutrophil chemotaxis. There is increased susceptibilty to infections and increased IgE serum levels. Retained primary teeth and lack of development of secondary teeth are characteristic findings.

question: Mutations in c-kit are associated with which of the following conditions?
explanation: Piebaldism is caused by mutations in c-kit. Waardenburg syndrome mutations include PAX3, MITF, EDNRB. Tuberous sclerosis mutations are in TSC1 (which encodes hamartin) and TSC2 (which encodes tuberin). Vogt-koyanagi-harada is an autoimmune condition. Cornelia de Lange Syndrome mutation is NIPBL.

question: Underlying defect for the disease shown in picture is
explanation: The disease shown in image is Hailey-Hailey disease (Familial Benign Pemphigus) which is an autosomal dominant genodermatosis, caused by mutation in ATP2C1, encoding a calcium pump protein related to SERCA2. It is characterized by recurrent vesicles and erosions, which most commonly appear on the sides and back of the neck, in the axillae, in the groin, and in the perianal regions. The disorder is not seen before puberty and usually has its onset in the late teens or early 20s. In the intertriginous area lesions tend to form erythematous plaques with dry crusting and soft, flat, and moist granular vegetations. Burning or pruritus is common, and, particularly in the intertriginous areas, lesions tend to become irritating, painful, and exceedingly uncomfortable. ATP2A2 is underlying defect in Darier's disease, other choices are defects seen in pemphigoid and epidermolysis bullosa.

question: A 16 year-old girl presents with a family history of Gardner syndrome. Her mother is very concerned that her daughter may have the syndrome as it runs in her family and she has many skin complaints. Gardner syndrome has been linked to defects in beta-catenin mediated transcription. Which of the following ocular finding is diagnostic for Gardner syndrome?

choices.C: Congenital Hypertrophy of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium

correct_text: Congenital Hypertrophy of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium
explanation: CHRPE (Congenital Hypertrophy of the Retinal Pigment Epithelium) is the characteristic eye finding for Gardner syndrome. Lisch nodules are seen in Neurofibromatosis I, Lester iris in Nail- Patella syndrome and angioid streaks are present in Pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Retinal detachment is not part of Gardner syndrome. 🔆 Clinical features of Gardner syndrome can be divided into two types, cutaneous and noncutaneous. The most noticeable cutaneous feature of Gardner syndrome is the appearance of epidermoid cysts. These cysts can be differentiated from ordinary epidermoid cysts by the following factors: • Epidermoid inclusion cysts of Gardner syndrome (50–65%) occur at an earlier age (around puberty) than ordinary cysts • Epidermoid cysts occur in less common locations such as the face, scalp and extremities compared to ordinary cysts • Cysts tend to be multiple in over half of the patients with Gardner syndrome • As with ordinary epidermoid cysts, cysts in Gardner syndrome are usually asymptomatic (without symptoms), however in some cases they may be pruritic (itchy) and/or inflamed, and they may rupture. • Sometimes the cysts have hybrid features with pilomatricoma-like histopathology Other cutaneous features include desmoid cysts, fibromas, lipomas, leiomyomas, neurofibromas and pigmented skin lesions. Non-cutaneous features include: • Gastrointestinal polyps that nearly always transform into colonic adenocarcinomas (colon cancer). • Osteomas – these benign bone tumours are essential in making the diagnosis of Gardner syndrome. They occur most commonly in the mandible (jawbone) but may also grow in the skull and long bones. • Dental abnormalities – as well as osteomas in the jaw there may be other dental abnormalities such as unerupted extra teeth and caries • Multifocal pigmented lesions of the fundus in the eye – seen in 80% of patients. These lesions may be present shortly after birth and can be the first marker of the disease.

question: An infant presents with poikiloderma on his face, buttocks, arms and legs. He is also noted to have a hypoplastic thumb and no radius. Yearly ophthalmologic examination is indicated because of the infant is at risk for developing:
explanation: The patient described has Rothmund-Thomson syndrome (or poikiloderma congentiale), an autosomal recessive disease localized to chromosome 8 and believed to be due to a DNA helicase mutation (RECQL4). 40-50% of patients will develop juvenile cataracts before puberty. Other clinical features include alopecia, dystrophic nails, short stature, hypogonadism and dental dysplasia. 🔆 Affected children may be identified early in life by their small size, their tendency to sunburn easily, and from the appearance of their skin, teeth and bones. Rothmund–Thomson syndrome is slightly more common in females than males. Skin Photosensitivity: sunburn-like redness, swelling and blisters on cheeks and face; may extend • to involve buttocks and extremities.
